docs.title: Ubunye Engine
docs.text:
Ubunye runs your data and ML jobs from a small folder of YAML and Python, the same way on a laptop, a cloud or Databricks.

  • Write it once. A task is one folder: a config.yaml and a transformations.py.
  • Run it anywhere. pandas with no Java, or Spark on your laptop, a cluster, AWS, GCP, Azure or Databricks.
  • Prove it's the same. Every run can leave a run record with a hash of every row, so two runs can be compared exactly.

Get started GitHub

docs.title: Try it in 60 seconds
docs.text:
On pandas, so all you need is Python (which version): no Java, no cloud account.

pip install "ubunye-engine[pandas]"
ubunye init -d pipelines -u demo -p starter -t filter_adults
ubunye run -d pipelines -u demo -p starter -t filter_adults --backend pandas --lineage
ubunye lineage list -d pipelines -u demo -p starter -t filter_adults

init makes a task folder with eight sample people in a CSV. run keeps the adults and writes them as Parquet. lineage list shows the run record the run left:

RUN_ID     STARTED              STATUS        DUR  ROWS
------------------------------------------------------------
a2da9fbd  2026-11-10T10:34:34  success      0.3s  in:8  out:5

Next: the Quickstart explains each step, then runs the same folder on Spark.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
The same task, unchanged, has given the same rows on pandas, local Spark, Kubernetes, AWS Glue, GCP Dataproc, Azure Container Apps and Databricks, checked from the run records by the proving ground (latest results).

New to the words below? Concepts explains use case, pipeline, task, profile, write mode, run record and backend in plain words.

  • Config first. Inputs, outputs and Spark settings live in YAML, so no credentials or paths are hard coded. Config overview
  • One config for every environment. A profile (DEV, PROD) changes the Spark settings per environment, chosen with -m. Values can be filled in with Jinja2, a small template language: {{ dt }} becomes the run date. Profiles, Jinja
  • Connectors you declare, not code. Hive, JDBC, files on S3 or local disk, Delta, REST APIs, binary files and Unity Catalog (Databricks' catalog of tables). Connectors
  • Backends. Run on Spark, Databricks, or pandas with no Java (--backend). ubunye backends lists what each can do. Execution backends
  • Checks before a run. ubunye validate (the config), ubunye plan (a dry run: what it will read and write) and ubunye doctor (this machine). Which command catches what
  • Bad data stopped early. Expectations check inputs, put bad rows aside (quarantine) and reconcile input with output. Expectations
  • Run records. --lineage writes one run record per run to .ubunye/lineage/: what ran, on what data, with a hash of every row. ubunye gate and ubunye prove compare them. Run records
  • Safe reruns. A batch that was already appended is refused unless you pass --rerun; --resume finishes a pipeline that stopped half way. Safe reruns
  • Models. A library-independent UbunyeModel contract and a built-in registry to version, promote, roll back and gate models. Model contract, Registry
  • Observability. Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, MLflow and JSON event logs through hooks (ubunye.hooks), and export of run records to OpenLineage (an open standard for sharing what a job read and wrote). Hooks, OpenLineage
  • Orchestration export. One command writes an Airflow DAG, a Databricks job or a Spark Declarative Pipeline from the same config. Orchestration
  • Deployment. ubunye deploy to Databricks, AWS Glue, GCP Dataproc, EMR Serverless, Kubernetes and Azure Container Apps. Deployment
  • Plugins. Add your own readers, writers, transforms and backends through entry points (a standard Python way for an installed package to announce plugins): ubunye.readers, ubunye.writers, ubunye.transforms, ubunye.backends and more. ubunye plugins lists what is installed. Writing your own
  • Agents. ubunye mcp serves the engine over MCP (Model Context Protocol, the way AI agents call tools). It only reads unless you pass --allow-run. Agents over MCP
  • Tested three ways. A unit tier with no Java, a Spark tier, and a parity tier that checks Spark and pandas agree. Contributing

docs.title: What Ubunye is not
docs.text:
• Not an agent framework. Use LangChain or CrewAI for that.
  • Not an orchestrator. Use Airflow, Prefect or Dagster. (ubunye export writes an Airflow DAG or a Databricks job for you.)
  • Not a compute engine. It runs on Spark, or on pandas for laptop-sized data.

Ubunye is the layer between your data sources and your applications that makes the plumbing the same everywhere, so you can focus on the logic.

docs.title: Two ways to run a task
docs.text:
CLIPython API (Databricks) 
ubunye run -d pipelines -u fraud -p etl -t claims -m PROD --lineage

import ubunye

outputs = ubunye.run_task(
    task_dir="pipelines/fraud/etl/claims",
    mode="PROD",
    dt="2024-06-01",
)

The Python API finds and reuses an active SparkSession on Databricks. When no session exists, it creates one, the same as the CLI. Pass backend="pandas" to run with no Spark at all.

docs.title: A Spark example with profiles
docs.text:
This task reads a Hive table and writes Delta, so it needs the Spark backend (Spark on your machine, a cluster or Databricks). For a pandas example, see Try it in 60 seconds above.

# pipelines/fraud/etl/claims/config.yaml
MODEL: etl
VERSION: "1.0.0"

ENGINE:
  profiles:
    DEV:
      spark_conf:
        spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: "4"
    PROD:
      spark_conf:
        spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: "200"

CONFIG:
  inputs:
    raw_claims:
      format: hive
      db_name: raw
      tbl_name: claims
  transform: {}
  outputs:
    clean_claims:
      format: delta
      path: s3://data-lake/clean/claims
      mode: overwrite

ubunye plan -d pipelines -u fraud -p etl -t claims -m PROD   # what it will read and write
ubunye run  -d pipelines -u fraud -p etl -t claims -m PROD

-m PROD picks the PROD profile. Leave -m out and run uses DEV. Profile names must match exactly, case included. Profiles

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: Run Ubunye tasks from Python instead of the CLI: in a notebook, a job, or a test. This page lists the public classes and functions, generated from their docstrings.

docs.title: Which API do I use?
docs.text:
You want to Use It returns Run one task, end to end ubunye.run_task(task_dir, ...) {output name: frame}: what the task wrote, as the backend's own frames (a pandas DataFrame on pandas, a Spark DataFrame on Spark) Run several tasks of one pipeline, in order ubunye.run_pipeline(usecase_dir, usecase, pipeline, tasks, ...) {task name: {output name: frame}}, without the tasks resume=True skipped Step through a task in a notebook: read, look, transform, look, write ubunye.notebook(task_dir, ...) A NotebookContext: read() gives {input name: frame}, transform() gives {output name: frame}, write() writes them, run() does all three Drive the engine yourself from a parsed config ubunye.core.runtime.Engine Engine.run(cfg) gives {output name: frame} (None with dry_run=True)

Most people want run_task. All of them take mode (the profile: DEV, PROD, ...; default DEV) and backend ("pandas", "spark", ...). See Execution backends and Profiles.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
The main use: Databricks notebooks and jobs, where a SparkSession already exists and the engine attaches to it.

import ubunye

# Run a single task
outputs = ubunye.run_task(
    task_dir="pipelines/fraud_detection/ingestion/claim_etl",
    mode="PROD",
    dt="202510",
)

# The same task with no Spark and no Java
outputs = ubunye.run_task("pipelines/sales/etl/daily", backend="pandas")

# Run multiple tasks in order
results = ubunye.run_pipeline(
    usecase_dir="pipelines",
    usecase="fraud_detection",
    pipeline="ingestion",
    tasks=["claim_etl", "feature_engineering"],
    mode="PROD",
    dt="202510",
)

docs.title: ubunye.api.run_task
docs.text:
run_task(task_dir, *, mode='DEV', dt=None, dtf=None, spark=None, backend=None, variables=None, lineage=False, lineage_dir='.ubunye/lineage', profile=None, hooks=None, rerun=False, lineage_backend=None)

Run a single Ubunye task and return the outputs map.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: task_dir : str Path to the task directory containing config.yaml and transformations.py. mode : str Run mode, used for Spark profile merging. Default "DEV". dt : str, optional Data timestamp, injected as {{ dt }} in Jinja templates. dtf : str, optional Data timestamp format, injected as {{ dtf }}. spark : SparkSession, optional Explicit SparkSession to reuse. If None, auto-detects an active session (Databricks) or creates a new one. backend : Backend or str, optional The backend to run on: a registered name ("pandas" for a run with no Spark and no Java, "spark", or any installed plugin) or an instance. If None: the spark session if given, else the platform's active session, else a new Spark session. variables : dict, optional Extra template variables for the config ({"region": "gauteng"} makes {{ region }} available), as --var does on the command line. May set dt or dtf; the same name with two values is refused. lineage : bool Record lineage for this run. lineage_dir : str Where lineage records go. For the filesystem store, a directory under the use case directory; for any other store, its location as given (a Delta table name or path). profile : str, optional Config profile for validation (passed to load_config). hooks : iterable of Hook, optional Hooks to add to the engine's own (the ubunye.hooks entry point, CONFIG.monitors and the run record). They never replace them. rerun : bool Replace a batch (same dt and variables) that a finished run already appended. Without it, such a run is refused, since it would append the batch twice. lineage_backend : str, optional The run record store, by name (ADR 011): "filesystem", "delta" or an installed plugin. If None: $UBUNYE_LINEAGE_BACKEND, else "filesystem".

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Dict[str, Any] Mapping of output name → DataFrame.

docs.title: ubunye.api.run_pipeline
docs.text:
run_pipeline(usecase_dir, usecase, pipeline=None, tasks=None, *, mode='DEV', dt=None, dtf=None, spark=None, backend=None, variables=None, lineage=False, lineage_dir='.ubunye/lineage', profile=None, hooks=None, rerun=False, lineage_backend=None, resume=False, package=None)

Run multiple tasks sequentially and return all outputs.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: usecase_dir : str Root directory for use cases (e.g. "./pipelines"). usecase : str Use case name. pipeline : str Pipeline name (the folder between the use case and the tasks). tasks : List[str] Task names to run in order. mode, dt, dtf, spark, backend, variables, lineage, lineage_dir, profile, hooks, rerun, lineage_backend Same as :func:run_task. One backend runs every task. resume : bool Finish a pipeline that stopped half way: a task that already finished this batch is skipped (with a warning, and is not in the result); the rest run. A task that appends knows it finished; one that only overwrites is known to have finished from its run records, so it is skipped only with lineage=True (its latest run of the batch succeeded). Without resume a finished append is refused (:class:~ubunye.core.runs.BatchFinished). package : str, optional Old name of pipeline. Still works, with a DeprecationWarning; removed in 1.0.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Dict[str, Dict[str, Any]] Mapping of task name → outputs map (without tasks skipped by resume).

docs.title: Job health and upstream checks
docs.text: Queries over run records (ADR 013).

docs.title: ubunye.api.job_health
docs.text:
job_health(usecase_dir, *, usecase=None, pipeline=None, tasks=None, max_age=None, stuck_after='6h', lineage_dir='.ubunye/lineage', lineage_backend=None, package=None)

Job health per task, from run records (ADR 013); what ubunye runs health prints.

Name the tasks (tasks=["uc/pipeline/task"]) or a use case (usecase=, with pipeline= to narrow it; package= is its old name, deprecated). Returns one :class:~ubunye.lineage.health.TaskHealth per task; .healthy is False when the task is failing, has a run likely dead (running past stuck_after) or, with max_age, has not succeeded recently enough.

docs.title: ubunye.api.wait_for_upstream
docs.text:
wait_for_upstream(usecase_dir, task, *, dt=None, variables=None, timeout=0, poll=60, lineage_dir='.ubunye/lineage', lineage_backend=None)

The run of task that succeeded for this batch, waiting up to timeout.

The batch is dt and variables; every one must match. Raises :class:~ubunye.lineage.upstream.UpstreamNotReady when there is none in time. What ubunye runs wait-for does; a task can ask the same in its config with CONFIG.requires.

docs.title: Notebook API (Interactive)
docs.text:
Step-by-step execution for prototyping in Databricks notebooks. Environment variables referenced via {{ env.VAR }} in config.yaml are auto-resolved from widgets and secrets, with no manual os.environ setup.

import ubunye

ctx = ubunye.notebook(
    "/Workspace/pipelines/claims/claim_etl",
    mode="PROD",
    dt="2026-01-01",
)

sources = ctx.read()
sources["raw_claims"].display()

outputs = ctx.transform(sources)
outputs["bronze_claims"].show()

ctx.write(outputs)

docs.title: ubunye.notebook.notebook
docs.text:
notebook(task_dir, *, mode='DEV', dt=None, dtf=None, spark=None, backend=None, variables=None, env=None, secrets_scope=None, secrets_map=None, lineage=False, lineage_dir='.ubunye/lineage', profile=None, auto_env=True, hooks=None, lineage_backend=None)

Create an interactive notebook context for step-by-step task execution.

All {{ env.VAR }} references in the task's config.yaml are auto-resolved from Databricks widgets and secrets — no manual os.environ setup needed.

backend picks the engine as in :func:ubunye.run_task: a registered name ("pandas") or an instance; by default the notebook's session. lineage_backend picks the run record store as in :func:ubunye.run_task.

write(outputs=None)

Write outputs to configured sinks, and record the run.

If outputs is None, uses the result of the last :meth:transform call. With lineage=True every write leaves a run record, exactly as ubunye.run_task does (before 0.7.0 a notebook recorded nothing).

close()

docs.title: ubunye.core.runtime.Engine
docs.text:
Executes a task by reading inputs, applying one or more transforms, and writing outputs.

Minimal required config structure

cfg[CONFIG][inputs] : mapping input_name -> reader cfg (must include 'format') cfg[CONFIG][outputs] : mapping output_name -> writer cfg (must include 'format') cfg[CONFIG][transform]: EITHER a single transform dict with 'type', OR a list of transform dicts to form a pipeline.

Observation (logging, metrics, tracing, user monitors) is delegated to :class:ubunye.core.hooks.Hook instances. Pass hooks= to override the default set.

docs.title: backend property writable
docs.text:
backend

The backend running this engine's tasks, resolved on first use.

docs.title: __init__
docs.text: __init__(backend=None, registry=None, context=None, hooks=None, extra_hooks=None, manage_backend=True)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: hooks : iterable of Hook, optional Replace the default hook set entirely. extra_hooks : iterable of Hook, optional Append these hooks to the default set. Ignored when hooks is also given. manage_backend : bool, default True If True (default), the engine calls backend.start() and backend.stop(). Set to False when the caller owns the backend lifecycle (e.g. Python API running multiple tasks on one session).

docs.title: apply_transforms
docs.text:
apply_transforms(sources, cfg)

Apply configured transforms to sources.

Returns a dict mapping output name to the backend's own frame type. Frames that did not come from :meth:read_inputs (a notebook's own sample, say) are checked against the input contracts and counted for a reconcile first, like read ones: a reconcile compares an output with the frames the transform actually got.

docs.title: read_inputs
docs.text:
read_inputs(cfg)

Read all inputs defined in CONFIG.inputs.

Returns a dict mapping input name to the backend's own frame type (a pandas.DataFrame on pandas) — suitable for interactive inspection before calling :meth:apply_transforms. The inputs' expectations (input contracts) are checked here, as in :meth:run, and the inputs a reconcile names are counted; both are kept for a later :meth:write_outputs.

docs.title: run
docs.text:
run(cfg, *, dry_run=False)

Run a task using the provided config mapping.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: cfg : dict Parsed task configuration (already rendered/validated). dry_run : bool, default False If True, validates and returns without executing readers/writers.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] Optionally returns the outputs map (None if dry_run).

docs.title: write_outputs
docs.text:
write_outputs(outputs, cfg, *, as_run=False, inputs=None)

Write outputs to the sinks defined in CONFIG.outputs.

With as_run=True the write is wrapped as a whole task for the hooks, so lineage and monitors record it exactly as they record run(). This is how a notebook that reads, transforms and writes step by step still leaves a run record. A reconcile compares with the inputs counted before the transform (by :meth:read_inputs or :meth:apply_transforms). inputs given here that were not counted then are counted now, after the transform: a transform that changed them in place hides its loss.

docs.title: Interfaces (Protocols)
docs.text: See the full Interfaces page for design principles, discovery, and auto-detection.

docs.title: ubunye.interfaces
docs.text:
Formal interfaces (typing.Protocol) for Ubunye's pluggable seams.

Each protocol defines the structural contract that backends must satisfy. Implementations are discovered at runtime via entry-point groups and auto-detect classmethods.

Cross-boundary dataclasses accompany each protocol so that callers never depend on a concrete backend's internal types.

docs.title: AuthBackend
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Structural interface for authentication backends.

Concrete implementations: TokenAuthBackend (built-in), ServicePrincipalAuthBackend (Phase 2).

docs.title: resolve
docs.text:
resolve(workspace_url, **kwargs)

Resolve credentials for the given workspace.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: workspace_url: The Databricks (or other) workspace host URL. **kwargs: Backend-specific hints (e.g. token_env="MY_TOKEN").

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Credentials Populated credentials ready for client construction.

docs.title: Raises
docs.text: ubunye.core.errors.AuthNotFoundError When credentials cannot be located (missing env var, etc.).

docs.title: validate
docs.text:
validate(credentials)

Validate that credentials are accepted by the workspace.

Returns True on success.

docs.title: Raises
docs.text: ubunye.core.errors.AuthInvalidError When the workspace rejects the credentials.

docs.title: Credentials dataclass
docs.text:
Resolved authentication credentials.

The auth_type field tells callers which fields are populated. metadata carries backend-specific extras (e.g. token expiry, scope, tenant ID) without polluting the core fields.

docs.title: DeployAdapter
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Structural interface for deployment backends.

Each adapter is responsible for:

  1. Validating that the target dict contains the fields it needs.
  2. Preparing artifacts (notebooks, config bundles) for the target.
  3. Uploading artifacts and creating/updating the remote job.
  4. Returning a :class:DeployResult with job metadata.

docs.title: name property
docs.text:
name

Short identifier for this adapter (e.g. "databricks").

docs.title: deploy
docs.text:
deploy(ctx, target, *, dry_run=False)

Deploy a task to the target environment.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: ctx: Task metadata, config dict, and filesystem paths. target: Adapter-specific target configuration (validated by the adapter via :meth:validate_target). dry_run: If True, build and return the job spec without making any remote API calls.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: DeployResult Job metadata including name, id, spec, and workspace path.

docs.title: get_job_url
docs.text:
get_job_url(job_id, target)

Return a browser URL to the deployed job.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: job_id: The job identifier returned by :meth:deploy. target: The same target dict, which typically contains the host URL.

docs.title: validate_target
docs.text:
validate_target(target)

Validate adapter-specific target config.

docs.title: Raises
docs.text: ubunye.core.errors.TargetNotFoundError When required keys are missing or values are invalid.

docs.title: DeployContext dataclass
docs.text:
Structured metadata for a deploy operation.

Callers construct this from CLI flags and the parsed config; the adapter never derives task identity from filesystem paths.

docs.title: DeployResult dataclass
docs.text:
Returned by :meth:DeployAdapter.deploy.

metadata carries adapter-specific extras (notebook source, cluster id, etc.) without polluting the core fields.

docs.title: LineageBackend
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Structural interface for lineage storage backends.

Concrete implementations: FilesystemLineageBackend (built-in), DeltaLineageBackend (Phase 2).

docs.title: compact
docs.text:
compact()

Optimize the underlying storage.

For filesystem backends this is a no-op. For Delta backends this triggers OPTIMIZE on the lineage table.

docs.title: get_run
docs.text:
get_run(run_id)

Load a single run record by ID.

docs.title: Raises
docs.text: ubunye.core.errors.LineageRecordNotFoundError When no record exists for run_id.

docs.title: record
docs.text:
record(record)

Persist a lineage record (non-blocking per Decision 1).

Creates or overwrites the record for the given run_id. Typically called twice per task: once at start (status="running") and once at end (status="success" or "error").

The actual write is dispatched to a background worker thread. On failure, the record is written to a fallback manifest (Decision 2).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: record: The lineage record to persist. Callers construct this with the current engine version and task metadata.

docs.title: search
docs.text:
search(*, task=None, usecase=None, pipeline=None, status=None, since=None, limit=100)

Search across recorded runs with optional filters.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: task: Filter by task name. usecase: Filter by use case. pipeline: Filter by pipeline. status: Filter by status ("success", "error", "running"). since: ISO-8601 datetime; only return runs recorded at or after. limit: Maximum number of records to return.

docs.title: LineageRecord dataclass
docs.text:
Cross-boundary lineage record (Decision 3 compliant).

Core columns are strict; everything else goes into metadata. Every record stamps engine_version so analysts can filter by writer version.

docs.title: ModelVersionInfo dataclass
docs.text:
Cross-boundary model version record (Decision 3 compliant).

Core fields are strict; everything else goes into metadata. Every record stamps engine_version so downstream consumers can filter by writer version.

docs.title: RegistryBackend
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Structural interface for model registries.

Concrete implementations: FilesystemRegistryBackend (built-in), MLflowModelRegistryBackend (mlflow, ADR 014).

docs.title: delete
docs.text:
delete(*, use_case, model_name, version)

Remove a version and its artifacts.

docs.title: demote
docs.text:
demote(*, use_case, model_name, version, to_stage)

Demote a version to a lower stage.

Never move a version up: refuse (RegistryError) a move to production, or to staging from below. Call :func:ubunye.models.lifecycle.check_demote first.

docs.title: get
docs.text:
get(*, use_case, model_name, version=None, stage=None)

Retrieve a model version by exact version or active stage.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: tuple of (artifact_path, ModelVersionInfo) artifact_path is an opaque string — it may be a local path, an MLflow artifact URI, or a cloud storage URL. Callers pass it to ModelClass.load(artifact_path).

docs.title: Raises
docs.text: ubunye.core.errors.VersionNotFoundError When no matching version exists.

docs.title: list_versions
docs.text:
list_versions(*, use_case, model_name)

List all registered versions, newest first.

docs.title: promote
docs.text:
promote(*, use_case, model_name, version, to_stage, gates=None, promoted_by=None)

Promote a version to a higher lifecycle stage.

If gates are provided, all checks must pass before the transition. On gate failure, raises :class:~ubunye.core.errors.PromotionBlockedError — this is NOT caught by the graceful degradation layer (auth and gate failures must propagate).

Metadata update is non-blocking per Decision 1.

docs.title: register
docs.text:
register(*, use_case, model_name, version, model, metrics, metadata=None, lineage_run_id=None)

Register a trained model as a new version.

Artifact writes are synchronous — the method returns only after the model is safely persisted. Index/metadata updates are non-blocking per Decision 1.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: use_case: Logical namespace (e.g. "fraud_detection"). model_name: Model identifier within the use case. version: Explicit semver string, or None for auto-increment. model: A trained model instance whose save()/metadata() methods will be called by the backend. metrics: Training metrics dict. metadata: Optional flexible key-value pairs (Decision 3). lineage_run_id: Optional lineage run ID for cross-referencing.

docs.title: RunRecordStore
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Where run records live (ADR 011). Four methods, no base class needed.

A task is named by its task_path, "usecase/package/task". Newest first means the record written last comes first. A store is built with one argument, its location (a directory, a table name, a URL), given unchanged.

docs.title: list_runs
docs.text:
list_runs(task_path, n=20)

The n newest records of one task, newest first.

docs.title: load
docs.text:
load(task_path, run_id)

One record, every field as saved.

Raises :class:ubunye.core.errors.LineageRecordNotFoundError when the task has no run with that id.

docs.title: save
docs.text:
save(ctx)

Create or replace the record of ctx.run_id for its task.

docs.title: search

docs.title: ubunye.core.backends
docs.text:
Backends are plugins, found by name (ADR 001) and resolved in one order (ADR 003).

Every backend, the shipped ones included, registers in the ubunye.backends entry point group::

[project.entry-points."ubunye.backends"]
spark = "ubunye.backends.spark_backend:SparkBackend"
pandas = "ubunye.backends.pandas_backend:PandasBackend"

so a third party engine plugs in the same way, with no edit here. This module never imports an engine: it loads the class a name points at, only when asked.

Which backend runs a task, in order:

  1. the one asked for by name (--backend on the CLI, backend= in the API);
  2. the platform's: a backend that finds an active session it should attach to (on Databricks, the notebook's SparkSession);
  3. :data:DEFAULT_BACKEND.

The task's config.yaml never names its engine; the same folder runs on any backend that can do what it asks.

docs.title: ubunye.models.base.UbunyeModel
docs.text:
Bases: ABC

Abstract contract every user model must implement.

The engine calls these methods during the pipeline lifecycle. Users implement them with whatever ML library they choose — the engine never imports or knows about the underlying library.

Minimal example::

from ubunye.models.base import UbunyeModel
import joblib

class FraudRiskModel(UbunyeModel):
    def __init__(self):
        self._clf = None

    def train(self, df):
        import pandas as pd
        from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier
        pdf = df.toPandas()
        X, y = pdf.drop("label", axis=1), pdf["label"]
        self._clf = GradientBoostingClassifier().fit(X, y)
        return {"accuracy": self._clf.score(X, y)}

    def predict(self, df):
        pdf = df.toPandas()
        pdf["score"] = self._clf.predict_proba(pdf)[:, 1]
        return spark.createDataFrame(pdf)

    def save(self, path):
        import pathlib, joblib
        pathlib.Path(path).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        joblib.dump(self._clf, f"{path}/clf.joblib")

    @classmethod
    def load(cls, path):
        import joblib
        m = cls()
        m._clf = joblib.load(f"{path}/clf.joblib")
        return m

    def metadata(self):
        import sklearn
        return {
            "library": "sklearn",
            "library_version": sklearn.__version__,
            "features": list(self._clf.feature_names_in_),
            "params": self._clf.get_params(),
        }

docs.title: task_end
docs.text:
task_end(*, context, config, outputs, status, duration_sec, inputs=None, expectations=None, timings=None, llm_calls=None, llm_budget=None, model_runs=None, hash_basis=None, source_versions=None, error=None)

Update the run record with final status, duration, and step hashes.

hash_basis is the engine's word, by output name, on whether each output frame is the rows that were written ("materialised") or will be computed again for the hash ("recomputed"). An output it does not name, and every input, gets the basis its frame type implies.

source_versions is each input's source version when it was read (:mod:ubunye.lineage.source_version). A recomputed input's version is taken again right after its hash; if it moved, the step says the digest is of a later state than the one read (F-046).

model_runs is each model the run trained or scored with: the version, the stage and, for training, the gate result (ADR 012).

error is why a failed run failed (the exception's type and message). It is kept in the record, with the values of secret-looking variables masked, so lineage show, OpenLineage and ubunye prove can say why (F-054).

docs.title: Execution backends
docs.text: A backend is the engine that runs your task. The task folder never names one, so the same folder runs on any backend that can do what it asks.

docs.title: See what you have
docs.text:
ubunye backends

databricks
  features:     catalog, partitioned_writes, path_io, records, remote_paths, spark
  file formats: any
  write modes:  any
  distributed:  yes   needs Java: yes
pandas
  features:     partitioned_writes, path_io, records
  file formats: csv, json, parquet
  write modes:  append, errorifexists, ignore, overwrite, overwrite_partitions
  distributed:  no   needs Java: no
spark (default)
  features:     catalog, partitioned_writes, path_io, records, remote_paths, spark
  ...

Add --json for a machine readable list.

docs.title: Choose one
docs.text:
Where How CLI ubunye run ... --backend pandas (also test run; validate and plan take it to check without running) Python ubunye.run_task(task_dir, backend="pandas") (also run_pipeline and notebook)

With no choice, Ubunye uses the platform's session if there is one (on Databricks, the notebook's), and otherwise starts Spark.

docs.title: Check before you run
docs.text:
ubunye validate -d pipelines -u sales -p etl -t daily --backend pandas

This checks every input and output against what the backend can do, without starting anything, and lists every problem at once:

  [FAIL] daily (on the pandas backend)
         - input 'orders' uses the 'hive' connector, which needs spark; the pandas backend does not provide it.
         - output 'report' uses mode 'merge'; the pandas backend can do append, errorifexists, ignore, overwrite, overwrite_partitions.

ubunye run makes the same check before it starts, so a task that cannot run stops in the first second, not halfway through.

docs.title: The shipped backends
docs.text:
Backend Use it for Install spark Local Spark, Kubernetes, EMR, Dataproc, spark-submit, CI. Starts its own SparkSession, or attaches to the one spark-submit made pip install 'ubunye-engine[spark]' databricks Reuses the SparkSession that already exists instead of making one (chosen for you on Databricks) included in the runtime pandas Small data on a laptop, CI, teaching: pandas and pyarrow, no Spark and no Java. Reads and writes local csv, json and parquet exactly as Spark does pip install 'ubunye-engine[pandas]'

The pandas backend reads and writes exactly as Spark does: see How the pandas backend reads and writes. The REST connector runs on it too (the records feature), with the same rows and types as on Spark. Its frames have Arrow backed columns, which makes a big merge slower on pandas 3; Big merges on Arrow columns says when that matters and the three lines that fix it.

docs.title: One transform for every engine
docs.text:
The config runs anywhere; the transform runs where its code does. A transform that calls the Spark API (F.col, groupBy) needs a Spark backend, and one written with pandas needs the pandas backend. To run the same task on both, write the transform once with Narwhals (pip install narwhals):

import narwhals as nw

from ubunye.core.interfaces import Task


class SurvivalByGroup(Task):
    def transform(self, sources):
        people = nw.from_native(sources["titanic"])  # pandas or Spark, as given
        summary = (
            people.with_columns(
                age_group=nw.when(nw.col("Age") < 18).then(nw.lit("child")).otherwise(nw.lit("adult")),
                # Spark widens every sum to a 64 bit integer; pandas keeps the
                # column's type. Cast first and both give the same type.
                Survived=nw.col("Survived").cast(nw.Int64),
            )
            .group_by("Pclass", "age_group")
            .agg(nw.len().alias("passengers"), nw.col("Survived").sum().alias("survivors"))
            .sort("Pclass", "age_group")
        )
        return {"summary": summary}  # returning the Narwhals frame is fine

Run it with --backend pandas and on Spark, and the two run records carry the same data hash: the same rows, values and types (the engine's own tests check this against Spark). The engine hands your transform its own frames and unwraps what you return, so writers, hooks and lineage never see Narwhals.

Narwhals gives one API, not one set of engine rules. Two differences are known:

  • A sum of whole numbers is bigint on Spark and keeps the column's type on pandas (int32 for small numbers read from CSV). Cast the column before the group by, as above. (Casting inside agg works too, but pandas then runs the sum the slow way, and Narwhals warns.)
  • Rounding a value exactly halfway: Spark rounds half up and pandas rounds half to even, so round(2) makes 0.125 into 0.13 on Spark and 0.12 on pandas. Other values round the same. Round for presentation, or where ties cannot occur.

The run record's data hash covers every value and type, so comparing the two runs' hashes (ubunye lineage compare) shows whether a transform really gives the same result on both.

You do not declare which engines a transform supports. ubunye plan reads the imports in transformations.py and says what it is written for:

  Transform  SurvivalByGroup  (transformations.py), written for narwhals

and with --backend pandas on a transform written for pyspark it warns before the run instead of failing on the first line. Why it works this way, and why SQL is not the answer yet: ADR 005.

docs.title: How the pandas backend reads and writes
docs.text:
The pandas backend runs a task with pandas and pyarrow: no Spark and no Java. Use it for small data, local development, CI and teaching:

ubunye run -d ./pipelines -u sales -p etl -t daily --backend pandas

The same config.yaml drives it. Reads and writes go through the generic s3 path connector for the formats pandas understands (csv, parquet, json); lakehouse formats (delta) and managed tables need Spark, and the engine says so rather than failing obscurely. The one caveat is your own logic: a transformations.py that calls the Spark DataFrame API needs Spark, so a task can run on pandas when its transform works on both (see One transform for every engine) or is written in pandas. Install the extra with pip install "ubunye-engine[pandas]" (on Windows it asks for pyarrow 24 or newer, the first that handles time zones there). Check a task can run on it first with ubunye validate ... --backend pandas.

docs.title: It reads data the way Spark does
docs.text:
The same folder must give the same data on both backends, so the pandas backend copies Spark's defaults instead of pandas' own:

What you read What you get (same as Spark) CSV, no options No header: the first line is data, columns are _c0, _c1, ... CSV with header: "true" Columns named from the first line, every value as text. A blank name becomes _c<position>; a repeated name (ignoring case) gets its position added to each copy, so a,a,,A reads as a0, a1, _c2, A3 CSV with inferSchema: "true" Spark's rules, over every file at once: int if every value fits, else bigint, a whole number past 64 bits, or one written 5. or 1.5E1, a decimal (read exactly); digits in any script count; double (Java's forms: 1.5d, 2 with a space, Inf, NaN; but inf is text), boolean in any case, date, timestamp (with or without an offset); an empty column is text An empty CSV field null, not an empty string (also when nullValue is set to other text) A CSV value of any length Read whole (Spark has no limit; pyarrow alone stopped past 1 MB) encoding (csv, json) One of the names Spark 4 accepts: UTF-8, ISO-8859-1, US-ASCII, UTF-16, UTF-16LE, UTF-16BE, UTF-32 (any case). Others (cp1252, latin1, utf8) are refused, as Spark 4 refuses them; Spark 3.5 took any Java name A CSV byte that is not valid in encoding (UTF-8 unless set) The character U+FFFD, one per broken sequence exactly as Java decodes it (an encoded surrogate, ED A0 80, is one); the read goes on Quotes in a CSV value Spark's escape is a backslash, so "Anna ""Annie""" stays exactly as written, and "a\"b" is a"b (set escape: '"' for doubled quotes); a line of only spaces is skipped JSON One object per line (multiLine: "true" for one big array, which Spark needs; pandas also reads a file holding one array across lines without it); columns and nested fields sorted by name; whole numbers are bigint (decimal past 64 bits); a field that is a number in one record and text in another is text, and a value read as text keeps its JSON (one object per line: its exact source text, 1.50 stays 1.50, as Spark 4 reads it; multiLine: as Jackson writes it back, 1.5, as Spark 3.5 does always); records whose names differ only by case merge into the names seen first (as Spark does; the other spelling then reads as null); a record that repeats a key is refused; empty names and empty objects are dropped, and a record left with no fields is still a row; dates stay text Parquet with unsigned columns uint8 as smallint, uint16 as int, uint32 as bigint, uint64 as decimal(20,0): Spark has no unsigned types A folder Every data file in it, skipping _SUCCESS and other _ or . files and empty files, so it reads what Spark wrote A partitioned folder (dt=2024-01-02/...) The partition columns, after the data columns, typed as Spark infers them (see below) A glob such as data/*.csv Every matching file Column names that differ only by case (Col, col) Refused, on read and on write, as Spark refuses them by default schema: "id INT, name STRING" Exactly those columns and types; an empty file or a folder with no data files gives zero rows of them mode: "FAILFAST", "DROPMALFORMED", "PERMISSIVE" What Spark does with a bad row: stop, skip it, or (the default) cut a row with too many fields and pad one with too few

The frame your task gets is an ordinary pandas DataFrame whose columns are backed by Arrow, so a whole number column with gaps stays whole numbers and a decimal stays a decimal, just as in Spark. Write plain pandas and return plain pandas:

class Enrich(Task):
    def transform(self, sources):
        orders = sources["orders"]
        return {"report": orders.assign(total=orders["price"] * orders["qty"])}

Timestamps written as text are read in spark.sql.session.timeZone from your ENGINE.spark_conf, the same setting Spark uses. If it is not set, the pandas backend uses UTC on every machine, while Spark would use the machine's own zone. Set it once and the two backends agree. A wall clock time that the zone skips (02:30 on the night clocks go forward) is read an hour later, and one that happens twice (01:30 on the night clocks go back) is read as the first of the two, as Java and so Spark read them.

docs.title: Big merges on Arrow columns
docs.text:
Arrow backed columns cost you speed in one place: merge. On pandas 3, a merge on an int64[pyarrow] key is about 2.8 times slower than the same merge on a NumPy int64 key. Filters, new columns, groupby, reads and writes run at the same speed. Measured on 5,000,000 rows joined to 900 (median of 3, dev box, pandas 3.0.6, pyarrow 25):

Merge on region Seconds Arrow keys, as the transform gets them 0.97 NumPy keys (pd.read_parquet) 0.29 Arrow keys, converted with the snippet below first 0.33

In the engine's scale test transform the merge took 0.98 s against 0.35 s, 2.8 times; alone, as above, 3.3 times. On pandas 2.3 the two took about the same time (0.93 and 0.97 s). Memory goes the other way: at 50,000,000 rows the whole job peaked at 9.1 GB with Arrow columns and 12.2 GB with NumPy ones. So this is a trade, and most tasks never notice.

If a merge is most of your task's time, convert the join keys yourself, in your transform, when they are whole numbers with no nulls:

def numpy_keys(frame, keys):
    """Whole number join keys with no nulls as NumPy int64; the rest as they are."""
    return frame.astype({k: "int64" for k in keys if not frame[k].hasnans})

class Detail(Task):
    def transform(self, sources):
        events = numpy_keys(sources["events"], ["region"])
        regions = numpy_keys(sources["regions"], ["region"])
        return {"detail": events.merge(regions, on="region")}

It works on pandas 2 and 3, and on both int64[pyarrow] and pandas' own nullable Int64. The values do not change, and a key with a null is left alone, so it stays a whole number column. The written data and its hash in the run record are the same either way. Convert both sides of the merge: with only one side converted the rows are still right, but do not count on the speed.

The engine does not do this for you, on purpose. Your transform gets the frames as they were read (ADR 004), with the types Spark would give: a whole number column with a null stays a whole number column. NumPy has no whole number that can be null, so it would turn that column into floats. Only your transform knows which keys never have nulls, so the choice is yours.

docs.title: It writes data the way Spark does
docs.text:
A path the pandas backend writes looks exactly like one Spark writes: a folder holding part-00000-....snappy.parquet (or .csv, .json) and a _SUCCESS file. So Spark can read what pandas wrote, and pandas can read what Spark wrote.

  • overwrite replaces the folder. The new data is written to a hidden folder first and swapped in only when it is complete, so a failed run never leaves you with half a table.
  • append adds new part files and leaves the old ones alone.
  • overwrite_partitions with partitionBy replaces only the partitions the new data fills (see below).
  • CSV is written the Spark way: no header unless header: "true", text quoted only when it has to be, numbers such as 2.0 and 1.0E10, timestamps such as 2024-01-02T03:04:05.000+02:00.
  • JSON is one object per line, and null fields are left out. A map column is written as an object and keeps its null values ({"a":null,"b":"x"}), as Spark writes a map.
  • Parquet timestamps are stored in microseconds, which is what Spark reads.

docs.title: Partition folders
docs.text:
partitionBy: [dt] writes Spark's folders, out/dt=2024-01-02/part-....parquet, with every mode, and the same task gives the same folders and rows on both backends (the engine's tests check this against Spark 4.2). What Spark does, this does:

  • One folder level per column, in partitionBy order. Characters a folder name cannot hold become % codes (a/b is a%2Fb; on Windows a space is %20, as Spark writes it there). A null or empty value is __HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__.
  • The partition columns are not in the data files; reading the folder puts them back after the other columns.
  • overwrite_partitions replaces each partition folder the new data fills and leaves every other partition alone. Each new partition is written to a hidden folder first, then swapped in; if a swap fails, the partitions already swapped are put back; an old partition that cannot be put back is kept, and the error says where. Rerunning a day this way replaces that day, so it is safe after a crash with no other help.
  • One window is left, as in Spark's own commit: a hard kill (power cut) between moving a partition's old folder aside and moving the new one in leaves that partition missing until the batch is rerun. Its old files are then in a hidden folder beside the target, .<name>.ubunye-<id>.old/<partition path>; the next write to the target warns and names it, and nothing deletes it.
  • A write whose values would share a folder is refused, as Spark's write fails on it: a null and the text __HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__, two timestamps that read the same on the wall clock when daylight saving ends, or folder names that differ only in case (also against folders already in the target), on every system, since Windows and macOS disks ignore case.
  • append claims every new file before it lands, so a failed or killed run has exactly its own files taken back (ADR 008). Spark does the same for a path on a local or shared disk: it writes the batch into a hidden folder inside the output (_ubunye-<id>, skipped by Spark, pyarrow, pandas and Ubunye's readers, as Spark's own _temporary is), and the files are claimed, then moved up into the output. On object storage a Spark append is not claimed, and the log says so. A job that overwrites the whole output while an append is being written removes that folder, and the append fails.

Reading a partitioned folder, a value becomes an int, bigint, decimal, double, timestamp, date or text, as Spark infers it. That inference is why some column types are refused as partition columns: Spark writes them, but reads them back as something else (a double column comes back as text or a decimal, a decimal as a double, binary as text). The pandas backend refuses double, decimal, binary, time and nested partition columns with a message saying so; cast the column to a string or a date first. Partition by strings, whole numbers, dates, booleans or timestamps. As on Spark, a boolean comes back as the text true or false, a small integer as int, and a timestamp with 2 to 6 decimal places of seconds makes the column text.

Three things differ from Spark, all rare:

  • A partition column whose every value is null reads back as all null text; Spark calls its type void, which pandas has no match for.
  • A folder value like 10:05:06 reads back as text; Spark 4.2 infers a time.
  • Folder names that differ only in case (p=1 and P=2) are one column on both; Spark takes the spelling from whichever folder it lists first, which is not a fixed order, so the name's case may differ.

ubunye plan --backend pandas and ubunye validate --backend pandas check these options before a run, so an option the pandas backend cannot honour is found then, not when the file is opened.

Anything the pandas backend cannot do the Spark way is refused by name, not ignored: an unknown reader option (dateFormat, for example), a nested schema type, or a cloud path such as s3a://. The error says which option or path and what to do instead.

docs.title: The run record uses helper processes
docs.text:
With --lineage, every input and output is hashed, every row (ADR 006). A table of 500,000 rows or more is hashed by helper processes: fresh Pythons, started from sys.executable, that load only the hash code. They are gone when the hash is done.

  • How many: the usable cores, at most 4. UBUNYE_HASH_WORKERS sets the cap; it is never more than the cores this process may use (its CPU affinity and, on Linux, a cgroup v2 cpu.max quota). 1 turns helpers off. Hashes running at the same time in one process (threads) share the cap.
  • Memory: each helper holds about 105 to 125 MB resident while it works (measured on Windows with a venv, where each helper is the venv launcher plus Python). Four helpers add about 0.5 GB on top of the run.
  • In a container with a memory limit, count that in, or set UBUNYE_HASH_WORKERS=2 (or 1). The CPU quota is read for you; a memory limit is not.
  • No helpers in a frozen app (PyInstaller and the like) or when sys.executable is not a Python interpreter; the hash then runs in the calling process, as it does for smaller tables.
  • Safe to fail: a helper that fails, gives no answer within its deadline, or runs other hash code or another pyarrow than the caller is stopped, and the calling process hashes the table itself. The digest is the same either way. Ctrl+C stops every helper at once. The reason is logged at debug level (ubunye.lineage.content_hash).

docs.title: Write your own
docs.text:
A backend is a subclass of ubunye.core.interfaces.Backend registered as an entry point. It says what it can do, and the engine does the rest.

from ubunye.core.capabilities import PATH_IO, Capabilities
from ubunye.core.interfaces import Backend


class MyBackend(Backend):
    name = "mine"
    CAPABILITIES = Capabilities(
        features=frozenset({PATH_IO}),
        file_formats=frozenset({"parquet"}),
        write_modes=frozenset({"append", "overwrite"}),
    )

    def __init__(self, app_name="ubunye", conf=None):
        self.conf = dict(conf or {})

    def start(self): ...
    def stop(self): ...
    def read_frame(self, file_format, path, *, options=None, schema=None): ...
    def execute_write(self, df, resolved, *, connector, file_format, **kw): ...

[project.entry-points."ubunye.backends"]
mine = "my_package.backend:MyBackend"

To serve the REST connector, declare records and implement frame_from_records(records, *, schema=None) (a list of dicts, and a Spark DDL string or None, to your frame) and iter_records(frame) (each row as a dict). A backend with a SparkSession (self.spark) that declares spark needs neither: spark implies records, and the REST connector falls back to the Spark way.

After pip install, ubunye backends lists it and --backend mine runs on it. If your constructor takes other arguments, override the create class method. If your engine should claim a session the platform already started, override from_platform. See the architecture decisions for why it works this way.

docs.title: Prove it: the conformance suite
docs.text:
The tests every backend must pass ship with the engine, and the Spark and pandas backends run them too. Subclass them in your backend's tests:

import pytest

from ubunye.testing.backend_conformance import BackendConformance


class TestMyBackend(BackendConformance):
    @pytest.fixture
    def backend(self):
        backend = MyBackend(conf={"spark.sql.session.timeZone": "UTC"})
        backend.start()
        yield backend
        backend.stop()

They check that it is registered under its name and declares what it can do; that transforms get its own frames and the engine a port whose count() means rows; that it reads a CSV file exactly as Spark does, leaving the same run record hash as every other engine for the same data; that what it writes it reads back unchanged; and that the write modes it claims behave as Spark's do. Anything your backend does not claim (a format, a write mode) is skipped, with the reason. For the hash to match, a port that is not Spark or pandas reports its column types by the run record's names (int32, int64, float64, bool, string, date, timestamp, ...; see ADR 006).

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
All notable changes to Ubunye Engine will be documented here.

The format is based on Keep a Changelog and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• One path for the model registry. ModelRegistry is now a thin front over the lifecycle layer for every backend, the filesystem included. The filesystem no longer keeps its own copy of the rules (version numbers, gates, one production version, rollback, archive). Same API, same files on disk: a store written by 0.9.0 reads and promotes the same (a fixture test pins it). Reading a version's stage no longer downloads its artifact from a remote store.
  • ModelRegistry.promotion_gates gives {} for a model with no versions on the filesystem too (it raised RegistryNotFoundError), like every other backend.
  • Metadata given through the FilesystemRegistryBackend protocol (kept nested under registry_metadata on disk, unchanged) now reads back flat from ModelRegistry, as it already did through the backend. A model whose own metadata() uses a version field's name (promoted_by, lineage_run_id, config_hash, the stage times) or registry_metadata reads back with that key in the field, as on every other backend; no shipped model does.

  • An unknown stage name given to the filesystem backend raises ValueError; it was written to registry.json as is.

  • ubunye deploy databricks defaults to Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS (17.3.x-scala2.13, Spark 4.0), the runtime ubunye export databricks already used, for a target in targets.yaml that does not set spark_version. The old default, 13.3 LTS, runs Spark 3.4, older than the engine supports (pyspark 3.5 or later). A target that sets spark_version is unchanged.

  • A first Delta append of a named batch makes no history lookups (F-100). The two DESCRIBE HISTORY calls around each keyed append, there only to warn that Delta skipped a batch an earlier run had committed, now run only when an earlier run of the batch could have: the run took over a dead run's lease, or a failed run that wrote the batch left a note beside it. Same warning, fewer steps.

  • The docs were reworked for clarity. Each topic now has one home page, and the others link to it. New pages: Concepts, Run records, Safe reruns, Troubleshooting, Upgrading from 0.8 and Azure. The README is a short front door. The home page has an intro film. Every page uses the same words (use case, pipeline, task, profile, run record), and internal ticket numbers are gone from user pages. Examples that did not run as written (drift detection, RAG, the registry gates, the hooks setup, the Databricks bundle) now run, and their output is real. The site has top tabs, tap to zoom on diagrams, link preview cards, and colours that match the diagrams.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• ubunye run on a task whose transformations.py has no Task class prints one [ERROR] Run refused line, not a traceback. ubunye doctor no longer suggests --backend databricks on a laptop (it only attaches to a cluster's session).

  • Saving a Delta run record from a CLI or pandas run is about twice as fast (F-116). With no active SparkSession the Delta run record store starts a local one, and Delta read the run record log in 50 tasks on every save. That session, and only that one, now sets spark.databricks.delta.snapshotPartitions=1 and turns off the Spark UI and console progress bar. Measured on the dev box (16 cores, 8 saves): about 1.35 s to 0.72 s per save. A session the user or the platform started is never changed.

  • Each command's help says its default profile plainly (F-115). ubunye export defaults to production (--profile prod for airflow and databricks, -m PROD for spark-pipeline) and ubunye run to DEV. The defaults are unchanged; the help of export spark-pipeline and run now says so, as export airflow and export databricks already did, and docs/cli.md says it once for all.

  • python -m ubunye documents only what works (F-114). Its docstring showed spark-submit ... -m ubunye (spark-submit takes a file, not -m) and a --task-dir s3a://... (only a local folder works); docs/deployment/anywhere.md said "path or bucket". Both now show the file path and a local task folder, and point to ubunye deploy glue|dataproc|emr-serverless for running from a bucket.

  • A task the backend cannot run is one [ERROR] line in ubunye run (F-113). A BackendCapabilityError (say, a hive input on --backend pandas) printed a full traceback box. It now ends in [ERROR] Run refused for <task>: ... with the hint and exit code 1, like the other refusals. Nothing ran, as before.

  • Spark with no usable Java fails in one clean message (F-112). The spark backend now looks for Java (JAVA_HOME, then java on PATH) and its version before it starts a session. No Java, or one older than the installed Spark needs, raises SparkSessionError with the versions that work, and ubunye run prints it as one [ERROR] line instead of pyspark's [JAVA_GATEWAY_EXITED] traceback. A session that is already running, or Spark Connect, is not checked. ubunye doctor and ubunye backends ask the same function, so the spark backend is no longer called usable with no Java. The Java versions are now right everywhere: Spark 4 runs on Java 17 or 21, Spark 3.5 on Java 8, 11 or 17 (the doctor's fix text said 17 or 11).

  • ubunye deploy dockerfile --out img/ writes img/Dockerfile (F-111). A path ending in / is a folder: it is made when missing. Before, a missing img/ gave a file named img.

  • The workflow from ubunye init github-actions works out of the box (F-110). ubunye deploy databricks --host now reads DATABRICKS_HOST, the secret the workflow sets, so the deploy step needs no committed targets.yaml (a targets.yaml, when there is one, still wins). The manual "Run job" step now starts the job with the new --run flag; before, it deployed again and started nothing. --run starts a run after the deploy and prints its link. The workflow's "Notebook output link" step is gone: the run step prints the link.

  • hooks= adds to the engine's hooks, it does not replace them (F-101). ubunye.run_task(..., hooks=[...]), run_pipeline and notebook dropped the run record (lineage=True) and the CONFIG.monitors hook when given hooks. Your hooks now run with them. Engine(hooks=...) is unchanged.

  • A unity read that names its table with db_name fails ubunye validate (F-102). It passed validation and failed at run time: the reader never read db_name. The message says what to use: table: 'catalog.schema.table', or catalog + schema + tbl_name (now accepted by validate, as the reader always read it), or sql. ubunye init --template databricks wrote such a read; it now writes table: main.raw_db.<task>_input, and a test checks that every template init writes passes ubunye validate.

  • ubunye validate reports a write mode the writer cannot do (F-103), with the message ubunye plan gives: a jdbc output with mode: merge, a merge with no merge_keys. Only plan and the write itself caught these. One check (write_modes.resolve_for) now serves both. A writer that declares no modes is not held to any, as before.

  • secret:// in ENGINE.spark_conf is checked and resolved (F-104). It reached Spark as literal text, and a misspelt provider passed ubunye validate. Validate now checks it (base and profiles), and a Spark backend gets the value, fetched when the backend is built, masked like any secret. A backend without Spark does not fetch it.

  • The pandas backend reads a JSON file holding one array (F-105), as Spark reads it with multiLine. It read JSON Lines only, so a pretty-printed array failed on its first line. JSON Lines, including an array on each line, reads as before.

  • The C01 proving workload runs on pandas without a Narwhals warning (F-106). Its counts and sums were cast inside the group-by, which made Narwhals fall back to a slow per-group apply and warn "Found complex group-by expression". The casts now follow the aggregation. Same outputs, same golden digest.

  • Registering with promotion_gates={} clears a model's stored gates on every backend. Before, only the default filesystem path cleared them; MLflow and the others kept the old gates.

  • A rollback keeps who promoted the version on every backend. Before, a filesystem backend named by object, and the deprecated MLflowRegistryBackend, set it to empty.

  • ubunye deploy and ubunye export end an expected error in one [ERROR] message (F-096), exit code 1, the way ubunye run does. No targets.yaml, no token, a cloud CLI not on PATH, a bad task list or a config that does not validate printed a full traceback; deploy k8s and deploy container-apps also printed their whole launcher script. A missing kubectl or az is now found before anything runs, and a failed launcher is named, never printed. A bug still shows its traceback. A config that does not validate now raises ConfigError (still a ValueError).

  • --resume skips a task that only overwrites once it finished the batch (F-098). Only a task with an append output was skipped, though the docs said every finished task is. With --lineage (lineage=True), a task whose latest run record for this batch (same -dt and --var) says success is now skipped with [SKIP], whatever it writes. Without run records an overwrite task runs again, as the docs now say.

  • The Delta run record store no longer grows one file per save for ever (F-099). A table it creates is clustered by task_path (liquid clustering) with auto compaction on (delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact), so Delta merges the small files each append leaves: 200 saves leave under 60 files, not 200. An existing table is used as it is; docs/cli.md shows the three statements that turn the same on for it.

  • A run record no store could write is kept, whatever the store (F-097). When the filesystem store could not write (its folder under a file), the record was lost with a log line, and ubunye sync lineage found nothing. Now every store's failed save goes one way, through the recorder, to ~/.ubunye/fallback/<run_id>/lineage.jsonl, and the warning names the ubunye sync lineage command that replays it. The Delta store's own copy of that code is gone; its save raises like any store's.

  • The docs say what 0.9.1 does. Merging the docs rework dropped some 0.9.1 facts and kept older text they made false. Back in place: deploy databricks --run and --host reading DATABRICKS_HOST (the Databricks guide also lost a stray copy of that text in "What success looks like", and no longer says to commit a targets.yaml for the workflow), --resume skipping an overwrite task with --lineage, the Delta run record table's clustering and the three statements for an existing table, the fallback manifest for every store, and python -m ubunye taking only a local --task-dir. Fixed: hooks= and OTelHook no longer said the run record is dropped, secret:// in spark_conf no longer said it is not read, validate -m no longer said a config with no profiles fails, registry.auto_version is marked deprecated, and the troubleshooting doctor output is the real 0.9.1 output (Java versions).

  • The CLI reference shows every command again. A code span broken across two lines put <table> at the start of a line, and Markdown read it as raw HTML: everything after "Where run records are stored" (lineage show, runs, models, prove, sync, deploy, export) showed as plain text. The same fix applies to ADR 008. The example catalog names on the deployment page are now neutral.
  • ubunye validate checks the profile the way run does. It uses DEV when no -m or --profile is given, refuses a name the config does not define, and accepts any name when the config has no profiles. Before, a config with profiles dev and prod passed validate and then stopped run. The error now lists the profiles and, when only the case differs, says which one you meant. run prints the same message instead of a traceback.
  • ubunye plan and ubunye doctor check -m too. plan -m XYZ said "Plan OK" on a config whose profiles are DEV and PROD, and doctor passed it. Both now refuse a profile the config does not define, with the message run gives, and accept any name on a config with no profiles.
  • load_config(profile=...) follows the same rule (and so run_task, run_pipeline and notebook, which pass profile= to it). It refused any profile on a config with no profiles, which run accepts. It now calls UbunyeConfig.check_profile, the one rule, and its error is the one run prints. It is still a ConfigProfileError.
  • prove observe before any run is a clean error (exit 2) that says to run the task with --lineage first, not a traceback. An unknown --run-id is too.
  • The warning for CONFIG.transform.type no longer says it became an error in 0.8.0. It says what happens (the task still runs transformations.py) and what to do instead.
  • The config that ubunye init writes spells {{ task_dir }} in its comment the way the config uses it.

docs.title: Deprecated
docs.text:
Nothing in Ubunye, its docs or examples uses these. They still work, warn with a DeprecationWarning, and go in 1.0:

  • registry.auto_version in a model transform. It never did anything: a version is made whenever registry.version is not set. Remove the key.
  • ubunye.core.planning.plan_problems, ubunye.proving.matrix.render_many, ubunye.plugins.ml.adapters.to_numpy_from_pandas and to_numpy_from_spark (use ensure_Xy_numpy), ubunye.cli.backend_choice.capabilities_or_exit, and ubunye.telemetry.otel.init_tracer (use setup).

docs.title: Removed
docs.text:
• The private module ubunye._internal.auto_detect (detect_registry_backend, detect_lineage_backend, detect_auth_backend). Nothing called it; the registry backend has been chosen by ubunye.models.backends.choose since 0.9.0 (ADR 010), and the lineage store by ubunye.lineage.stores (ADR 011).
  • Dead private code: a second copy of the engine version lookup in ubunye plan (it now reads ubunye.__version__), and two attributes that were set and never read (notebook()'s task object, SklearnModel._last_metrics).

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Job health and upstream checks, from run records (ADR 013). ubunye runs health shows, per task, the last status, when it last succeeded, runs in a row that failed, and runs left running past --stuck-after (likely dead); it exits 1 when a task is failing, stuck, or older than --max-age, so it can be a scheduled check. CONFIG.requires: [{task: uc/pkg/t, variables: [month]}] refuses to start a task until the upstream succeeded for the same batch, with an optional wait; ubunye runs wait-for is the same check as a command. Both read only the run record store (any store, ADR 011), so jobs that share no disk can check each other; no platform plugin. Also ubunye.api.job_health, ubunye.api.wait_for_upstream and the MCP tools health and upstream. A task with no requires runs, and hashes, exactly as before.
  • The run record names the model (ADR 012). A ModelTransform train puts the model, the version it registered, the stage it reached and the gate result on the record (model_runs): passed, or blocked with the gate, metric, value and threshold. A predict puts the version and stage it used. A blocked promotion still fails the run, and the failed run's record now says why; registry.on_blocked: record keeps the run going instead. ubunye lineage trace prints a MODELS section; lineage show includes the entries. The lineage conformance suite checks every store keeps them.
  • Scored rows can name their model. registry.stamp_columns: true adds model_version and model_stage columns to a ModelTransform predict, the same on pandas and Spark. Off by default.

  • Features are checked at predict (ADR 012). A frame without a feature the model version declares is logged and recorded before the model is called, and a model that then fails gets a note naming the missing columns. registry.check_features: true refuses the frame with FeatureContractError; false skips the check. A model that declares no features works as before.

  • Model registry backends are plugins, found by name (ADR 010). The ubunye.registry_backends entry points existed but nothing used them, so a third party registry could be installed and never reached. Now ubunye models * takes --backend / -b, a model transform takes registry.backend, and ModelRegistry(store, backend=...) and ubunye.models.resolve_registry() exist. The order is: the name asked for, else UBUNYE_REGISTRY_BACKEND, else filesystem. With neither set, nothing changes. A backend implements six methods; rollback, archive, compare, version numbers, stored promotion gates and one production version at a time are done by Ubunye on top of them, for every backend.

  • --backend mlflow now uses the MLflow Model Registry (ADR 014). Before, the mlflow backend kept models in a folder and only logged a best effort MLflow run. Now each version is a registered model version ({use_case}.{model_name}, or the UBUNYE_MLFLOW_MODEL_NAME template), the saved model is the version's artifact, and the stage, metrics, metadata, gates and lineage run id are version tags. staging and production are MLflow aliases, so models:/<name>@production works. The MLflow stage API is never called, so the backend fits Unity Catalog. MLflow is found through MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI / MLFLOW_REGISTRY_URI; --store names the experiment. The old class, MLflowRegistryBackend, still works from Python and warns that it is deprecated.
  • ubunye.testing.registry_conformance, the suite a registry backend runs to prove itself. The filesystem and MLflow backends pass it, and so does a third party one installed through a real entry point.
  • Run records can live in a shared store (ADR 011). The store is a plugin in ubunye.lineage_backends, chosen by --lineage-backend (on run, test run, lineage *, gate, mcp, sync lineage), lineage_backend= (on run_task, run_pipeline, notebook), LineageRecorder(backend=), then the UBUNYE_LINEAGE_BACKEND variable, then filesystem. With --lineage-backend delta --lineage-dir main.ops.ubunye_runs, jobs that share no disk write their receipts to one Delta table and can read each other's. Nothing changes if you set nothing: records stay in <usecase_dir>/.ubunye/lineage.
  • ubunye.testing.lineage_conformance: the tests a run record store must pass (every field read back equal, newest first, limit, status, missing run id, tasks kept apart). The filesystem store passes it in the unit tier, Delta on live Spark.
  • RunRecordStore in ubunye.interfaces: the four methods a store provides.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• CLI docs and help say what the commands do (F-094). docs/cli.md said python -m ubunye runs the same CLI; it is a separate runner for spark-submit (--task-dir, --mode, --dt), and the page now says so. The version example shows 0.9.0, the middle level is called a pipeline where the page still said package, and ubunye config --help says it validates (it never showed anything).

  • export databricks defaults are current (F-095). With no wheel_dbfs_path the job named the wheel ubunye_engine-0.1.0; it now names the installed version's wheel. The default job cluster runtime moves from 13.3.x-scala2.12 (Spark 3.4, past end of support, older than the pyspark>=3.5 the engine needs) to 17.3.x-scala2.13 (Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS). Set spark_version or wheel_dbfs_path under ORCHESTRATION.databricks to choose your own. export airflow and export databricks help now says --profile defaults to prod, unlike run, which defaults to DEV.

  • deploy dockerfile --out makes its folder, and takes a folder (F-093). The documented --out build/Dockerfile failed with FileNotFoundError when build/ did not exist, and --out build failed with IsADirectoryError. Missing folders are now made, and a folder gets <folder>/Dockerfile.

  • prove options with fixed values reject a wrong value cleanly (F-092). prove skip --status nonsense and prove observe --cost-basis bogus printed a raw ValueError traceback, and prove observe --kind bogus was kept silently. Each is now a usage error (exit 2) that lists the valid choices.

  • models demote can no longer move a version up past its gates (F-091). ubunye models demote --to production put a version in production without checking its promotion gates, and without the promotion_forced mark. Demote now only moves a version down: --to takes development, staging or archived, and staging only from production. The library refuses the same moves (ModelRegistry.demote and every built in registry backend raise RegistryError), and the registry conformance suite checks it for every backend. models promote --to now takes only staging or production, as its help said. A wrong --to is a usage error (exit 2) that lists the choices.

  • Rerun safety reads the run record store you chose (ADR 008, ADR 011). With --lineage-backend delta (or any store other than the filesystem), a run that took over a dead run's lease looked for its record in local files, found none, and could take back the appends of a run that had in fact recorded success. It now reads and marks the record through the chosen store, and refuses if the store cannot be read.

  • A Delta append of a batch lands once, and a rerun can correct it (F-071). A run killed or failed after its Delta commit was appended again by the rerun, and --rerun appended a finished batch twice. A Delta append (path or table, through the delta, s3, hive or unity writer) of a named batch is now Delta's idempotent write, keyed by task, output and batch: a retry commits nothing, and says so if the table did not change. Set replace_where on the append (for example "month = '{{ dt }}'") and each run replaces that batch's rows in one commit instead, so a retry or --rerun writes the corrected batch. Behaviour change: replace_where on an append was ignored before. See ADR 008. On Spark 3.5 the replace of a table batch uses writeTo(table).overwrite(...), since saveAsTable cannot replace rows there.

  • A JDBC append with replace_where lands its batch once (F-072). Spark's JDBC writer commits each partition on its own, so a failed run left part or all of the batch and the rerun inserted it again. With replace_where the batch is written to a staging table, then one database transaction deletes the batch's rows and inserts the staged ones; the staging table is dropped. A JDBC append without it is unchanged.

  • The Databricks examples run on serverless again. Four example configs set spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode, which serverless refuses. Since the engine stopped ignoring refused keys, the scheduled jhb_weather job failed every day from 2026-09-26. The key is removed; serverless never applied it, so the writes behave as before.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• -p/--pipeline replaces --package. The middle level of use case, pipeline, task is called a pipeline everywhere now. Every CLI command that took -p/--package takes -p/--pipeline ("Pipeline name."). --package still works until 1.0: it is hidden from --help and prints one warning to stderr. Giving both is an error. In Python, run_pipeline() and job_health() take pipeline=; package= still works with a DeprecationWarning, and both is a TypeError. The positional order of run_pipeline() is unchanged. The MCP health tool takes pipeline and still accepts package. Run records keep their package field.
  • The Delta lineage store keeps the whole run record. It used to store a LineageRecord, which dropped steps, hashes, timings, expectations and the environment. It now writes the record as JSON plus index columns, only appends, and needs Spark: a record it cannot write goes to the fallback manifest with a warning, never quietly to local files. DeltaLineageBackend.search() returns run records; the old search is search_records(), and search(task=, usecase=, pipeline=) still reaches it with a DeprecationWarning.
  • LineageRecorder(store=...) is now LineageRecorder(backend=...); store= still works, with a DeprecationWarning (store="s3" keeps the stub, as before). A failed record write is now logged instead of silently dropped.
  • ubunye sync lineage replays whole run records, the last one kept for each run, into the store named by --lineage-backend and --lineage-dir.
  • LineageStore.search() takes limit.
  • Clearer docs diagrams. Project Structure zooms from a use case into a pipeline (its tasks run in order) and into a task (config.yaml and transformations.py), and colour-matches the folder path to the -u, -p and -t flags. The home page shows a task written once, run unchanged on a laptop, a cloud or Databricks, each run leaving a record that ubunye prove compares. Connectors shows inputs:, your transform and outputs: with the names you write in YAML, and which also work on pandas. They keep the look of the original slides (dark stage, stacked cards, logos) and are drawn as SVG by the scripts in scripts/diagrams/.
  • More diagrams, and one on the README. New pictures for the parts of config.yaml (Config Overview), what expectations do with bad rows (Expectations), the run receipt and ubunye gate (Gate Pull Requests, ADR 006) and the model stages (Model Registry). The README shows the home diagram.
  • Diagrams for the rest of the key ideas. Rerun safety (CLI, ADR 008), profiles (Engine and Profiles), how a backend is chosen (Execution Backends, ADR 003), ubunye export (Orchestration), agents over MCP, and the RAG and feature store guides, whose text arrows become pictures.
  • The Databricks example notebooks use the notebook API. They now open a context with ubunye.notebook() and run ctx.read(), ctx.transform() and ctx.write() in separate cells, so you can see the data between steps. Catalog and schema come from the widgets on their own (no os.environ), and the notebooks install ubunye-engine==0.8.0.
  • The registry backend is no longer picked from the host. The private detect_registry_backend() returned mlflow on Databricks; it now follows the ADR 010 order and is deprecated. Set UBUNYE_REGISTRY_BACKEND=mlflow to keep MLflow.
  • FilesystemRegistryBackend.register keeps the metadata it is given (it was returned once and dropped), and stores promotion_gates with the model.

The hardening release. Ubunye was tested against real use: newcomers given only the public docs, real open data (Olist, WFP food prices), a scale ladder to 50 million rows, awkward data of ten shapes, and seven environments. Every fix below has a test that failed before it, and every engine fix was reviewed by an adversarial skeptic. The same three workloads (C01, R1, R2) give identical digests on pandas, Spark, AWS Glue, Azure Container Apps, Databricks, GCP Dataproc and Kubernetes (42 of 42 checks).

docs.title: Upgrade notes (read these first)
docs.text:
• Digests change for map columns (maps are now unordered: entries sorted by key, null values kept) and for text holding control characters such as U+000B (the escape is written in upper case, as Spark writes it). A ubunye gate against a 0.7 record may report these columns as changed once.
  • Delta reads are pinned to the version seen when the input is read, so every output of a run sees one snapshot.
  • New refusals, each before anything is written: a Spark task that overwrites a folder it reads; a lease or finished note that exists but cannot be read; charset names Spark 4 refuses (it accepts UTF-8, ISO-8859-1, US-ASCII, UTF-16, UTF-16LE, UTF-16BE and UTF-32); column names that differ only by case, on file reads and writes.
  • Input contracts name timestamps by their real type (timestamp or timestamp_ntz), as Spark 3.4 and later do.
  • New settings: UBUNYE_HASH_WORKERS, UBUNYE_SOURCE_VERSION_TIMEOUT, UBUNYE_LLM_PROGRESS.
  • Recording a run costs 1.9 times the plain job on Spark and 6.4 times on pandas at 5 million rows (it was 2.5 and 9.8 times). The 1.5 times target is not met yet.
