A requirement is met by a record of that task with status success whose variables match this run's batch. Batch means the same thing as in rerun safety (ADR 008): every variable but mode and dtf. The check runs in execute_user_task, before the task is loaded, so the CLI, run_task, run_pipeline and every deploy target share it. When the upstream has not succeeded the run is refused with what is missing, which batch, the upstream's latest run of that batch, and what to try. With wait it looks again every poll (default 60 s) until the time is up. A task with no requires does nothing new, and its config dumps and hashes as before. 4. The store the check reads is the one the run records into (--lineage-backend, --lineage-dir); with no store named, the filesystem one under the use case folder. A non-filesystem store chosen only by UBUNYE_LINEAGE_BACKEND, with no location, is an error that says to name it. 5. A new command group, ubunye runs, holds health and wait-for, not ubunye lineage. The lineage commands show what records say and exit 0 when they find them. runs commands answer a yes or no question for a scheduler, and their exit code is the answer. wait-for is the same check as requires, for a job that cannot change its config or is not an Ubunye task. 6. The same functions everywhere: ubunye.api.job_health, ubunye.api.wait_for_upstream, and the read-only MCP tools health and upstream.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A team gets job health and an upstream gate on any platform, from the records it already writes, by pointing jobs at one shared store.
  • The upstream must record its runs (--lineage) into the store the downstream reads. A run that was never recorded cannot be seen.
  • Any successful run of the batch counts, even if a later rerun of that batch is under way or failed: rerun safety replaces a batch only after the new run succeeds, so the earlier data stands until then.
  • Health reads the newest 50 runs per task, and searches further back only for the last success. On a large Delta table each task is one filtered read.
  • Not done: a lease or lock between the upstream and the downstream. The check is made once, when the downstream starts.

docs.title: ADR 014: The MLflow registry backend uses aliases
docs.text: Status: accepted, 0.9.0

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The mlflow registry backend did not use the MLflow Model Registry. It kept every model in a folder (the filesystem registry) and, on register and promote, logged a best effort MLflow run with params and metrics. No registered model, no model version, no alias. A team on MLflow could not load a Ubunye model with models:/..., and the run logging failed silently.

MLflow's fixed stages (Staging, Production, Archived) are deprecated, and Unity Catalog has none: only aliases and tags.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
mlflow (MLflowModelRegistryBackend) keeps models in the MLflow Model Registry and implements only the six protocol methods (ADR 010). Rollback, archive, compare and one production version come from the lifecycle layer.

  • Where MLflow is comes from MLflow itself (MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI, MLFLOW_REGISTRY_URI). The store string is the experiment that holds one run per version; the run's model artifact is the saved model and the version's source.
  • A Ubunye model is the registered model {use_case}.{model_name}, or the template in UBUNYE_MLFLOW_MODEL_NAME.
  • A Ubunye version is a model version. Its Ubunye version string, stage, metrics, metadata, gates and lineage run id are version tags under ubunye.. MLflow's own version numbers stay MLflow's.
  • The stage tag is the truth for every version. staging and production are also aliases, held by the version moved there last. When that version leaves the stage, the alias moves to another version still in it, or is removed. development and archived have no alias: many versions sit in them.
  • The stage API (transition_model_version_stage, get_latest_versions) is never called. The tests forbid it.

The old class stays as MLflowRegistryBackend, works as before when built in Python, and warns that it is deprecated. The mlflow entry point name became reachable only in 0.9 (ADR 010), so no released config changes meaning.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• models:/<name>@production works for any MLflow client, serving included.
  • The conformance suite runs against a local MLflow (SQLite and a file artifact store), no server.
  • Unity Catalog should work by naming the model catalog.schema.model through UBUNYE_MLFLOW_MODEL_NAME. Not tried on a workspace yet. Unity Catalog also wants an MLmodel file with a signature in the source; Ubunye's saved models have none, so registering there may be refused until the artifact carries one.
  • Every call lists the model's versions (paged), fine for the tens of versions a model has.
  • Like ADR 010, the alias moves are a read then a write, not atomic.

docs.title: Engine & Profiles
docs.text: The ENGINE section holds Spark settings, and profiles: named sets of overrides for each environment (DEV, PROD), picked with -m. This page is for anyone who runs one task in more than one place without copying its config.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
ENGINE:
  spark_conf:                          # base Spark settings (all profiles)
    spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: "200"
    spark.executor.memory: "4g"

  profiles:
    DEV:                               # overrides applied with -m DEV (the default)
      spark_conf:
        spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: "4"
        spark.executor.memory: "512m"
    STAGING:
      spark_conf:
        spark.executor.memory: "8g"
    PROD:
      spark_conf:
        spark.executor.memory: "32g"
        spark.executor.cores: "8"

The memory and cores keys here take effect only when Ubunye starts Spark itself. See Spark keys fixed at session start.

docs.title: EngineConfig
docs.text: Field Type Default Description spark_conf Dict[str, str] {} Base Spark configuration keys applied in all profiles profiles Dict[str, EngineProfile] {} Named profiles that override spark_conf, catalog and schema_name catalog string null Catalog to switch to before the task runs (USE CATALOG) schema_name string null Schema to switch to before the task runs (USE SCHEMA)

docs.title: EngineProfile
docs.text:
Field Type Default Description spark_conf Dict[str, str] {} Spark conf overrides for this profile catalog string null Replaces ENGINE.catalog for this profile schema_name string null Replaces ENGINE.schema_name for this profile

catalog and schema_name apply on a Spark backend only. Open-source Spark has no USE CATALOG; when the switch fails, the engine logs it and carries on, so fully qualified table names still work.

docs.title: Profile merge rules
docs.text:
When -m <name> (--mode) is passed, the engine builds the Spark settings like this:

  1. Start with the base ENGINE.spark_conf dict.
  2. Update with the named profile's spark_conf (profile values win on conflict).

Profile-only keys are additive; base keys not overridden by the profile are kept. A profile's catalog or schema_name, when set, replaces the base value.

docs.title: Using profiles at runtime
docs.text:
run picks a profile with -m (--mode). validate takes -m or --profile (the same thing). The name must match a key under profiles: exactly, including its case: -m prod does not find a profile named PROD.

-m defaults to DEV (upper case). When a config defines profiles: and the mode names none of them, the run stops with ConfigProfileError and lists the valid names. Name your profiles DEV and PROD so the default finds one. A config with no profiles: ignores the mode and uses the base spark_conf.

# Development: small cluster, few shuffle partitions (-m DEV is the default)
ubunye run -d pipelines -u fraud -p etl -t claims -m DEV

# Production: full cluster
ubunye run -d pipelines -u fraud -p etl -t claims -m PROD

validate checks the profile the same way run does, and also defaults to DEV. So a config whose profiles are dev and prod fails validate before it can fail a run:

Profile 'DEV' not found.

  Profile:   DEV
  Available: ['dev', 'prod']
  Hint: This config's profiles are: dev, prod. Names match exactly, case included; did you mean 'dev'? Pass -m dev. With no -m, run, validate, plan and doctor use DEV.

Validate with the profile you will run: ubunye validate ... -m PROD. plan and doctor check it the same way.

docs.title: Common Spark settings
docs.text:
These keys can be changed on any Spark session, so they work everywhere, Databricks included:

ENGINE:
  spark_conf:
    # Shuffle tuning
    spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: "200"
    spark.sql.adaptive.enabled: "true"
    spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled: "true"

    # Delta
    spark.databricks.delta.optimizeWrite.enabled: "true"
    spark.databricks.delta.autoCompact.enabled: "true"

Memory and Hive keys are fixed when Spark starts; see the next section.

Note

All values must be strings: Spark's configuration API accepts only strings. Use "true" not true, "200" not 200.

docs.title: Spark keys fixed at session start
docs.text:
Some Spark keys are read once, when the Spark session starts, and can never be changed after. Examples:

  • spark.jars, spark.jars.packages (JDBC drivers, Delta jars)
  • spark.sql.extensions, spark.sql.catalogImplementation, spark.sql.warehouse.dir (Delta, Hive)
  • spark.driver.*, spark.executor.memory, spark.executor.memoryOverhead, spark.executor.cores (memory and cores)
  • spark.master

Where such a key works depends on who starts the session:

Who starts Spark A fixed key in ENGINE.spark_conf Ubunye (ubunye run on the spark backend, no session running yet) applied The platform (Databricks, EMR, Dataproc, Glue, spark-submit, a notebook) refused with SparkSessionError, naming each key

Where the platform starts Spark, set these keys there instead: the cluster settings, a cluster policy, the job's conf, or spark-submit --conf / --jars. The engine refuses them rather than ignoring them, so a task never believes it enabled Delta or chose a cluster when it did not. A config may not set spark.master when the platform already chose one; see Deployment for that rule.

A setup where Ubunye starts Spark itself, with Hive:

ENGINE:
  spark_conf:
    spark.executor.memory: "8g"
    spark.driver.memory: "4g"
    spark.executor.memoryOverhead: "1g"
    spark.sql.catalogImplementation: "hive"
    spark.sql.warehouse.dir: "/user/hive/warehouse"

docs.title: ENGINE is optional
docs.text:
If you omit ENGINE entirely the engine uses Spark defaults:

MODEL: etl
VERSION: "1.0.0"
CONFIG:
  inputs:
    ...
  outputs:
    ...

docs.title: Expectations
docs.text:
CONFIG.expectations states what an output must look like: rules such as "this column is never empty". This page is for anyone who wants bad data to stop a run instead of landing in a table. The engine checks every output after the transform and before anything is written, on Spark and on pandas alike. It can also state what an input must look like: see Input contracts.

CONFIG:
  inputs:
    transactions: {format: s3, path: "data/transactions.csv", file_format: csv}
  outputs:
    clean_transactions: {format: s3, path: "out/clean", file_format: parquet}
    quarantined_transactions: {format: s3, path: "out/quarantine", file_format: parquet}

  expectations:
    clean_transactions:                      # the output being checked
      quarantine: quarantined_transactions   # where bad rows go
      max_quarantine_rate: 0.05              # more than 5% bad: stop the run
      rules:
        - not_null: transactionID            # severity fail is the default
        - unique: transactionID
        - between: {column: quantity, min: 1}
          severity: quarantine
        - one_of: {column: paymentMethod, values: [visa, mastercard, amex]}
          severity: quarantine
        - matches: {column: cardNumber, pattern: '^\d{4}$'}
          severity: warn
        - row_count: {min: 1}

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
Rule Passes when Per row? not_null: col the value is present yes between: {column, min, max} min <= value <= max (either bound may be left out) yes one_of: {column, values} the value is in the list yes matches: {column, pattern} the value matches the regular expression yes unique: col or [col, ...] no two rows share the value(s) no row_count: {min, max} the number of rows is in range no columns: {col: type, ...} each column exists with that type; see Input contracts no

A missing value passes every rule except not_null, as in SQL. When a value must be present and valid, write both rules. In a float column NaN counts as missing, like null, on every backend: pandas stores a missing float as NaN and cannot tell the two apart, so this is the one rule both backends can keep. not_null breaks on NaN; between and one_of let it pass.

Each rule is named after its column and kind (quantity_between), or give it a name:. Names must be unique within an output.

docs.title: What a broken rule does
docs.text:
severity Effect fail (default) The run stops. Nothing is written, for any output. quarantine The breaking rows move to the quarantine: output, with a _ubunye_failed_rules column naming every rule each row broke, and only those, in the order they are declared (quantity_between,paymentMethod_one_of), the same on every backend. The rest are written. Only per-row rules can quarantine. warn The rows stay; the breach is logged.

The quarantine output is always written, empty when no row broke a rule, so a downstream job can rely on it. The transform must not return it: the engine fills it.

max_quarantine_rate turns "a few bad rows" into "the source has changed": if a larger share of rows is quarantined, the run fails and nothing is written.

docs.title: When it fails
docs.text:
ExpectationError: Expectations failed, so nothing was written:
  clean_transactions: transactionID_not_null (not_null) broken by 1 of 891 rows
  Hint: Fix the data or the source, or change the rule's severity to quarantine
  or warn if this is expected.

The hint names only what the broken rules can do:

Broken rule The hint suggests a rule on rows (not_null, between, one_of, matches) quarantine or warn a reconcile a share (max_lost: "1%") or warn unique, row_count, columns (these cannot quarantine) warn

What you see:

  • ubunye run prints the message and exits with code 1, with no traceback: the data broke a rule, the engine did not crash.
  • An ExpectationError about the setup, such as narwhals not installed, still shows its traceback.
  • From Python, the error carries every rule's result, passed or not (err.results). A rule that breaks zero rows today and thousands tomorrow is the earliest warning that something upstream moved.

docs.title: Reconcile: nothing lost on the way
docs.text:
A join can drop rows and the run still succeeds. reconcile compares an output with an input the transform received, before anything is written:

  expectations:
    enriched:
      reconcile:
        - input: orders
          rows: {max_lost: 0}                    # every order reaches enriched
          sum: {column: amount, tolerance: 0.01} # and so does its amount
Key Meaning input an input in CONFIG.inputs rows: {max_lost, max_gained} how many rows may be lost, or gained (a join that fans out). A number of rows, or a share of the input: "1%". A bound left out is not checked. sum: {column, input_column, tolerance} the column's sum must match the input's. input_column is the input's name for it, if different. tolerance is a number, or a share of the input's sum ("0.1%"); default 0. severity fail (default) or warn

Each check is reported like a rule, named rows_from_orders and amount_sum_from_orders, with what was found:

ExpectationError: Expectations failed, so nothing was written:
  enriched: rows_from_orders (reconcile): 1000 rows read from orders, 900 reached
  enriched: 100 lost, 0 gained (at most 0 lost)
  • The input is counted before the transform runs. A pandas transform can change its input in place (drop(..., inplace=True), orders["amount"] = 0); counting afterwards would hide the very loss a reconcile is for.
  • Quarantined rows count as carried over. They were set aside with a reason, not lost. The output is counted before any row moves to its quarantine output.
  • Counting rows sees the net change only. A join that loses 5 rows and duplicates 5 others shows 0 lost and 0 gained. max_gained bounds a fan out, and a unique rule on the key catches the duplicates.
  • A filter that drops rows on purpose needs a share (max_lost: "30%"), or no row reconcile at all; max_lost: 0 would stop every run.
  • Sums are exact for integers (no wrap past 2**63) and decimals (no rounding through a float); the message prints them in full. A sum leaves out missing values (null, and NaN in a float column) on both sides, as the rules do. Two equal totals match, infinities included. Float sums can differ in the last digits when rows move, so give a float sum a small tolerance.
  • Two checks against one input need a name (the results are then <name>_rows and <name>_sum), for example a warning at 1% and a stop at 5%:
      reconcile:
        - {input: orders, name: early, rows: {max_lost: "1%"}, severity: warn}
        - {input: orders, name: stop, rows: {max_lost: "5%"}}
  • Cost: one pass over each reconciled input, for its row count and sums, however many outputs reconcile with it. On pandas that is in memory. On Spark it reads the input again, because inputs are not held in memory. On the output side the rows are counted in the same pass as the other rules, and sums in a pass of their own over the held output. On Spark an integer sum is taken as decimal(38,0); a decimal sum past 38 digits fails (ANSI) or comes back null.
  • In a notebook the check compares with what the transform got: the frames read() returned, or the ones you passed to transform(). They are counted when transform() starts.

docs.title: Input contracts
docs.text:
A source can change under you. When price arrived as text, pandas computed qty * price as "11.011.0" and the run succeeded. Name the input under expectations, and its rules run right after it is read, before the transform:

  expectations:
    orders:                                  # an input, not an output
      rules:
        - columns: {order_id: int64, qty: int64, price: float64}
          extra: allow                       # default; forbid refuses other columns
        - not_null: order_id

ExpectationError: An input broke its expectations, so the transform did not run
and nothing was written:
  orders: columns (columns): price: expected float64, found string

The columns rule:

  • Type names are the run record's, the same on Spark and pandas: int8, int16, int32, int64, float32, float64, bool, string, binary, date, timestamp, timestamp_ntz, decimal(p,s), list<...>, map<...,...>, struct<name:type,...>. Spark's double is float64, bigint is int64; ubunye validate says so if you write the other name. Nested names are checked part by part (list<banana> is refused). A frame can also report uint8 to uint64, null (a column of nulls only), mixed (a pandas column of mixed Python values), time64[us] and the like; those can be declared too.
  • A timestamp is named by what it is: with a zone timestamp, without one timestamp_ntz, on pandas as on Spark 3.4 and later, at every depth. So a source that switches between naive and UTC is caught. This differs from the run record, which writes every pandas timestamp as an instant and names it timestamp; the record (and its schema hash) is unchanged.
  • CSV: with inferSchema, a whole number column is int32 when every value fits, else int64, on both engines. A column that may grow, declare as [int32, int64]. Without inferSchema every column is string.
  • Types match exactly. int32 is not int64: a narrower or wider type is a changed source, and it changes what the task writes. To accept more than one, list them: qty: [int32, int64].
  • Nulls are not part of the type. A column of int64 with gaps is int64.
  • A column that is missing, has another type or (with extra: forbid) is not declared is named, each on its own. The result's detail holds them all.
  • It reads the schema only; no row is read. If a columns rule with severity fail breaks, the other rules on that frame are not run.

Any rule can go on an input: not_null, between, unique, and so on. They cost one pass over the input; on Spark that reads the source again, since inputs are not held in memory. The results are in the run record with side: input.

An input cannot quarantine rows (yet), and cannot have a reconcile (that goes on the output). A name that is both an input and an output cannot have expectations: rename one. columns works on an output too, to pin what the task writes.

docs.title: Checked when the config loads
docs.text:
ubunye validate refuses:

  • an expectation that names no input or output, or a name that is both;
  • an input with a quarantine or a reconcile;
  • a columns type that is not one of the names above;
  • a quarantine output that does not exist, or is the output itself;
  • two outputs sharing one quarantine output;
  • a rule with no kind, or two kinds;
  • a quarantine rule with no quarantine: output;
  • a matches pattern that is not a valid regular expression;
  • a reconcile that names no real input, checks nothing, or has a bound that is not a number or a percentage.

Why inputs are read again on Spark instead of held: ADR 009.

docs.title: Inputs & Outputs
docs.text:
This page is for anyone writing a task's config.yaml. It shows how to say what a task reads (CONFIG.inputs) and writes (CONFIG.outputs), and it is the home page for write modes: how an output treats data already in its target.

Each entry has a name you choose and a block that names a connector with format:. A connector is the built-in code that reads or writes one kind of storage (see Connectors).

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
CONFIG:
  inputs:
    <logical_name>:
      format: <format_type>
      # format-specific fields...

  outputs:
    <logical_name>:
      format: <format_type>
      mode: append | overwrite | errorifexists | ignore | merge | overwrite_partitions
      # format-specific fields...
  • At least one input and one output are required.
  • Logical names are arbitrary; they are passed to your transform as dict keys.

docs.title: Supported formats
docs.text:
format Direction Connector hive read / write Hive Metastore tables via Spark jdbc read / write Any JDBC-compatible database unity read / write Databricks Unity Catalog s3 read / write Any path: S3, ADLS, GCS, HDFS, local (Parquet, CSV, JSON...) delta read / write Delta Lake tables by path or name binary read Raw binary files rest_api read / write HTTP REST endpoints

format may also name any connector installed as a plugin. ubunye plugins lists what is installed; an unknown format is refused with that list.

docs.title: Common fields
docs.text:
These fields apply to most formats:

Field Type Description format string Required. One of the format types above. options dict Spark reader/writer options (e.g. header, delimiter). mode see Write modes Write mode (outputs only). merge_keys list or string Key columns for mode: merge (outputs only). replace_where string Delta predicate for mode: overwrite_partitions (outputs only). On a Delta or JDBC append, the rows of the run's batch: each run replaces them, so a rerun corrects the batch instead of adding it twice.

docs.title: hive
docs.text:
format: hive
db_name: raw             # required if sql is not set
tbl_name: claims         # required if sql is not set
sql: "SELECT ..."        # alternative to db_name + tbl_name (inputs only)

As an output, hive needs db_name + tbl_name.

docs.title: jdbc
docs.text:
format: jdbc
url: "jdbc:postgresql://host:5432/db"   # required
table: public.claims                    # required unless sql is set (always for outputs)
sql: "SELECT * FROM public.claims"      # alternative to table (inputs only)
user: "{{ env.DB_USER }}"
password: "secret://env/DB_PASS"        # see Secrets
options:
  fetchsize: "10000"
  partitionColumn: id
  lowerBound: "1"
  upperBound: "1000000"
  numPartitions: "8"

docs.title: unity
docs.text:
format: unity
table: main.fraud.claims       # three-part Unity Catalog name
# or:
sql: "SELECT ..."              # inputs only
# outputs also take catalog + schema + tbl_name instead of table

docs.title: s3 / delta
docs.text:
# S3: path-based; file_format picks the file type (default parquet)
format: s3
path: s3://my-bucket/data/claims/
file_format: csv
options:
  header: "true"

# Delta: by path
format: delta
path: s3://my-bucket/delta/claims
mode: overwrite

# Delta: by table name
format: delta
table: main.fraud.claims
mode: append

docs.title: binary
docs.text:
format: binary
path: /mnt/raw/documents/
path_glob_filter: "*.pdf"   # optional
recursive: true             # optional

docs.title: rest_api
docs.text:
format: rest_api
url: "https://api.example.com/v1/records"
auth:
  type: bearer
  token: "secret://env/API_TOKEN"
pagination:
  type: cursor
  cursor_response_key: next_cursor
headers:
  Accept: application/json

See REST API Connector for the full REST API reference.

docs.title: Connector keys are checked
docs.text:
An input or output block carries whatever keys its connector reads, and the whole block is passed to the connector. This is how the REST API connector receives auth, pagination and headers without schema changes.

Each built-in connector declares the keys it reads, so any other key is refused by ubunye validate, with the closest real one:

outputs.clean: 'paht' is not a setting of 's3'; did you mean 'path'?

Each connector also says what it requires (s3 needs path, jdbc needs url, and so on), checked the same way. Options for Spark itself go under options. A third-party connector that declares no keys accepts any key.

docs.title: Write modes
docs.text:
The write mode (mode: on an output) says what happens to data already in the target. The first four are Spark's own save modes. merge and overwrite_partitions are added by Ubunye: Spark has no save mode for either.

Mode Behaviour append Insert new rows without touching existing data overwrite Drop existing data and replace entirely errorifexists Fail if the target already exists (alias: error) ignore Do nothing if the target already exists merge Delta MERGE (upsert) on merge_keys. Creates the target on first run overwrite_partitions Replace only the partitions present in the DataFrame; leave the rest of the table intact

Not every connector can honour every mode. Asking for one it cannot do raises SinkWriteError before any rows are written. It is never silently downgraded.

ubunye plan catches this before a run. ubunye validate does not check write modes against the connector, so a jdbc output with mode: merge passes validate and fails plan:

  problem: outputs.predictions: Write mode 'merge' is not supported by the 'jdbc' connector.
Connector Supported modes Default delta all six append unity all six append s3 all six (merge and replace_where need file_format: delta) append hive all six (merge needs file_format: delta) append jdbc native four only: no merge / overwrite_partitions append rest_api append (a REST sink has no table to merge into) append binary none: read-only, rejected in CONFIG.outputs none

Every writer defaults to append: the mode that cannot destroy data you did not mean to destroy. Set mode explicitly when you want anything else.

docs.title: merge
docs.text:
Requires merge_keys: the columns that identify a row. Matched rows are updated, unmatched rows inserted. On the first run the target does not exist yet, so the engine creates it with a plain overwrite instead of a MERGE.

    customer_features:
      format: s3
      path: s3://my-bucket/delta/features/
      file_format: delta
      mode: merge
      merge_keys: [id, dt]        # or options.merge_keys: "id,dt"

docs.title: overwrite_partitions
docs.text:
The backfill mode: re-run one day without wiping the rest of the table. Three ways to say which partitions to replace:

    # 1. Dynamic: replace whatever partitions the DataFrame contains
    daily_sales:
      format: s3
      path: s3://my-bucket/sales/
      mode: overwrite_partitions
      partitionBy: [dt]

    # 2. Predicate: replace exactly what the expression matches (Delta only)
    daily_sales:
      format: delta
      path: s3://my-bucket/delta/sales/
      mode: overwrite_partitions
      replace_where: "dt = '{{ dt }}'"

    # 3. A table: INSERT OVERWRITE of just the incoming partitions
    daily_sales:
      format: hive
      db_name: clean
      tbl_name: sales
      mode: overwrite_partitions
      partitionBy: [dt]

Without partitionBy or replace_where, dynamic overwrite silently degrades to a full-table wipe, so the engine refuses it instead. ubunye plan reports this before a run (validate does not):

  problem: outputs.daily_sales: Write mode 'overwrite_partitions' requires 'partitionBy' or 'replace_where'.

The partitionBy form also runs on the pandas backend; replace_where needs Delta, so Spark.

docs.title: replace_where on an append
docs.text:
On a Delta or JDBC append, replace_where names the rows of the run's batch, so a rerun replaces the batch instead of adding it twice. Each connector page owns the details: Delta appends and JDBC appends.

Under the hood

Checking a mode against what a connector supports is done once, the same way on every backend. Running merge and overwrite_partitions is Spark work (MERGE INTO, dynamic partition overwrite), done by the Spark backend.

For overwrite_partitions the engine picks the mechanism the target actually supports: Delta's own write option for Delta, INSERT OVERWRITE for an existing table, and Spark's partitionOverwriteMode=DYNAMIC for a path. Each route is covered by an integration test against a real Spark session.

docs.title: Jinja Templating
docs.text: Ubunye fills in Jinja2 expressions ({{ ... }}) in your config.yaml before the config is checked against its schema. This lets you inject environment variables, CLI arguments, dates, and computed values without changing the schema.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. load_config(path, variables) (in ubunye.config) parses the YAML.
  2. The resolver renders every string value through Jinja2.
  3. The result is checked against the config schema (see Validation).

Jinja expressions can appear in any string value: paths, table names, SQL, header values, tokens, etc. Jinja renders values, not structure: keys and {% if %} blocks around keys are not templated.

The variables a template can use:

Variable Where it comes from dt -dt / --data-timestamp (or --var dt=...) dtf -dtf / --data-timestamp-format mode -m / --mode (default DEV) task_dir the task's own folder, always set env the environment: {{ env.NAME }} any other name --var name=value

A flag that was not given leaves its variable undefined, so | default(...) works for it.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
CONFIG:
  inputs:
    source:
      format: jdbc
      url: "{{ env.JDBC_URL }}"
      user: "{{ env.DB_USER }}"
      password: "secret://env/DB_PASS"   # a secret: not templated, see Secrets

env is a dict-like object populated from os.environ at load time. Use it for settings, not for passwords: a templated value becomes part of the rendered config, while a secret:// reference is read only when the connector runs.

docs.title: The task's own folder: {{ task_dir }}
docs.text:
Every config gets {{ task_dir }}, the absolute path of the folder that holds it. Use it for files that live next to the task:

CONFIG:
  inputs:
    people:
      format: s3
      path: "{{ task_dir }}/data/people.csv"

A relative path is resolved by the engine's own filesystem: pandas reads it from the folder you ran the command in, and Spark from where its JVM started (on a cluster, its default filesystem). {{ task_dir }} means the same thing everywhere, so prefer it for anything next to the task.

docs.title: CLI-injected variables
docs.text:
Pass arbitrary key-value pairs with --var (repeatable):

ubunye run -d pipelines -u fraud -p etl -t claims \
    --var dt=2024-06-01 \
    --var env_name=prod

Reference them directly:

CONFIG:
  inputs:
    events:
      format: hive
      tbl_name: "events_{{ dt | replace('-', '_') }}"

--var works on every command that renders a config: run, validate, plan, config and test run. From Python, pass the same thing as variables=:

ubunye.run_task("pipelines/fraud/etl/claims", variables={"env_name": "prod"}, dt="2024-06-01")

A few rules, so a typo is caught instead of rendering the wrong thing:

  • A name must be a valid template name: letters, digits and underscores, not starting with a digit (env_name, not env-name).
  • env is reserved for the environment ({{ env.NAME }}), task_dir for the task's folder, and mode is set with -m.
  • --var dt=... works like -dt; giving both with different values is refused.
  • A value arrives as text: --var min_age=30 gives the string '30', and a rendered value stays text even with | int. Convert it in your Python code (int(params["min_age"])).
  • The variables a run used are kept in its run record (--lineage).

docs.title: Default filter
docs.text:
Use | default(value) to provide a fallback when a variable is not set:

db_name: "{{ env.HIVE_DB | default('raw') }}"
tbl_name: "events_{{ dt | default('2024-01-01') | replace('-', '_') }}"

docs.title: String filters
docs.text:
Any Jinja2 filter works:

path: "s3://{{ env.BUCKET | lower }}/{{ mode | lower }}/{{ dt | replace('-', '/') }}/"

Common filters:

Filter Description default(val) Fallback if variable is undefined upper Convert to UPPERCASE lower Convert to lowercase replace(a, b) Replace substring a with b trim Strip leading/trailing whitespace int, float Number conversion inside an expression ({{ (n \| int) + 1 }}); the rendered value is still text

docs.title: Conditional expressions
docs.text: mode: "{{ 'overwrite' if env.RESET | default('false') == 'true' else 'append' }}"

docs.title: Multi-line SQL
docs.text:
sql: >-
  SELECT id, amount, event_date
  FROM raw.claims
  WHERE event_date = '{{ dt | default('2024-01-01') }}'
    AND status = '{{ env.CLAIM_STATUS | default('OPEN') }}'

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
Never commit secrets

Never hardcode passwords, tokens, or keys in config.yaml, and do not template them in with {{ env.SECRET }} either. Use a secret:// reference (secret://env/DB_PASS reads the same environment variable). See Secrets.

Validate after templating

ubunye validate renders the template and validates the result. Run it in CI to catch missing variables early: 

ubunye validate -d pipelines -u fraud -p etl -t claims \
    --var dt=$(date +%F)

A templated value is always a string

The YAML is parsed first, then each string is rendered. The result is not parsed again, so "{{ n }}" gives the string "8", never the number 8, and a rendered "true" stays text. Write a value that must be a number or a list without a template.

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
MODEL: etl
VERSION: "1.0.0"

ENGINE:
  spark_conf:
    spark.sql.warehouse.dir: "{{ env.HIVE_WAREHOUSE | default('/user/hive/warehouse') }}"

CONFIG:
  inputs:
    raw_events:
      format: hive
      db_name: "{{ env.RAW_DB | default('raw') }}"
      tbl_name: "events_{{ dt | default('2024-01-01') | replace('-', '_') }}"

  transform: {}

  outputs:
    clean_events:
      format: delta
      path: "s3://{{ env.BUCKET }}/clean/events/dt={{ dt | default('2024-01-01') }}/"
      mode: "{{ 'overwrite' if full_refresh | default('false') == 'true' else 'append' }}"

docs.title: Orchestration
docs.text: The ORCHESTRATION section says when and how a scheduler should run your task: a schedule, retries, an owner. This page is for anyone handing a task to Airflow or a Databricks job. It does not affect how ubunye run executes the task: it is used only by ubunye export airflow and ubunye export databricks.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
ORCHESTRATION:
  type: airflow           # required. Implemented today: airflow, databricks
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"  # cron expression
  retries: 3
  owner: data-engineering
  tags:
    - fraud
    - etl
  databricks:             # Databricks job cluster settings
    spark_version: "17.3.x-scala2.13"
    node_type_id: "Standard_DS3_v2"
    num_workers: 4

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
Field Type Default Description type airflow or databricks required Target platform. prefect and dagster are accepted by the schema but have no exporter yet schedule string null Cron expression for the DAG/workflow schedule retries int 2 Number of automatic retries on failure (Airflow) owner string null Team or person responsible (shown in Airflow UI) tags list of strings [] Labels for filtering in the orchestration UI databricks dict null Databricks job settings, read by export databricks

No other key is allowed: a typo under ORCHESTRATION is refused by ubunye validate.

When a field is left out, the Airflow DAG uses its own default: schedule @daily, owner ubunye, tags [ubunye]. With no ORCHESTRATION block at all, export airflow still works and uses 1 retry.

The keys export databricks reads from databricks: are spark_version (default 17.3.x-scala2.13, Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS), node_type_id (default i3.xlarge), num_workers (default 2), spark_conf, aws_attributes, job_name, wheel_dbfs_path (default dbfs:/libs/ubunye_engine-<installed version>-py3-none-any.whl) and timezone_id (default UTC). Other keys there are ignored.

docs.title: Which profile an export uses
docs.text:
Each export writes a profile name into the command it generates. The defaults differ, in name and in case:

Command Flag Default ubunye run -m DEV ubunye export airflow --profile prod (lower case) ubunye export databricks --profile prod (lower case) ubunye export spark-pipeline -m PROD (upper case)

A profile name must match a key under ENGINE.profiles exactly, case included (see Engine & Profiles). So name your profiles DEV and PROD, and always pass the profile to export airflow and export databricks (--profile PROD) rather than relying on its lower-case default. A config with no profiles: ignores the name.

docs.title: Airflow export
docs.text:
ubunye export airflow \
    -c pipelines/fraud/etl/claims/config.yaml \
    -o dags/claims_etl.py \
    --profile PROD

The generated DAG contains a single BashOperator that runs:

ubunye run -d <pipelines folder> -u fraud -p etl -t claims -m PROD -dt {{ ds }}

--profile on export becomes -m in the command (ubunye run has no --profile). {{ ds }} is Airflow's logical date, so each scheduled run gets its own dt. The pipelines folder is the absolute path of the one the config sits in; pass --usecase-dir when Airflow sees it at another path. --backend and --lineage on export airflow are added to the command too.

Schedule, retries, owner, and tags are read from ORCHESTRATION.

docs.title: Databricks export
docs.text:
ubunye export databricks \
    -c pipelines/fraud/etl/claims/config.yaml \
    -o jobs/claims_etl.json \
    --profile PROD

The generated JSON can be submitted with the Databricks CLI:

databricks jobs create --json-file jobs/claims_etl.json
databricks jobs run-now --job-id <ID>

Cluster settings from ORCHESTRATION.databricks are embedded in the job JSON. The job runs the CLI with -d -u -p -t and -m <profile>. ORCHESTRATION.schedule becomes the job's quartz_cron_expression, so write it in Quartz syntax ("0 30 1 * * ?"), not five-field cron.

docs.title: Example: full Airflow config
docs.text:
MODEL: etl
VERSION: "1.0.0"

CONFIG:
  inputs:
    raw:
      format: hive
      db_name: raw
      tbl_name: claims
  transform: {}
  outputs:
    clean:
      format: delta
      path: s3://datalake/clean/claims
      mode: overwrite

ORCHESTRATION:
  type: airflow
  schedule: "30 1 * * *"    # 01:30 UTC daily
  retries: 2
  owner: fraud-team
  tags:
    - fraud
    - daily
    - etl

docs.title: Spark Declarative Pipelines (Spark 4.1+)
docs.text:
Spark 4.1 ships its own pipeline format. ubunye export spark-pipeline writes a task in it, so the task can run where only Spark is installed, or be handed to a team that standardised on it:

ubunye export spark-pipeline -c pipelines/shop/orders/clean/config.yaml -o clean-pipeline -dt 2026-07-13 -m PROD
cd clean-pipeline && spark-pipelines run      # needs pyspark[connect] 4.1+

It writes spark-pipeline.yml, a transformations/ module and a copy of the task in task/. Every input becomes a temporary view that reads what the config says, the task's transform() runs unchanged, and every output becomes a materialized view of the same name. The config is rendered at export time (-dt, --var, the environment).

What does not carry over is reported when you export: a merge (or any non-overwrite) mode becomes a full recompute, outputs go to the pipeline's catalog rather than their paths, and CONFIG.expectations are not applied. A task that uses secret:// references is refused (the pipeline would hold them in plain text). Supported readers: s3 and delta paths, binary files, hive and unity tables.

The run-anywhere example exported this way and run by spark-pipelines on Spark 4.2 wrote the same data, row hash for row hash, as Glue, Dataproc, Kubernetes and Azure Container Apps.

docs.title: Config Reference: Overview
docs.text: Every Ubunye task is driven by a single config.yaml file. This page is for anyone writing one: it explains the top-level keys, which command catches which mistake, and links to a page for each section.

docs.title: Top-level keys
docs.text:
MODEL: etl          # optional: job type, etl | ml (defaults to etl)
VERSION: "1.0.0"    # optional: semver string (defaults to "0.0.0-dev")

ENGINE: ...         # optional: Spark settings and per-profile overrides
CONFIG: ...         # required: inputs, transform, outputs, expectations
ORCHESTRATION: ...  # optional: metadata for `ubunye export`
Key Type Required Default Description MODEL etl | ml No etl Declares the job type VERSION semver string No "0.0.0-dev" Pipeline version (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, optional -prerelease suffix) ENGINE EngineConfig No none Spark conf, catalog and schema, per-profile overrides CONFIG TaskConfig Yes none Inputs, transform, outputs, expectations ORCHESTRATION OrchestrationConfig No none Export metadata for orchestrators

CONFIG holds five keys: inputs and outputs (both required, at least one entry each), transform (optional), expectations (optional) and requires (optional: upstream tasks that must have succeeded for this batch first, see Job health and upstream checks).

Set MODEL and VERSION explicitly in production pipelines where job type or version is load-bearing (lineage records, model registry, orchestrator metadata). For quick local iteration the defaults are fine.

docs.title: Jinja templating
docs.text:
Config values are filled in by Jinja2 ({{ ... }} placeholders) before the config is checked. You can use environment variables, CLI-injected variables, and filters in any value in the YAML:

CONFIG:
  inputs:
    events:
      format: hive
      db_name: "{{ env.HIVE_DB | default('raw') }}"
      tbl_name: events_{{ dt | default('2024-01-01') | replace('-', '_') }}

See Jinja Templating for all supported syntax.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Ubunye checks the rendered YAML against a strict schema, written with Pydantic (a Python library that checks data against declared fields and types). Unknown fields are rejected with typo suggestions; undefined Jinja variables fail immediately. Run validation before deploying:

ubunye validate -d pipelines -u fraud -p etl -t claims

docs.title: Which command catches what
docs.text:
Three commands check a task before it runs. Each catches different mistakes, so run validate in CI, and plan and doctor on the machine that will run the task.

Mistake validate plan doctor Unknown or misspelt key, wrong type (schema) yes yes yes A connector key that connector does not read (paht: on s3) yes yes yes A template variable that is not set yes yes yes, and names each missing environment variable A secret:// provider name that does not exist yes yes yes A secret provider whose package is not installed no no yes A write mode the connector cannot do (jdbc with mode: merge) no yes no overwrite_partitions with no partitionBy or replace_where no yes no A local input path with nothing there no yes no A connector the backend cannot serve (jdbc on pandas) with --backend with --backend no A profile name that is not under ENGINE.profiles (default DEV) yes no no Missing packages: Java, Delta, a backend, a plugin no no yes

validate and run check the profile name the same way, and both default to -m DEV. See Engine & Profiles.

docs.title: Strict field checking
docs.text:
Every config section rejects unknown keys. A typo like ENGNE triggers a ConfigFieldError with a "Did you mean?" suggestion.

Input and output blocks are checked by their connector. Each built-in connector declares the keys it reads, so a typo such as paht: on an s3 input is refused with the closest real key. A third-party connector that declares no keys accepts any key. See Writing a Plugin.

docs.title: Strict template variables
docs.text: A {{ var }} that is not given as a CLI variable or environment variable stops the config from loading, instead of silently becoming an empty string. (Jinja calls this mode StrictUndefined.) Use | default(...) for optional values.

docs.title: Reference pages
docs.text: Section Description Inputs & Outputs CONFIG.inputs and CONFIG.outputs: connector format and options Expectations CONFIG.expectations: checks on inputs and outputs Upstream checks CONFIG.requires: do not start until an upstream task succeeded for this batch Engine & Profiles ENGINE: Spark conf, catalog, schema and profiles Transform CONFIG.transform: the task class and its params Orchestration ORCHESTRATION: schedule, retries, tags, platform-specific settings Jinja Templating Variable interpolation, filters, and best practices Secrets secret:// references to a secret store

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
This page shows how to give a task a password, token or key without writing it in config.yaml. A config names a secret; it never holds one. Every password, token and key example in these docs uses a secret:// reference.

CONFIG:
  inputs:
    orders:
      format: jdbc
      url: "jdbc:postgresql://db.internal:5432/shop"
      table: public.orders
      user: reporting
      password: "secret://aws-sm/prod/shop-db#password"

The value is fetched only at the moment a connector reads or writes, and only into the copy of the config that connector receives. Everywhere else the reference stays a reference: the config hash, ubunye plan, ubunye config, run records and logs. So a secret cannot leak through a printed plan or a run record, and rotating a password does not change the config hash.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
Reference Where the secret lives Install secret://env/NAME an environment variable nothing secret://file/PATH a file, e.g. a mounted secret: secret://file//run/secrets/db nothing secret://databricks/SCOPE/KEY a Databricks secret scope (dbutils on a cluster, the Databricks SDK elsewhere) ubunye-engine[databricks] off-cluster secret://aws-sm/NAME AWS Secrets Manager ubunye-engine[aws] secret://gcp-sm/PROJECT/SECRET[/VERSION] Google Secret Manager (latest version by default) ubunye-engine[gcp] secret://azure-kv/VAULT/SECRET[/VERSION] Azure Key Vault ubunye-engine[azure]

For a JSON secret, #field picks one field: secret://aws-sm/prod/shop-db#password.

The cloud providers log in the way each cloud's own SDK does (a profile, a role, workload identity, a managed identity, environment variables). The engine never takes a credential itself.

ENGINE.spark_conf (and a profile's spark_conf) takes references too, for a storage key or a token Spark needs:

ENGINE:
  spark_conf:
    fs.azure.account.key.myacct.dfs.core.windows.net: "secret://azure-kv/vault/acct-key"

They are fetched when a Spark backend starts, and handed only to Spark. A backend without Spark (pandas) does not fetch them.

The whole value must be the reference; a secret is not spliced into a longer string. Put a password in its own field (password:), not inside a URL.

References are read in input and output blocks (any key, at any depth, such as password: or auth.token:) and in ENGINE.spark_conf (above). For cloud storage keys, letting the platform log in (an instance role, workload identity) is still simpler than setting keys in spark_conf.

docs.title: Checked before a run, fetched during it
docs.text:
ubunye validate refuses a reference to a provider that is not installed, with the closest name (secret://aws-smm/...: did you mean aws-sm?). Nothing is fetched at validation.

ubunye doctor with a task lists each provider the task uses and whether its package is installed:

ubunye doctor -d pipelines -u fraud -p etl -t claims

[FAIL] task claims: secret provider aws-sm: needs boto3
       fix: pip install boto3
[OK] task claims: secret provider env: installed (the secret itself is read at run time)

It does not read the secrets: the login they need may only exist where the task really runs. -t needs -d, -u and -p with it.

A secret that cannot be read stops the run with the reference and the provider's error, never the value:

SecretError: Could not read secret secret://aws-sm/prod/shop-db: ClientError: AccessDeniedException ...
  Provider:  aws-sm
  Reference: prod/shop-db
  Hint: pip install 'ubunye-engine[aws]'; the login is the AWS SDK's (profile, role, env).

docs.title: What is recorded
docs.text:
A resolved secret never reaches the run record, the lineage record, an OpenLineage event or ubunye plan output: only the secret:// reference is kept. A test puts a marker in every place a secret can go and searches everything a run leaves behind.

--var is not for secrets: variables are recorded, because the record says what the run was given. Pass a secret through secret:// instead. As a safety net, Ubunye masks secrets it can recognise in everything it records, sends or prints:

  • a --var whose name says it is a secret (token, db_password, api_key, client_secret and the like) is recorded as ***;
  • a password written into a URL (jdbc:postgresql://user:password@host/db, ;password=..., ?token=...);
  • a failed run's error message.

docs.title: A failed run's error
docs.text: A failed run's record keeps why it failed: the error's type and message. That message is masked before it is recorded, sent to OpenLineage or printed, and cut to its first 4,096 characters. Details are in "Under the hood" below.

docs.title: The config hash
docs.text:
The config hash is taken over the config as rendered, so a templated secret is part of it. The hash cannot be reversed for a long token, but a short password could be guessed against it: another reason to use secret://, which is hashed as the reference.

Under the hood: how masking works

Variables. A variable whose name says it is a secret is recorded as ***, and its value is masked wherever it was templated in (a JDBC URL, a REST query). Names about a secret rather than holding one (max_token, auth_mode, secret_scope) are kept.

URLs. A password written into a URL is masked in every recorded location. Lineage tools have leaked JDBC passwords this way before.

A failed run's error. A failed run's record keeps why it failed (the error's type and message), and OpenLineage sends it, lineage trace prints it and ubunye prove shows it. An error message can quote anything, so it is masked before any of them sees it, by one function (the same one the REST connector uses for its logs and errors). It masks:

  • every secret the run knows of: secret-looking --var values, every value a secret:// reference resolved to in this process, literal secrets in the config (under a secret-looking key, an Authorization header, an auth block), and the values of environment variables with secret-looking names (a config can template one in with {{ env.DB_PASSWORD }});
  • each of them URL-encoded, in base64 (also inside user:password, as Basic auth codes it), and broken across a line or a space;
  • the usual shapes of a secret, known or not: scheme://user:password@host, a secret-named parameter in a URL or a JDBC string (?api_key=, &sig=, ?key=, ;password=), and the value of an Authorization, Proxy-Authorization or X-Api-Key header.

The error is kept to its first 4,096 characters, then ... (N more characters): a 5 MB message made a 5 MB record. It is masked before it is cut, so the cut cannot leave half a secret showing.

Limits: a value shorter than 4 characters is not masked word for word (it would shred the text), so a 3 character password in a message stays. An environment variable with a secret-looking name is masked even when it is not one (a path in PASSWORD_STORE_DIR). The Python API still raises the original exception to your code: only what is recorded, sent or printed is masked.

docs.title: Writing a provider
docs.text:
A provider is a class with get(ref) -> str, registered under the ubunye.secrets entry point group; its entry point name is the provider name in secret://NAME/.... Declare REQUIRES_MODULES = (("module", "pip-package"), ...) so ubunye doctor can say what is missing.

[project.entry-points."ubunye.secrets"]
vault = "my_package.secrets:HashiCorpVault"

A notebook that calls a connector itself resolves the config first: from ubunye.core.secrets import resolve, then reader.read(resolve(cfg), backend).

docs.title: Transform
docs.text: CONFIG.transform is the part of config.yaml that sits between reading inputs and writing outputs. This page is for anyone writing a task: it shows where your code goes, how to give it settings, and how to train a model inside a task.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
CONFIG:
  transform: {}

A task folder always runs the Task subclass in its transformations.py. That holds for ubunye run, run_task, run_pipeline and notebooks. Leave transform as {}, or give it params (below).

docs.title: The Task class
docs.text:
transform: {}

transformations.py:

from ubunye.core.interfaces import Task

class MyTask(Task):
    def transform(self, sources: dict) -> dict:
        df = sources["input_name"]
        cleaned = df.filter("value IS NOT NULL").dropDuplicates(["id"])
        return {"output_name": cleaned}

The logical names in sources and the returned dict must match the keys declared under CONFIG.inputs and CONFIG.outputs.

docs.title: Settings for your Task: params
docs.text:
Put your own settings under transform.params and read them from self.config, the whole config as a dict. Jinja variables work here too, so a setting can come from --var or the data timestamp.

A value that comes from --var arrives as text: --var min_amount=30 gives the string '30', not the number 30. Convert it in your code (int(params["min_amount"])). A number written straight into the YAML (min_amount: 10) stays a number.

CONFIG:
  transform:
    params:
      only_states: ["SP", "RJ"]
      min_amount: 10

class MyTask(Task):
    def transform(self, sources: dict) -> dict:
        params = self.config["CONFIG"]["transform"]["params"]
        orders = sources["orders"]
        orders = orders[orders["customer_state"].isin(params["only_states"])]
        return {"orders_out": orders}

params is the only key besides type (see the note at the end of this page); any other key under transform is refused by ubunye validate with the list of valid fields.

docs.title: Training a model
docs.text:
Train and register the model in transformations.py. A model registered inside a run records that run's id (lineage_run_id), so ubunye lineage show finds the data it was trained on. See Model Contract and Model Registry.

# transformations.py
from ubunye.core.interfaces import Task
from ubunye.models.registry import ModelRegistry, ModelStage

from model import FraudRiskModel  # model.py in the task folder


class TrainFraudModel(Task):
    def transform(self, sources: dict) -> dict:
        features = sources["features"]
        model = FraudRiskModel()
        metrics = model.train(features)

        registry = ModelRegistry(".ubunye/model_store")
        mv = registry.register("fraud_detection", "FraudRiskModel", None, model, metrics)
        registry.promote(
            "fraud_detection",
            "FraudRiskModel",
            mv.version,
            ModelStage.STAGING,
            gates={"min_auc": 0.85, "min_f1": 0.80},
        )
        # Write what the model was trained on, so the run record hashes it.
        return {"training_set": features}

A gate that fails raises PromotionBlockedError, which fails the run. The version stays registered in development. Catch the error if the run should still succeed.

To have the run record name the model, its version, stage and gate result, train with ModelTransform from transformations.py instead (see Model Registry: the run record names the model). There, registry.on_blocked: record keeps a blocked run going.

docs.title: ModelTransform from Python
docs.text:
ModelTransform trains or scores a model from a settings dict. Call it yourself, for example from a notebook or from your Task. It takes the settings flat or under params:. The third argument is the run's backend; pass None when you call it outside a run.

from ubunye.plugins.transforms.model_transform import ModelTransform

ModelTransform().apply(
    {"features": df},
    {
        "action": "train",
        "model_class": "model.FraudRiskModel",
        "registry": {"store": ".ubunye/model_store", "use_case": "fraud_detection"},
    },
    None,  # the backend: None when you call it yourself
)
Field Type Default Description action train | predict required Whether to train or score model_class string required module.ClassName of the UbunyeModel subclass model_dir string null Folder holding the model file; defaults to sys.path model_path string null Path to a saved artifact (predict without a registry) input_name string null Key in inputs to train or score on registry registry settings null Model registry settings

docs.title: Registry settings
docs.text: Field Type Default Description store string required Path or URI of the model store backend string null Where the registry keeps models. Not set: the UBUNYE_REGISTRY_BACKEND environment variable, else filesystem. See Model Registry use_case string "default" Logical grouping for the model version string null Explicit version; generated for you if null auto_version bool true Deprecated: it never had an effect, warns, and goes in 1.0. A version is generated whenever version is null. Remove the key promote_to development | staging | production null Promote after registration use_stage development | staging | production "production" Stage to load from (predict only) promotion_gates dict null Metric thresholds that must pass before promotion on_blocked raise | record raise What a promotion the gates block does. raise fails the run. record keeps the run going; the version stays in development and the run record says which gate blocked it stamp_columns bool false Predict only: add model_version and model_stage columns to the scored rows check_features bool null Predict only: compare the frame with the model's declared features. Not set: warn and call the model. true: refuse the frame before the model is called. false: no check

docs.title: Transform plugins
docs.text: Classes registered under the ubunye.transforms entry point run when you build an Engine yourself and pass it a config; a task folder does not run them. See Writing a Plugin.

docs.title: type: in a task's config.yaml is not run
docs.text:
A type: line only gets a warning

A task's config may name a transform plugin (transform: {type: model}, or your own). In 0.9.0 the type is still not run: transformations.py runs instead. ubunye validate, ubunye plan and ubunye run print a warning about it, and the run carries on. Move the logic into transformations.py (see Training a model) and remove the type line. type: noop is accepted and does nothing.

docs.title: Hive Connector
docs.text: Reads and writes tables in a Hive metastore (the catalog that maps a database.table name to files) through Spark SQL. Use it on a Spark cluster that has a Hive metastore configured (spark.sql.catalogImplementation: hive).

docs.title: Read
docs.text:
CONFIG:
  inputs:
    raw_claims:
      format: hive
      db_name: raw          # database name
      tbl_name: claims      # table name

Alternatively, supply a sql query:

    raw_claims:
      format: hive
      sql: >-
        SELECT id, amount, event_date
        FROM raw.claims
        WHERE event_date >= '{{ dt }}'

Requirement

For a read, either (db_name + tbl_name) or sql is required. For a write, db_name + tbl_name is required. Anything else is a validation error.

docs.title: Write
docs.text:
CONFIG:
  outputs:
    clean_claims:
      format: hive
      db_name: clean
      tbl_name: claims
      mode: overwrite
      file_format: parquet
      options:
        compression: snappy

docs.title: Fields
docs.text: Field Type Required Description format "hive" Yes Selects this connector db_name string Conditional Database name (required unless a read sets sql) tbl_name string Conditional Table name (required unless a read sets sql) sql string Conditional SQL query, reads only (alternative to db_name + tbl_name) file_format string No Writes only: parquet (default), orc, delta mode see Write modes No Default append. All six modes supported; mode: merge requires file_format: delta merge_keys list | string Conditional Required for mode: merge partitionBy list No Writes only: partition columns replace_where string No With file_format: delta: on an append, the batch's rows, replaced by each run (Delta appends) options dict No Spark reader/writer options

docs.title: Spark configuration for Hive
docs.text:
ENGINE:
  spark_conf:
    spark.sql.catalogImplementation: "hive"
    spark.sql.warehouse.dir: "/user/hive/warehouse"
    hive.metastore.uris: "thrift://metastore-host:9083"

These keys are fixed when the Spark session starts. Where the platform starts it (Databricks, EMR, spark-submit), set them there instead. See Spark keys fixed at session start.

docs.title: Partitioned writes
docs.text:
partitionBy is a top-level list, not a Spark option:

  outputs:
    events_partitioned:
      format: hive
      db_name: clean
      tbl_name: events
      mode: overwrite
      partitionBy: [event_date]

To re-run a single day without dropping the rest of the table, use mode: overwrite_partitions instead of overwrite. How each write mode behaves, merge included (it needs file_format: delta on hive), is on the Inputs & Outputs page.

  outputs:
    events_partitioned:
      format: hive
      db_name: clean
      tbl_name: events
      mode: overwrite_partitions
      partitionBy: [event_date]

docs.title: JDBC Connector
docs.text: Reads and writes any database that has a JDBC driver (Java's standard way to talk to a database): PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server, Redshift, Snowflake, and more. Needs Spark. Passwords are given as secret:// references.

docs.title: Read
docs.text:
CONFIG:
  inputs:
    customers:
      format: jdbc
      url: "jdbc:postgresql://db-host:5432/mydb"
      table: public.customers          # or use sql:
      user: "{{ env.DB_USER }}"
      password: "secret://env/DB_PASS"
      options:
        fetchsize: "10000"

Parallelised read (requires a numeric partition column). The tuning keys can be top-level keys or go under options; both reach Spark the same way:

    large_table:
      format: jdbc
      url: "jdbc:postgresql://db-host:5432/mydb"
      table: public.transactions
      user: "{{ env.DB_USER }}"
      password: "secret://env/DB_PASS"
      options:
        partitionColumn: id
        lowerBound: "1"
        upperBound: "10000000"
        numPartitions: "16"
        fetchsize: "50000"

Custom SQL:

    recent_orders:
      format: jdbc
      url: "jdbc:postgresql://db-host:5432/mydb"
      sql: "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '{{ dt }}'"
      user: "{{ env.DB_USER }}"
      password: "secret://env/DB_PASS"

Requirement

url is required. A read needs table (or dbtable) or sql. A write needs table.

docs.title: Write
docs.text:
CONFIG:
  outputs:
    predictions:
      format: jdbc
      url: "jdbc:postgresql://db-host:5432/mydb"
      table: ml.predictions
      user: "{{ env.DB_USER }}"
      password: "secret://env/DB_PASS"
      mode: append
      options:
        batchsize: "5000"
        truncate: "true"

docs.title: A batch that lands once
docs.text:
Spark's JDBC writer commits each partition on its own, so a plain append that fails part way leaves part of the batch, and a rerun inserts it again. Name the batch's rows with replace_where and the append lands once:

    payments:
      format: jdbc
      url: "jdbc:postgresql://db-host:5432/billing"
      table: billing.payments
      mode: append
      replace_where: "month = '{{ dt }}'"

Spark writes the batch into a staging table beside the target (ubunye_stage_<id>, same schema), then one database transaction deletes the rows the predicate selects and inserts the staged rows. It commits or changes nothing, and the staging table is dropped. A retry after a crash, and --rerun of a finished batch, replace the batch from the current data. The predicate is SQL in your database's dialect. The database user needs to create and drop a table in the target's schema. A staging table a killed run left behind holds no target data; the next run of the batch replaces it. Without replace_where an append is Spark's own, as before.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text: Field Type Required Description format "jdbc" Yes Selects this connector url string Yes JDBC connection URL table string Conditional Fully qualified table name (required for writes; for reads unless sql is set) dbtable string No Spark's own name for table; reads accept either sql string Conditional SQL query, reads only (alternative to table) driver string No JDBC driver class, e.g. org.postgresql.Driver user string No Database username password string No Database password, as a secret:// reference (secret://env/DB_PASS, secret://aws-sm/prod/db#password) fetchsize, partitionColumn, lowerBound, upperBound, numPartitions string or int No Read tuning, passed to Spark mode append | overwrite | errorifexists | ignore No Default append. Spark's native save modes only; merge and overwrite_partitions are refused by this connector. ubunye plan catches that before a run; ubunye validate does not (write modes) replace_where string No On an append: SQL selecting the batch's rows; the batch is staged, then those rows are replaced in one transaction (above) options dict No Spark JDBC options, applied last

docs.title: JDBC URLs by database
docs.text: Database URL pattern PostgreSQL jdbc:postgresql://host:5432/db MySQL jdbc:mysql://host:3306/db Oracle jdbc:oracle:thin:@host:1521/SID SQL Server jdbc:sqlserver://host:1433;databaseName=db Redshift jdbc:redshift://cluster.id.region.redshift.amazonaws.com:5439/db

docs.title: JDBC driver setup
docs.text:
The JDBC driver JAR must be on the Spark classpath:

ENGINE:
  spark_conf:
    spark.jars: "/opt/spark/jars/postgresql-42.7.0.jar"
    # or for multiple JARs:
    # spark.jars: "/opt/spark/jars/pg.jar,/opt/spark/jars/mysql.jar"

spark.jars is fixed when the Spark session starts (see Spark keys fixed at session start). On Databricks, install the driver via the cluster Libraries UI; elsewhere pass it to spark-submit --jars.

docs.title: Connectors: Overview
docs.text: A connector reads or writes one kind of storage for you. You write format: s3 (or jdbc, delta, ...) on an input or output in config.yaml; the connector does the reading before your transform runs, and the writing after. Your code only sees data frames. This page lists the connectors and links to each one's settings.

docs.title: Built-in connectors
docs.text:
Format Reader Writer Notes hive Yes Yes Hive Metastore via Spark SQL jdbc Yes Yes PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server, ... unity Yes Yes Databricks Unity Catalog (3-part names) s3 Yes Yes S3, ADLS, GCS, HDFS, local: any path. Also runs on the pandas backend delta Yes Yes Delta Lake by path or table name; time travel binary Yes No Raw files (PDFs, images). Spark's binaryFile source is read-only, so format: binary in CONFIG.outputs is rejected at config load rest_api Yes Yes HTTP REST with auth, pagination, retry. Also runs on the pandas backend

s3 and rest_api work on every shipped backend (spark, databricks, pandas). The others need Spark. ubunye validate --backend pandas says before a run when a task uses a connector its backend cannot serve.

docs.title: Which connectors are installed
docs.text:
ubunye plugins

lists every connector this machine can use: the built-in ones above, plus any installed from another package. An unknown format: is refused by ubunye validate, with that list. How connectors are found and registered (entry points) is in Writing a Plugin.

docs.title: Connector config structure
docs.text:
Every connector is declared as an IOConfig block:

CONFIG:
  inputs:
    <name>:
      format: <format>          # selects the connector
      # connector-specific fields below
      options: {}               # raw Spark reader/writer options

  outputs:
    <name>:
      format: <format>
      mode: append              # the default; see Write modes
      options: {}

Connector-specific keys (e.g. auth, pagination) are passed to the connector unchanged. Every built-in connector declares the keys it reads, so a key it does not read is refused by ubunye validate. See Inputs & Outputs and its write modes.

docs.title: Writing your own connector
docs.text: See Writing a Plugin for a step-by-step guide to building a custom Reader or Writer and registering it with the entry point system.

docs.title: Writing a Plugin
docs.text: This page is for Python developers who want Ubunye to read or write a system it does not support yet, or to add a transform, monitor or secret provider. You write a small class, declare it in your package's pyproject.toml (an "entry point"), and pip install the package: Ubunye finds it with no change to Ubunye itself.

docs.title: Plugin types
docs.text: Type Interface Entry point group Reader ubunye.core.interfaces.Reader ubunye.readers Writer ubunye.core.interfaces.Writer ubunye.writers Transform ubunye.core.interfaces.Transform ubunye.transforms Monitor ubunye.telemetry.monitors.Monitor (a protocol) ubunye.monitors Secret provider a class with get(ref) -> str (see Secrets) ubunye.secrets

docs.title: Writing a Reader
docs.text:
# my_package/readers/my_api.py
from ubunye.core.interfaces import Reader

class MyApiReader(Reader):
    CONFIG_KEYS = frozenset({"url", "token"})   # see "Declare your settings" below

    @classmethod
    def validate_config(cls, cfg):
        # Problems found here are reported by `ubunye validate`, before any run.
        return [] if cfg.get("url") else ["format 'my_api' requires 'url'"]

    def read(self, cfg: dict, backend):
        rows = _fetch_all(cfg["url"], cfg.get("token", ""))   # a list of dicts
        # The backend builds its own frame: Spark on spark, pandas on pandas.
        return backend.frame_from_records(rows)

cfg is this input's block from the config as a dict: format, options and every other key in the YAML. secret:// references in it are already resolved. validate_config and CONFIG_KEYS are optional; leave them out and the connector accepts any block.

docs.title: Writing a Writer
docs.text:
# my_package/writers/my_sink.py
from ubunye.core.interfaces import Writer

class MySinkWriter(Writer):
    CONFIG_KEYS = frozenset({"url"})

    def write(self, df, cfg: dict, backend) -> None:
        url = cfg["url"]
        mode = cfg.get("mode") or "append"
        # iter_records works on every backend: each row as a dict,
        # from a Spark frame or a pandas one.
        rows = list(backend.iter_records(df))
        _send_to_sink(rows, url, mode)

df is a Spark DataFrame on the spark and databricks backends and a pandas DataFrame on pandas. Going through backend (see Backend reference) keeps one writer working on all of them. Calling df.toPandas() instead would work on Spark only: a pandas frame has no toPandas().

docs.title: Writing a Transform
docs.text:
# my_package/transforms/my_transform.py
from ubunye.core.interfaces import Transform

class MyTransform(Transform):
    def apply(
        self,
        inputs: dict,           # {logical_name: DataFrame}
        cfg: dict,              # TransformConfig.params dict
        backend,                # the run's backend (see Backend reference)
    ) -> dict:                  # {logical_name: DataFrame}
        df = inputs["source"]
        threshold = cfg.get("threshold", 0.5)
        return {"output": df.filter(f"score > {threshold}")}

A task folder does not run transform plugins: ubunye run always runs the task's transformations.py, and transform.type in its config.yaml only gets a warning. A transform plugin runs when you build an Engine (ubunye.core.runtime.Engine) yourself and pass it a config, or when your Task calls it. See Transform.

docs.title: Registering via entry points
docs.text:
In your package's pyproject.toml:

[project.entry-points."ubunye.readers"]
my_api = "my_package.readers.my_api:MyApiReader"

[project.entry-points."ubunye.writers"]
my_sink = "my_package.writers.my_sink:MySinkWriter"

[project.entry-points."ubunye.transforms"]
my_transform = "my_package.transforms.my_transform:MyTransform"
Under the hood: the built-in connectors are registered the same way

Ubunye finds connectors at startup through Python entry points. Its own are declared in Ubunye's pyproject.toml:

[project.entry-points."ubunye.readers"]
hive     = "ubunye.plugins.readers.hive:HiveReader"
jdbc     = "ubunye.plugins.readers.jdbc:JdbcReader"
s3       = "ubunye.plugins.readers.s3:S3Reader"
delta    = "ubunye.plugins.readers.delta:DeltaReader"
binary   = "ubunye.plugins.readers.binary:BinaryReader"
unity    = "ubunye.plugins.readers.unity:UnityTableReader"
rest_api = "ubunye.plugins.readers.rest_api:RestApiReader"

[project.entry-points."ubunye.writers"]
s3       = "ubunye.plugins.writers.s3:S3Writer"
delta    = "ubunye.plugins.writers.delta:DeltaWriter"
hive     = "ubunye.plugins.writers.hive:HiveWriter"
jdbc     = "ubunye.plugins.writers.jdbc:JdbcWriter"
unity    = "ubunye.plugins.writers.unity:UnityTableWriter"
rest_api = "ubunye.plugins.writers.rest_api:RestApiWriter"

Any installed package that declares these entry points is picked up the same way, with no change to Ubunye.

After pip install -e . (or publishing to PyPI):

ubunye plugins
# Should list: my_api, my_sink, my_transform

docs.title: Using your plugin in a config
docs.text:
CONFIG:
  inputs:
    data:
      format: my_api          # matches the entry point key
      url: "https://..."
      token: "secret://env/MY_API_TOKEN"

  transform:
    params:
      threshold: 0.7          # read in transformations.py from self.config

  outputs:
    result:
      format: my_sink
      url: "https://..."

ubunye validate checks that format names an installed reader (for an input) or writer (for an output). An unknown name is refused with the list of installed ones.

docs.title: Declare your settings, so typos fail early
docs.text:
Input and output blocks accept keys the engine does not know, because your connector reads its own settings. That also means a typo (tokne:) is silently ignored, unless you say which keys you read:

class MyApiReader(Reader):
    CONFIG_KEYS = frozenset({"url", "token"})

With CONFIG_KEYS declared, ubunye validate rejects any other key in a block that uses your connector and names the closest real one (inputs.data: 'tokne' is not a setting of 'my_api'; did you mean 'token'?). You do not list format or options (every block may have them), nor, for a writer, mode, merge_keys and replace_where (the engine reads those for every output). Leave CONFIG_KEYS out and any key is accepted, as before. Every built-in connector declares its keys.

docs.title: Backend reference
docs.text:
The backend argument passed to read, write, and apply is the run's backend: SparkBackend, DatabricksBackend or PandasBackend (ubunye backends lists them). What every backend offers:

backend.is_spark                                  # True on spark and databricks
backend.frame_from_records(rows, schema=None)     # list of dicts -> frame (schema: Spark DDL)
backend.iter_records(frame)                       # frame -> each row as a dict
backend.read_frame(file_format, path, options=..., schema=...)

A Spark backend also has backend.spark (the SparkSession). A connector that needs Spark should get the session with spark_of, which raises a clear error on the pandas backend. Declare that it needs Spark too, so ubunye validate and ubunye plan with --backend pandas say so before a run:

from ubunye.adapters.spark.session import spark_of
from ubunye.core.capabilities import SPARK
from ubunye.core.errors import SourceReadError

class MySparkReader(Reader):
    REQUIRES = frozenset({SPARK})   # also: PATH_IO, RECORDS

    def read(self, cfg: dict, backend):
        spark = spark_of(backend, "my_spark", error=SourceReadError)
        return spark.read.table(cfg["table"])

docs.title: Testing your plugin
docs.text:
Ubunye's own tests prove that the plugin system works with a connector the engine has never seen: tests/unit/config/test_third_party_connector.py registers one from outside and uses it. It makes a good model for your own test.

Write Spark-free unit tests using mock DataFrames:

import pytest
from my_package.transforms.my_transform import MyTransform

class MockBackend:
    pass

class MockDF:
    def filter(self, expr):
        return self  # stub

def test_apply_passes_threshold():
    t = MyTransform()
    out = t.apply({"source": MockDF()}, {"threshold": 0.5}, MockBackend())
    assert "output" in out

For integration tests with real Spark:

from ubunye.backends.spark_backend import SparkBackend

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def spark():
    with SparkBackend(app_name="plugin_test") as be:
        yield be.spark

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text:
Package your plugin as a normal Python package and publish to PyPI. Users install it alongside ubunye-engine:

pip install ubunye-engine my-ubunye-plugin

Entry points are discovered automatically: no code changes required in Ubunye.

docs.title: REST API Connector
docs.text:
Reads records from an HTTP API, and posts records to one. Use it when a task's data lives behind a web API rather than in files or a database. It handles pagination, authentication, rate limits, retries, and an optional schema.

It runs on every shipped backend: spark, databricks and pandas. On a laptop, --backend pandas pulls from an API with no Spark and no Java. Both backends give the same rows and types (see Types). For worked scenarios, see REST API patterns.

It needs the requests package: pip install "ubunye-engine[rest]".

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
CONFIG:
  inputs:
    customers:
      format: rest_api
      url: "https://api.example.com/v1/customers"

docs.title: A typical read
docs.text:
Most APIs need a token, return records under a key, and split them over pages:

CONFIG:
  inputs:
    customers:
      format: rest_api
      url: "https://api.example.com/v1/customers"
      auth:
        type: bearer
        token: "secret://env/API_TOKEN"   # see Secrets
      response:
        root_key: data                    # records are in response["data"]
      pagination:
        type: cursor
        cursor_response_key: next_cursor
