The sections below explain each part. The full example shows every read setting.

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
CONFIG:
  inputs:
    customer_data:
      format: rest_api
      url: "https://api.example.com/v1/customers"
      method: GET                        # GET (default) | POST
      # body: {...}                      # JSON body, for POST

      headers:
        Accept: application/json

      params:                            # query string parameters
        since: "{{ dt | default('2025-01-01') }}"
        status: active

      auth:
        type: bearer                     # bearer | api_key_header | api_key_query | basic
        token: "secret://env/API_TOKEN"

      pagination:
        type: offset                     # offset | cursor | next_link
        page_size: 100
        max_pages: 50

      response:
        root_key: data                   # extract records from response["data"]

      rate_limit:
        requests_per_second: 10
        retry_on: [429, 503]
        max_retries: 3

      schema:                            # optional; inferred if omitted
        - name: customer_id
          type: string
        - name: created_at
          type: string          # text; convert it in the transform
        - name: email
          type: string

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Bearer tokenAPI key (header)API key (query param)Basic auth 
auth:
  type: bearer
  token: "secret://env/API_TOKEN"

auth:
  type: api_key_header
  header: X-Api-Key          # the default
  key: "secret://env/API_KEY"

auth:
  type: api_key_query
  param: api_key             # the default
  key: "secret://env/API_KEY"

auth:
  type: basic
  username: "{{ env.API_USER }}"
  password: "secret://env/API_PASS"

Give the token, key or password as a secret:// reference; it is read only when the connector runs.

Secrets stay out of logs and error messages. The auth token, key and password, an Authorization header or a header with a secret-looking name, and a query parameter with a secret-looking name (access_token, api_key...) are masked as *** in every log line the connector and the HTTP library write, and in every error it raises. An api_key_query key travels in the URL, so this matters most there. A secret under a plain parameter name (key, sig) is masked only when it is the auth key; put keys in auth, not in params.

An auth type the connector does not know is refused by ubunye validate and before any request, so a typo never sends a request without its key. The old name type: api_key still works, with a warning: it means api_key_header when header is set and api_key_query when param is set.

docs.title: Pagination strategies
docs.text:
OffsetCursorNext linkNone (single request)

Sends offset (name it with offset_param) starting at 0, and adds page_size after each page, until a page comes back empty or max_pages is reached. page_size is not sent to the API: put the API's own page size parameter under params if it needs one.

params:
  limit: 200
pagination:
  type: offset
  page_size: 200
  max_pages: 100      # safety cap

Reads a cursor from each response and sends it as a query parameter in the next request, until the cursor is missing or empty.

pagination:
  type: cursor
  cursor_response_key: next_cursor   # the response's key holding the cursor (default)
  cursor_param: cursor               # the query parameter it is sent as (default)
  max_pages: 100

Follows a URL in each response until it is missing or null. The URL must be a top level key of the response body; a dotted path and the HTTP Link header are not read.

pagination:
  type: next_link
  next_key: next                 # the response's key holding the next URL (default)

Omit the pagination key entirely.

The old names cursor_field (for cursor_response_key) and link_field (for next_key) still work, with a warning. The cursor, like the next link, must be a top level key of the response body. An unknown pagination type stops the read with an error.

docs.title: Response extraction
docs.text:
If the API returns records nested inside a key:

{ "data": [...], "meta": { "total": 500 } }

response:
  root_key: data

Without root_key, the entire response body is treated as the record (or list of records).

docs.title: Schema
docs.text:
Declare the schema for production pipelines. Only the declared columns are kept, in the declared order, and a missing field is null:

schema:
  - name: id
    type: long
  - name: name
    type: string
  - name: score
    type: double
  - name: created_at
    type: string          # text; convert it in the transform

Supported types: string, integer, long, float, double, boolean, timestamp, date, binary. The short names str, int, bigint and bool work too.

A value must have the column's kind, as Spark checks it. A whole number in a double or float column is read as that decimal number (1 becomes 1.0), on both backends, when a double holds it exactly; a whole number past 2**53 that a double cannot hold is refused. timestamp, date and binary columns refuse text, which is all JSON can send. Read such a field as string and convert it in the transform.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Without a schema, the column types are inferred from the records, by the same rules on Spark and pandas, so a task gives the same frame on both. Some records are refused on both, for example a field that is null in every record, or a whole number in one record and a decimal in another. Declare such a field under schema (string takes any value, as text).

Spark vs pandas details

Without a schema, the types come from every record, by Spark's own rules (createDataFrame). The pandas backend follows the same rules, so a task gives the same frame on both:

JSON value Column type whole number bigint decimal number double text string true / false boolean object map<string, ...> (not a struct) array array<...>
  • Columns are in name order. A key that first appears in a later record goes last.
  • A field that is a number in some records and text in others is string: 7 becomes "7", true becomes "true".
  • A map has no entry order. pandas keeps the JSON's order. Spark does not keep one you can rely on: Spark classic takes it from a Java HashMap, and that order changed between Java 11 and Java 21; Spark Connect keeps the JSON's. Do not depend on it. The run record's hash sorts maps by key, so it does not either. On pandas a map cell is a list of (key, value) pairs; dict(cell) makes it a dict.

Spark refuses some records, and so does pandas, with the same error:

  • a field that is a whole number in one record and a decimal in another (CANNOT_MERGE_TYPE);
  • a field that is null in every record (CANNOT_DETERMINE_TYPE);
  • a field that is an object in one record and a number in another.

For any of these, declare the field under schema. string takes any value, as text.

Known differences, on records where Spark 3.5 and Spark 4 also disagree:

  • Spark 3.5 writes a large or tiny decimal number in a text column the Java way (1.0E7), where Spark 4 and pandas write 10000000.0.
  • Spark 3.5 takes a map's value type from its first non-null entry only. Spark 4 and pandas look at every entry, so {"a": 1, "b": "x"} is map<string,string> there. On Spark 3.5, give a map one kind of value.

Records with no fields ([{}, {}]) give one row each and no columns, on both.

A whole number outside the 64 bit range (past 9223372036854775807) is refused on pandas, with the field's name. Spark classic stores null there without a word. Declare the field as string to keep it as text on both.

One difference from every Spark: a record that is a JSON array ([1, "a"]) instead of an object. Spark reads it as a row with columns _1, _2...; pandas refuses it. Point response.root_key at the list of objects instead.

docs.title: Write
docs.text:
CONFIG:
  outputs:
    predictions_api:
      format: rest_api
      url: "https://api.example.com/v1/predictions"
      headers:
        Content-Type: application/json
      auth:
        type: bearer
        token: "secret://env/API_TOKEN"
      batch_size: 100            # records per request
      rate_limit:
        requests_per_second: 5
        retry_on: [429, 503]               # default for writes: [429, 500, 503]
        max_retries: 3

The writer always sends POST. It accepts url, headers, auth, batch_size (default 100), rate_limit, and mode: append (the default; merge and overwrite_partitions are refused, other save modes only warn). A batch that still fails after its retries is counted, and the write fails at the end with the number of failed batches.

The writer batches rows into JSON payloads of batch_size records and POSTs each batch as {"records": [...]}. A map column is sent as an object. Spark and pandas send the same payloads, with one JSON form for each kind of value:

Value Sent as NaN, Infinity, -Infinity null (JSON has none of them) timestamp (an instant) ISO 8601 text in UTC: "2024-01-02T01:04:05.123456Z" timestamp_ntz (wall clock time, Spark) ISO 8601 text without an offset date "2024-01-02" decimal its exact text, as a string: "12.50" (a JSON number could lose digits) binary base64 text

On pandas a naive timestamp is an instant in the backend's time zone, as everywhere on the pandas backend, so it is sent with Z too.

Each batch is encoded whole before any of it is sent. A row holding a value that has no JSON form stops the write with an error naming the row and the field; none of its batch is posted (earlier batches were, and the error says how many).

docs.title: Read fields reference
docs.text:
Field Type Default Description url string required API endpoint URL method GET | POST GET HTTP method headers dict {} Additional HTTP headers params dict {} Query string parameters body dict null JSON request body auth dict null Authentication config pagination dict null Pagination strategy: type, page_size (default 100), max_pages (default 0, no cap), offset_param, cursor_response_key, cursor_param, next_key response.root_key string null Key to extract records from rate_limit dict null requests_per_second (default 0, no limit), retry_on (default [429, 503]), max_retries (default 3) schema list of dicts null Field name + type declarations

A retry waits 1 second, then 2, then 4, and so on.

docs.title: Example: customer sync pipeline
docs.text:
MODEL: etl
VERSION: "1.0.0"

CONFIG:
  inputs:
    crm_customers:
      format: rest_api
      url: "https://crm.example.com/api/v2/customers"
      auth:
        type: bearer
        token: "secret://env/CRM_TOKEN"
      pagination:
        type: next_link
        next_key: next
      response:
        root_key: results

  transform: {}

  outputs:
    customers_delta:
      format: delta
      path: s3://datalake/crm/customers/
      mode: overwrite

docs.title: Files and Delta (s3, delta, binary)
docs.text:
This page covers the three connectors that read and write files: by path (s3), as Delta Lake tables (delta), and as raw bytes (binary). Use it when a task reads or writes files in cloud storage, HDFS or a local folder.

  • s3: any path (S3, ADLS, GCS, HDFS, local). Supports Parquet, CSV, JSON, ORC, Avro and Delta. It also runs on the pandas backend (no Spark, no Java).
  • delta: Delta Lake tables, accessed by path or by table name. Needs Spark.
  • binary: raw files (PDFs, images), one row per file. Read only. See Fields: binary.

docs.title: Read
docs.text:
CONFIG:
  inputs:
    raw_events:
      format: s3
      path: s3://my-bucket/raw/events/dt=2024-06-01/
      options:
        mergeSchema: "true"

Default file format is Parquet. Choose another with file_format (format is already taken: it picks the connector). Reader options go under options:

    csv_data:
      format: s3
      path: s3://my-bucket/exports/customers.csv
      file_format: csv
      options:
        header: "true"
        inferSchema: "true"

To skip schema inference, give schema as a DDL string: schema: "id BIGINT, name STRING".

docs.title: CSV with text that holds quotes or line breaks
docs.text:
Ubunye reads CSV the way Spark does, on both backends, so the same file gives the same rows. Spark's default escape character is a backslash. Most CSV files written by pandas, Excel or a database escape a quote by doubling it (""), and hold line breaks inside quoted text. Read such a file with Spark's defaults and some rows split in the wrong place: values land in the wrong columns, and inferSchema then reads a number column as text, without a warning. Tell the reader how the file is written:

      options:
        header: "true"
        inferSchema: "true"
        multiLine: "true"   # quoted text may span lines
        escape: '"'         # a quote inside quoted text is written as ""

A sign you need this: an expectation such as between says a number column is text, or the row count differs from pandas.read_csv on the same file. A UTF-8 byte order mark at the start of a file is dropped, as Spark does.

docs.title: Write
docs.text:
CONFIG:
  outputs:
    clean_events:
      format: s3
      path: s3://my-bucket/clean/events/
      mode: overwrite
      partitionBy: [event_date]     # a top-level list, not an option
      options:
        compression: snappy

docs.title: Read by path
docs.text:
CONFIG:
  inputs:
    transactions:
      format: delta
      path: s3://my-bucket/delta/transactions/

docs.title: Read by table name
docs.text:
transactions:
      format: delta
      table: main.finance.transactions    # or db_name + tbl_name

docs.title: Time travel
docs.text:
transactions:
      format: delta
      path: s3://my-bucket/delta/transactions/
      version_as_of: 12                   # or timestamp_as_of: "2026-01-01"

options: {versionAsOf: 12} (or timestampAsOf, in any case) works the same.

docs.title: One version per run
docs.text: A Delta read that names no version is pinned to the version the table is at when the task reads it (versionAsOf, taken from DESCRIBE HISTORY ... LIMIT 1). Every output and the run record then see that one snapshot, even if another job appends while the task runs. Without this pin, a Delta frame would read the latest version each time Spark computes it, so two outputs of one input could come from two versions. This applies to format: delta and to format: s3 with file_format: delta. A sql: input and a catalog table read through hive or unity are not pinned. If the version cannot be read (no Delta SQL extension, no permission to see the history), the read is left unpinned, as before. The run record says which it was (pinned_by: engine or config).

docs.title: Write
docs.text:
CONFIG:
  outputs:
    predictions:
      format: delta
      path: s3://my-bucket/delta/predictions/    # or table: main.fraud.predictions
      mode: overwrite
      options:
        mergeSchema: "true"
        overwriteSchema: "true"

format: delta and format: s3 + file_format: delta are equivalent; use whichever reads better. The delta connector addresses a table (by name or path); the s3 connector addresses a path that happens to hold Delta files. Both support all six write modes.

docs.title: Write modes
docs.text:
All six write modes work on delta, and on s3 with file_format: delta. The Inputs & Outputs page owns how each mode behaves. One example, a MERGE (upsert) on Delta:

    customer_features:
      format: delta
      path: s3://my-bucket/delta/features/
      mode: merge
      merge_keys: [id, dt]        # or options.merge_keys: "id,dt"

For backfills that replace only some partitions, see overwrite_partitions. Its partitionBy form also runs on the pandas backend, with the same folders and the same result as Spark; replace_where needs Delta, so Spark. See the pandas backend.

docs.title: Appends that land once, and reruns that correct
docs.text:
A Delta append of a named batch (a run with -dt or a --var) lands once. A run killed or failed after its commit leaves the rows; the next run of the batch commits nothing (Delta's idempotent write, keyed by the task, the output and the batch). If the table did not change, the run says the batch was already there.

To make a rerun correct a bad batch, name the batch's rows with replace_where:

    payments:
      format: delta
      table: main.billing.payments
      mode: append
      replace_where: "month = '{{ dt }}'"

Each run then replaces the rows the predicate selects, in one commit: a retry after a crash, and --rerun of a finished batch, write the batch from the current data. Delta refuses data outside the predicate, so a wrong predicate fails the run and deletes nothing. A second plain run of a finished batch is still refused (pass --rerun). Without replace_where, --rerun of a finished batch appends it again and says so. See ADR 008.

docs.title: Fields: s3
docs.text: Field Type Required Description format "s3" Yes Selects this connector path string Yes S3 / ADLS / GCS / HDFS / local path file_format string No parquet (default), delta, csv, json, orc, avro schema string No Reads only: a DDL schema string; skips inference mode see Write modes No Default append. All six modes supported; merge and replace_where require file_format: delta partitionBy list No Partition columns; required for mode: overwrite_partitions unless replace_where is set merge_keys list | string Conditional Required for mode: merge replace_where string No Delta predicate for mode: overwrite_partitions; on a Delta append, the batch's rows, replaced by each run options dict No Spark reader/writer options (e.g. mergeSchema)

docs.title: Fields: delta
docs.text: Field Type Required Description format "delta" Yes Selects this connector path string Conditional Delta table path (required unless a table is named) table string Conditional Table name, e.g. main.fraud.claims db_name + tbl_name string Conditional The table name in two parts, instead of table sql string No Spark SQL query, reads only. Give path or a table name too mode see Write modes No Default append. All six modes supported partitionBy list No Partition columns merge_keys list | string Conditional Required for mode: merge replace_where string No Predicate for mode: overwrite_partitions; on an append, the batch's rows, replaced by each run (above) version_as_of int No Time travel by version (reads only) timestamp_as_of string No Time travel by timestamp (reads only) options dict No Spark reader/writer options

docs.title: Fields: binary
docs.text:
Reads raw files (PDFs, images, audio) one row per file, with columns path, modificationTime, length, content. Spark's binaryFile source is read-only: format: binary in CONFIG.outputs is rejected at config load.

Field Type Required Description format "binary" Yes Selects this connector path string Yes Directory or file path path_glob_filter string No Only read matching files, e.g. "*.pdf" recursive bool No Descend into sub-directories options dict No Spark reader options

docs.title: Spark configuration for S3
docs.text:
ENGINE:
  spark_conf:
    spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.access.key: "{{ env.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }}"
    spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.secret.key: "{{ env.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }}"
    spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.endpoint: "s3.amazonaws.com"
    # For Delta Lake on open-source Spark. Match the Delta build to your Spark:
    # (Spark 4.0: delta-spark_2.13:4.0.0; Spark 3.5: delta-spark_2.12:3.2.0)
    spark.jars.packages: "io.delta:delta-spark_2.13:4.0.0"
    spark.sql.extensions: "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension"
    spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog: "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog"

spark.jars.packages and spark.sql.extensions are fixed when the Spark session starts: where the platform starts it (EMR, Dataproc, spark-submit), set them there. See Spark keys fixed at session start. The Python package is pip install "ubunye-engine[delta]".

The two key lines template environment variables because secret:// references are not read in ENGINE.spark_conf (see Secrets). Better still, leave them out and let Spark use the platform's login (an instance role, workload identity).

On Databricks, Delta and S3 are pre-configured, so no extra Spark settings are needed.

docs.title: Partitioned paths with Jinja
docs.text:
outputs:
    daily_events:
      format: delta
      path: "s3://my-bucket/delta/events/dt={{ dt | default('2024-01-01') }}/"
      mode: overwrite

docs.title: Unity Catalog Connector
docs.text: Reads and writes Databricks Unity Catalog tables, named in three parts (catalog.schema.table). Use it for tasks that run on Databricks with Unity Catalog enabled.

docs.title: Read
docs.text:
CONFIG:
  inputs:
    features:
      format: unity
      table: main.fraud.feature_store     # three-part name (preferred)

Alternatively, use a SQL query:

    features_filtered:
      format: unity
      sql: >-
        SELECT * FROM main.fraud.feature_store
        WHERE dt = '{{ dt }}'

Requirement

A read needs table, sql, or catalog + schema + tbl_name. db_name is a Hive key: ubunye validate refuses it on a unity read.

docs.title: Write
docs.text:
CONFIG:
  outputs:
    predictions:
      format: unity
      table: main.fraud.model_predictions
      mode: append

A write needs table, or catalog + schema + tbl_name. Tables are written as Delta unless file_format says otherwise.

docs.title: Table comment, properties and maintenance
docs.text:
claims_curated:
      format: unity
      table: main.fraud.claims_curated
      options:
        comment: "Curated fraud claims"     # COMMENT ON TABLE after the write
        tblproperties:
          quality: "silver"                 # ALTER TABLE ... SET TBLPROPERTIES
      optimize:
        enabled: true                       # OPTIMIZE after the write
        zorder_by: [policy_id]              # ... ZORDER BY (policy_id)
      vacuum:
        hours: 168                          # VACUUM ... RETAIN 168 HOURS

optimize and vacuum need a Delta table. If the engine cannot run them, the data is still written and a warning says the maintenance was skipped.

docs.title: Write modes
docs.text:
All six write modes work on unity; the Inputs & Outputs page owns how each behaves. One example, a partition overwrite for a backfill, which replaces only the partitions in the incoming data:

    claims_daily:
      format: unity
      table: main.fraud.claims_daily
      mode: overwrite_partitions
      partitionBy: [ds]
      # or, as a Delta predicate:
      # replace_where: "ds = '{{ dt }}'"

A merge updates matched rows on merge_keys and inserts the rest; the first run creates the table. See merge.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text: Field Type Required Description format "unity" Yes Selects this connector table string Conditional Three-part Unity Catalog name catalog, schema, tbl_name string Conditional Writes only: the name in three parts, instead of table sql string Conditional Reads only: Spark SQL query file_format string No Writes only: delta (default) or parquet mode see Write modes No Default append. All six modes supported partitionBy list No Partition columns; required for mode: overwrite_partitions unless replace_where is set merge_keys list | string Conditional Required for mode: merge replace_where string No Delta predicate for mode: overwrite_partitions; on a Delta append, the batch's rows, replaced by each run (Delta appends) optimize dict No Writes only: enabled, zorder_by vacuum dict No Writes only: hours of history to keep options dict No Spark writer options; comment and tblproperties are applied to the table

docs.title: Spark configuration for Unity Catalog
docs.text: On Databricks, Unity Catalog is the default catalog when configured in the workspace. The engine uses the session that is already running there (--backend databricks, or the default on Databricks). It does not open a remote connection to a workspace itself, so run Unity tasks on Databricks. ENGINE.catalog and ENGINE.schema_name set the default catalog and schema (see Engine & Profiles).

docs.title: Access control
docs.text: Unity Catalog enforces column-level and row-level security. Ensure the service principal or user has SELECT (read) and MODIFY (write) privileges on the target table via the Databricks Catalog Explorer or GRANT SQL statements.

docs.title: Differences from hive
docs.text: hive unity Name resolution Two-part (db.table) Three-part (catalog.schema.table) Governance None beyond Hive ACLs Column masking, row filters, audit logs Delta by default No Yes Databricks required No Yes

docs.title: Deploying anywhere with spark-submit
docs.text:
If your platform can run spark-submit, it can run your tasks. This page is for EMR, Dataproc, YARN clusters and self-managed Spark, where no ubunye deploy command fits.

  • The problem: a cluster runs a Python file through spark-submit. It has no shell, so it cannot call the ubunye command.
  • When to use it: your platform takes spark-submit jobs, and you launch them yourself.
  • The one command:
spark-submit --py-files deps.zip run_ubunye.py \
  --task-dir pipelines/sales/etl/daily --mode PROD --dt 2026-07-14

docs.title: 1. The entry point
docs.text:
The engine ships a small runner, python -m ubunye, for exactly this. Its flags:

Flag Default Description --task-dir (required) The task folder, the one holding config.yaml. A local folder: a bucket URI (s3://, gs://) does not work --mode PROD The profile --dt The {{ dt }} for the config --lineage off Write a run record --log-level INFO Log level

spark-submit needs a file, so either point it at the engine's own /path/to/site-packages/ubunye/__main__.py, or keep a two line file of your own next to your job (this is run_ubunye.py above):

import sys
from ubunye.__main__ import main

sys.exit(main())

Where you do have a shell, python -m ubunye --task-dir ... --mode PROD --dt ... does the same.

It does not create a Spark session on purpose. spark-submit already made one, with the platform's master, executors and settings, and the engine attaches to it. Creating a second would quietly ignore the cluster and run everything on one machine.

The task folder must be on the driver's own disk: baked into the image, on a mounted shared disk, or copied down before the run. A bucket URL such as s3a://... does not work as --task-dir. The ubunye deploy commands for Glue, Dataproc and containers do all of this for you: they ship the task as a zip with a small ubunye_entry.py (One command to the cloud).

docs.title: 2. Ship the engine: --py-files deps.zip
docs.text:
The cluster's Python needs the engine. The simplest way is to install it on the cluster (a bootstrap step, or a container image): pip install ubunye-engine. Its dependencies are pyyaml, jinja2, pydantic, typer and narwhals.

If you cannot install packages there, ship the engine with the job. --py-files puts a zip on the Python path of the driver and every executor:

pip install --target deps --no-deps ubunye-engine
cd deps && zip -qr ../deps.zip . -x '*.pyc' && cd ..
spark-submit --py-files deps.zip run_ubunye.py --task-dir pipelines/sales/etl/daily --mode PROD

Python cannot import compiled code from a zip. pydantic needs pydantic-core, which is compiled, so the dependencies must already be on the cluster (install them at cluster start, or in the image). Add deps.zip only for what is plain Python, such as the engine itself and helper modules your transforms import.

What success looks like: the run log names the task's Spark app, Submitted application: ubunye:sales.etl.daily, and the job exits 0.

docs.title: 3. Leave spark.master to the platform
docs.text: Do not set spark.master in any config: the platform owns it, and the engine refuses a config that tries. Why: Deployment.

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text:
Any scheduler that can run a command can own the timetable. For Airflow, the engine generates the DAG for you:

ubunye export airflow -c pipelines/sales/etl/daily/config.yaml -o dags/sales_daily.py

The generated file is one DAG (Airflow 2.4+ and 3) with one BashOperator that calls ubunye run ... -m prod -dt {{ ds }}. --profile sets the profile (default prod, lower case: pass --profile PROD if your profiles are upper case), --usecase-dir sets the pipelines folder as Airflow sees it, and --backend and --lineage are passed on to the run. Review it, commit it to your Airflow repository, done.

docs.title: The checklist for a new platform
docs.text:
1. Can it run spark-submit or an equivalent? Then compute is solved.
  2. Where does data live? Set UBUNYE_DATA_ROOT to a path or bucket the platform can reach.
  3. Where do models live? Give the registry a mounted path or an s3:// or gs:// location.
  4. Do not set spark.master in any config. The platform owns it.

That is the whole integration. If you build one for a platform we have not listed, the connectors, stores and backends are all pluggable entry points, and a pull request with your runner script is very welcome.

No Spark at all? A task can run on the pandas backend, with no Java: How the pandas backend reads and writes.

docs.title: Deploying on AWS
docs.text:
This page shows the ways to run a task on AWS, starting with the one that is proven. It is for anyone with an AWS account who wants a task to run there.

Way Command Status (who says) AWS Glue 5 ubunye deploy glue Proven: the proving ground runs its workloads on Glue and gets the same data as local Spark EMR Serverless, engine command ubunye deploy emr-serverless Tested as a plan only: an AWS account on the free plan cannot use EMR EMR Serverless, companion repo scripts platforms/aws/submit.sh Written and wired into CI, never run, for the same reason Classic EMR on EC2 (YARN) SPARK_MASTER=yarn Not yet run

docs.title: AWS Glue (proven)
docs.text:
The problem: you want a task to run on AWS with no cluster to manage. When to use it: this is the default way onto AWS. The command:

ubunye deploy glue -d pipelines -u shop -p orders -t clean \
  --bucket my-bucket --role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/glue-job \
  --record-out glue.json

Glue pre-creates a Spark session, and the engine uses it, the same way it does on Databricks. Glue installs the engine with pip; you build no image.

Before you start, the flags, and the real --dry-run output are on One command to the cloud.

docs.title: EMR Serverless with the companion repo's scripts (not yet run)
docs.text:
EMR Serverless is AWS's run-Spark-without-a-cluster service. It gives you no shell. It takes a Python file and hands it to spark-submit, which is why the engine ships python -m ubunye as an entry point (see Anywhere with spark-submit).

For the engine's own command, ubunye deploy emr-serverless, see One command to the cloud. The rest of this section is the older script path. The scripts live in the examples repository (platforms/aws/), not in this one. They are written and wired into CI there, but have not been run, because a free plan account cannot use EMR. The CI jobs say in plain words when they were skipped rather than run.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• A clone of the examples repository, and the aws CLI signed in (aws configure or aws sso login) as someone with AWS admin rights, for the one-time setup only.
  • Four values. setup.sh (below) creates them and prints them; put them in your shell, or as GitHub secrets for the examples repo's CI:
Variable What it is Required AWS_S3_BUCKET the bucket for code, data and output yes AWS_EMR_APPLICATION_ID the EMR Serverless application yes AWS_EMR_JOB_ROLE_ARN the IAM role the job runs as yes AWS_REGION the AWS region no, defaults to eu-west-1

For CI, setup.sh also prints how to let GitHub sign in to AWS: an OIDC role (AWS_ROLE_TO_ASSUME) or, less safe, access keys.

docs.title: 1. One-time setup
docs.text:
bash platforms/aws/setup.sh

This creates an S3 bucket, an IAM role allowed to touch that one bucket and nothing else, and an EMR Serverless application. It prints the four values above. The person running it needs AWS admin rights; the values it produces do not.

docs.title: 2. Submit a task
docs.text:
bash platforms/aws/submit.sh examples/11_run_anywhere pipelines/portable/ingestion/document_index

The script copies the code and data to S3 and starts the job. It never passes spark.master, because EMR sets it; see the spark.master rule.

docs.title: 3. Machine learning pipelines
docs.text: EMR Serverless accepts a custom container image. This path uses the companion repo's Dockerfiles (platforms/docker/Dockerfile.ml), not ubunye deploy dockerfile. The same ML image Kubernetes uses, pushed to ECR, gives EMR the open source models with the weights inside, so jobs in a private subnet with no internet still work. The exact commands are comments at the top of platforms/aws/submit.sh.

docs.title: What about SageMaker?
docs.text:
SageMaker is not a place these pipelines run. It trains and hosts models; it is not a Spark runtime.

Where SageMaker fits is after the pipeline: a model that the registry trained, gated and promoted could be pushed to a SageMaker endpoint for live serving. That adapter does not exist yet. It is listed as planned on the deployment map so the decision is visible rather than forgotten.

docs.title: What about EMR on EC2, or Glue?
docs.text:
Classic EMR clusters use YARN: set SPARK_MASTER=yarn in the examples repository's launcher and the same task runs. This path has not been run yet, and this page will say so until it has.

Glue is covered by ubunye deploy glue, above.

docs.title: Deploying on Azure
docs.text:
This page shows how to run a task on Azure Container Apps with one command. It is for anyone with an Azure subscription. Azure Container Apps is proven: the proving ground runs its workloads there and gets the same data as local Spark.

The problem: you want a task to run on Azure, on a schedule or on demand, with no Spark cluster to manage. When to use it: any task that fits on one machine. The job runs Spark in local mode inside one container. The command:

ubunye deploy container-apps -u shop -p orders -t clean \
  --image myacr.azurecr.io/ubunye-jobs:1 -g my-rg --environment my-env \
  --registry-server myacr.azurecr.io \
  --registry-identity /subscriptions/<sub id>/resourceGroups/my-rg/providers/Microsoft.ManagedIdentity/userAssignedIdentities/pull \
  --record-out aca.json

Azure Container Apps runs containers for you. A Container Apps job is a container that runs to the end and stops, rather than a web app that stays up.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
1. The Azure CLI, signed in: az login. The command calls az containerapp and az monitor log-analytics. Add the Container Apps extension once: az extension add --name containerapp.
  2. Docker, to build the image.

  3. In Azure:

    You need Why a resource group (-g) holds the job a Container Apps environment (--environment) with a Log Analytics workspace the job runs in it; its logs are where the run record is read back from a container registry, such as Azure Container Registry (--registry-server) holds your image a user-assigned managed identity with the AcrPull role on that registry (--registry-identity) lets the job pull the image with no password

    Your own sign-in needs rights to create and start Container Apps jobs in the resource group, and to query the Log Analytics workspace.

  4. Where the data goes. The container's disk is gone when the job ends. Several tasks in one launch can share it (see Several tasks in one launch), but anything you want to keep must go to storage that outlives the container. Point your task's outputs there, for example with --env.

docs.title: 1. Build and push the image
docs.text:
This target builds its image with the engine's own ubunye deploy dockerfile (not the companion repo's Dockerfiles). Run it in the folder that holds your pipelines/ folder:

ubunye deploy dockerfile container --pipelines pipelines --out Dockerfile
docker build -t myacr.azurecr.io/ubunye-jobs:1 .
az acr login -n myacr
docker push myacr.azurecr.io/ubunye-jobs:1

The first command prints [OK] wrote Dockerfile and ubunye_entry.py. The image carries Java 17, Spark 3.5 in local mode, Delta, the engine and your pipelines, copied to /app/pipelines. That is why container-apps takes no -d: the pipelines are already inside. Rebuild and push the image when a task changes.

docs.title: 2. Preview with --dry-run
docs.text:
ubunye deploy container-apps -u shop -p orders -t clean \
  --image myacr.azurecr.io/ubunye-jobs:1 -g my-rg --environment my-env \
  --registry-server myacr.azurecr.io \
  --registry-identity /subscriptions/0000/resourceGroups/my-rg/providers/Microsoft.ManagedIdentity/userAssignedIdentities/pull \
  --dry-run

Real output, with the launcher script cut to ...:

{
  "platform": "container-apps",
  "job": "ubunye-clean",
  "uploads": [],
  "commands": [
    [
      "python",
      "-c",
      "...create or update the job, start it, wait, read the logs...",
      "{\"job\": \"ubunye-clean\", \"resource_group\": \"my-rg\", \"environment\": \"my-env\", \"image\": \"myacr.azurecr.io/ubunye-jobs:1\", \"cpu\": \"2\", \"memory\": \"4Gi\", \"timeout\": 1800, \"registry_server\": \"myacr.azurecr.io\", \"registry_identity\": \"/subscriptions/0000/resourceGroups/my-rg/providers/Microsoft.ManagedIdentity/userAssignedIdentities/pull\", \"env\": [\"UBUNYE_ENTRY_ARGS=[\\\"--task\\\", \\\"shop/orders/clean\\\", \\\"--mode\\\", \\\"PROD\\\"]\"], \"wait\": true}"
    ]
  ]
}

[DRY RUN] container-apps plan for 'ubunye-clean'. Nothing ran.

docs.title: 3. Run it
docs.text:
Drop --dry-run and add --record-out aca.json. The command:

  1. creates the job the first time (manual trigger, no retries, one replica), or updates its image, size and environment after that;
  2. starts one run and prints execution <name>;
  3. with --wait (the default), prints the run state every 20 seconds until it ends;
  4. reads the job's output from Log Analytics. Output reaches Log Analytics a few minutes after the job ends, so the command keeps asking for up to about 13 minutes, until the whole run record is there.
Flag Default What it does --job from the task name the Container Apps job name --cpu 2 CPU for the replica --memory 4Gi memory for the replica --timeout 1800 seconds a replica may run, for all tasks together --no-wait start the run and return

Plus the shared flags -m, -dt, --env, --var, --record-out and --dry-run: see One command to the cloud and the CLI reference.

docs.title: What success looks like
docs.text:
The last lines name the task and each output, with its row count and data hash:

[OK] container-apps run success: shop/orders/clean
  <output name>: <rows> rows, <data hash>
  run record: aca.json

aca.json is a normal run record. Compare it with a local run, or another cloud, to check the data is the same:

ubunye gate --baseline local.json --candidate aca.json

In the Azure portal the job is under your resource group, named ubunye-clean; Execution history lists each run and links to its logs.

If the run fails, the line says [FAIL] and the command exits with a non-zero code.

A rare first-create failure

Once, creating the job failed with "unable to pull image using Managed identity", and the same command passed when run again. If you see it, check the identity has AcrPull on the registry, then run the command again.

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text: ubunye deploy container-apps creates a job with a manual trigger: it runs when this command (or someone in Azure) starts it. Running it again updates the job and starts a new run. To run on a schedule, start the command from a scheduler you already use, such as a CI workflow on a timer. The engine does not set a schedule on the Azure job.

docs.title: Deploy to Databricks
docs.text: This page shows how to run a task as a Databricks job. It is for anyone with a Databricks workspace, from Free Edition to a paid workspace.

docs.title: Two ways to deploy, and which to pick
docs.text:
ubunye deploy databricks Databricks Asset Bundles What it is One engine command that uploads one task and creates or updates its job Jobs written as YAML files in your repo, deployed with the Databricks CLI (databricks bundle deploy) Files you write targets.yaml (where to deploy) databricks.yml, job files, a notebook that calls the engine Sign in A personal access token only A token, or a service principal with OAuth Good for Getting one task running fast; small teams Several tasks in one job, reviewed job definitions, production CI

Databricks Asset Bundles (often called DABs) are Databricks' own way to keep jobs as code. A personal access token (PAT) is a password-like string tied to one user. A service principal is a robot user for CI. See Databricks authentication for both.

Both ways run the same task folder. The rest of this page covers ubunye deploy databricks first, then bundles.

docs.title: ubunye deploy databricks
docs.text:
The problem: you have a task that runs on your laptop and you want it as a Databricks job. When to use it: one task per job, signed in with a personal access token. The command:

ubunye deploy databricks -d pipelines -u shop -p orders -t clean --target dev

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
1. Install the engine with the Databricks extra:

    pip install "ubunye-engine[databricks]"

  2. Make a personal access token in the workspace (User Settings → Developer → Access tokens → Generate new token) and put it in an environment variable. The default name is DATABRICKS_TOKEN:

    export DATABRICKS_TOKEN="dapi..."

    You can use another name: set token_env in targets.yaml, or pass --token MY_VAR_NAME.

  3. Tell the command which workspace to use. There are two ways:

    • a targets.yaml file (below), chosen with --target; or
    • --host https://... for a one-off deploy. With no --host, the DATABRICKS_HOST environment variable is used.

    A targets.yaml, when there is one, wins. With neither a targets.yaml nor a host, it stops with No targets.yaml found and no --host flag provided.

docs.title: Create targets.yaml
docs.text:
Put targets.yaml in the use case folder, so every pipeline and task in it shares the same targets. This is the layout ubunye init -d pipelines -u shop -p orders -t clean makes, with targets.yaml added:

pipelines/
    shop/
        targets.yaml              ← use case level targets
        orders/
            clean/
                config.yaml
                transformations.py

# pipelines/shop/targets.yaml
targets:
  dev:
    host: "https://adb-dev-123.azuredatabricks.net"
    token_env: DATABRICKS_TOKEN        # env var holding the PAT
    workspace_path: /Workspace/ubunye   # where files are uploaded
    # serverless: true is the default: the job gets no cluster block

  prod:
    host: "https://adb-prod-456.azuredatabricks.net"
    token_env: DATABRICKS_TOKEN_PROD
    workspace_path: /Workspace/ubunye
    serverless: false                   # run on a job cluster instead
    spark_version: "17.3.x-scala2.13"
    node_type_id: "i3.2xlarge"
    num_workers: 4

Serverless compute means Databricks starts and stops the machines for you; you pick no cluster. With serverless: true (the default) the cluster fields (spark_version, node_type_id, num_workers, spark_conf, aws_attributes) are not used. Set serverless: false to get a job cluster built from them.

docs.title: Task level overrides
docs.text:
A task can change some fields with its own targets.yaml in the task folder:

# pipelines/shop/orders/clean/targets.yaml
targets:
  prod:
    num_workers: 8                     # this task needs more compute
    spark_conf:
      spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: "200"

The task file is merged on top of the use case file. Fields you don't set are kept.

docs.title: Preview with --dry-run
docs.text:
ubunye deploy databricks -d pipelines -u shop -p orders -t clean \
    --target dev --dry-run

It prints the job spec and touches nothing in Databricks. Real output, with the dev target above:

{
  "name": "ubunye-shop-orders-clean-dev",
  "tags": {
    "ubunye_managed": "true",
    "ubunye_usecase": "shop",
    "ubunye_pipeline": "orders",
    "ubunye_task": "clean",
    "ubunye_target": "dev"
  },
  "max_concurrent_runs": 1,
  "tasks": [
    {
      "task_key": "run_ubunye_task",
      "notebook_task": {
        "notebook_path": "/Workspace/ubunye/shop/orders/clean/run_clean"
      }
    }
  ]
}

[DRY RUN] Job spec for 'ubunye-shop-orders-clean-dev' printed above. No changes made to Databricks.

There is no cluster block, so the job runs on serverless compute.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
ubunye deploy databricks -d pipelines -u shop -p orders -t clean --target dev

This:

  1. Checks the task's config.yaml.
  2. Signs in to the workspace with the token.
  3. Uploads config.yaml, transformations.py and helper files to /Workspace/ubunye/shop/orders/clean/.
  4. Writes a small notebook there, run_clean, that installs the engine and calls ubunye.run_task(). If transformations.py imports Narwhals (one transform for every engine, see Execution backends), the notebook installs it too: the runtime brings Spark and pandas, not Narwhals.
  5. Creates the job ubunye-shop-orders-clean-dev, or updates it in place if a job with that name exists.

Every job it makes is tagged ubunye_managed: "true", plus ubunye_usecase, ubunye_pipeline, ubunye_task and ubunye_target, so you can find it later.

Schedule. If the task's config.yaml has ORCHESTRATION.schedule, the job gets that schedule, in UTC. The value is a Quartz cron expression, the format Databricks uses: it starts with seconds, and uses ? for "any day". For example 0 0 6 1 * ? means 06:00 on the first day of every month. With no schedule, the job runs only when you start it.

docs.title: What success looks like
docs.text:
The command prints one line:

[OK] Job 'ubunye-shop-orders-clean-dev' deployed (id=<job id>, target=dev)

Then start the job and look at it:

  • From the same command: add --run. It starts a run once the job is deployed and prints the run's link.
  • In the workspace: open Jobs & Pipelines (called Workflows in older workspaces), search for ubunye-shop-orders-clean-dev, and press Run now. The job page is also at <host>/#job/<job id>.
  • From a terminal, with the Databricks CLI: databricks jobs run-now <job id>.
  • The files are under /Workspace/ubunye/shop/orders/clean/ in the workspace browser, next to the run_clean notebook.

If the token variable is empty the command stops with AuthNotFoundError. A token the workspace refuses gives AuthInvalidError. See Errors.

docs.title: One-off deploy without targets.yaml
docs.text:
Pass the host directly, or set DATABRICKS_HOST (--host reads it). The host is used only when there is no targets.yaml:

ubunye deploy databricks -d pipelines -u shop -p orders -t clean \
    --host "https://adb-123.azuredatabricks.net" --dry-run

The target name is then dev, and the job is ubunye-shop-orders-clean-dev.

docs.title: Deploy from GitHub Actions
docs.text:
ubunye init github-actions writes a workflow that runs this command:

ubunye init github-actions -d pipelines -u shop -p orders -t clean

It writes .github/workflows/shop_orders.yml. One job does everything: on a pull request it checks the config and runs tests; on a push to main it also deploys. The important parts, trimmed:

jobs:
  test-and-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      PIPELINE_DIR: pipelines/shop/orders
      DATABRICKS_HOST:  ${{ secrets.DATABRICKS_HOST }}
      DATABRICKS_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DATABRICKS_TOKEN }}
    steps:
      # ... checkout, Python 3.11, Java 17, pip install -e ".[spark,dev]"
      - name: Validate config
        run: ubunye validate -d pipelines -u shop -p orders --all
      # ... unit tests from pipelines/shop/orders/tests, if that folder exists
      # ... skip the deploy when DATABRICKS_HOST or DATABRICKS_TOKEN is empty
      - name: Deploy to Databricks
        if: ${{ steps.check_secrets.outputs.has_secrets == 'true' && github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' }}
        run: |
          ubunye deploy databricks \
            -d pipelines -u shop -p orders -t clean \
            --target nonprod
      # ... "Run job (manual trigger)": the same command with --run

Before it can deploy:

  • Add the secrets DATABRICKS_HOST and DATABRICKS_TOKEN to the repository (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions).
  • That is all. With no targets.yaml the deploy reads the workspace from the DATABRICKS_HOST secret. A committed targets.yaml with a nonprod target (change it with --target) wins when there is one.
  • To deploy and start the job by hand, run the workflow from the Actions tab with run_after_deploy ticked. The run step prints the run's link.

Run ubunye init github-actions --help for --extras, --target, --no-deploy and --output.

docs.title: targets.yaml fields
docs.text:
Field Type Default Description host str required Databricks workspace URL token_env str DATABRICKS_TOKEN Environment variable holding the PAT workspace_path str /Workspace/ubunye Root path for uploaded files serverless bool true Run on serverless compute; false builds a job cluster from the fields below spark_version str 17.3.x-scala2.13 Databricks Runtime version (job cluster only); 17.3 LTS, as ubunye export databricks node_type_id str i3.xlarge Instance type (job cluster only) num_workers int none, sent as 0 Number of workers, 0 = single node (job cluster only) spark_conf dict {} Spark configuration overrides (job cluster only) aws_attributes dict {} AWS-specific cluster attributes (job cluster only) max_concurrent_runs int 1 How many runs of the job may run at once

Unknown fields are refused.

docs.title: CLI flags
docs.text:
ubunye deploy databricks --help lists them; the full table is in the CLI reference.

Flag Short Default Description --usecase-dir -d required The pipelines folder --usecase -u required Use case name --pipeline -p required Pipeline name --task -t required Task name --target dev Deploy target name --mode -m PROD Profile for the job --data-timestamp -dt Data timestamp passed to the task --dry-run false Print job spec without deploying --host One-off workspace URL (skips targets.yaml) --token DATABRICKS_TOKEN Env var name that holds the token

docs.title: Databricks Asset Bundles
docs.text:
The problem: you want jobs reviewed as code, several tasks in one job, or CI that signs in as a service principal. When to use it: production on a paid workspace, or any team that already uses bundles. The command: databricks bundle deploy --target nonprod, run by the Databricks CLI.

Bundle files (databricks.yml, bundles/) belong in your repo, the one that holds your pipelines, not in the engine repo. The engine is the runtime; your repo defines the jobs.

A full working bundle is in the engine repo: examples/production/titanic_databricks. The snippets below follow it.

docs.title: The flow
docs.text:
Push code -> GitHub Actions checks it -> Merge to main -> GitHub Actions deploys the bundle -> Databricks runs it on schedule
Stage Where What happens Pull request GitHub Actions ubunye validate --all and pytest Merge to main GitHub Actions databricks bundle deploy --target nonprod Production deploy GitHub Actions (started by hand) databricks bundle deploy --target prod Run Databricks The job runs the task on its schedule

docs.title: databricks.yml (your repo's root)
docs.text:
It names the bundle, declares its variables and lists the targets:

bundle:
  name: my-usecase-pipelines

include:
  - bundles/*.yaml

variables:
  catalog:
    description: Unity Catalog catalog the tasks write to.
    default: dev_catalog

targets:
  nonprod:
    mode: development
    default: true
    # No workspace.host here: the Databricks CLI reads it from DATABRICKS_HOST.

  prod:
    mode: production
    variables:
      catalog: prod_catalog

Two rules the Databricks CLI enforces:

  • Don't write host: ${DATABRICKS_HOST}. The CLI refuses variables in sign-in fields ("Variable interpolation is not supported for fields that configure authentication"). Leave workspace.host out and set the DATABRICKS_HOST environment variable, or write the URL itself.
  • Declare every variable under variables: before a target sets it.

Unity Catalog is Databricks' catalog of tables, volumes and who may use them. A catalog holds schemas; a schema holds tables.

docs.title: Job files (bundles/*.yaml)
docs.text:
Each file in bundles/ defines jobs. The job runs a small notebook that calls the engine:

resources:
  jobs:
    monthly_orders:
      name: ubunye-monthly-orders
      max_concurrent_runs: 1
      schedule:
        quartz_cron_expression: "0 0 6 1 * ?"   # 06:00 on day 1 of each month
        timezone_id: "UTC"
      tasks:
        - task_key: run_pipeline
          notebook_task:
            notebook_path: ./notebooks/run_task.py
            base_parameters:
              task_dir: ${workspace.file_path}/pipelines/shop/orders/clean
              mode: "PROD"
              catalog: ${var.catalog}
          # No cluster block: the task runs on serverless compute.

${workspace.file_path} is where the bundle uploads your repo's files. Add sync: include: [pipelines/**, notebooks/**] to databricks.yml so the pipelines and notebook travel with the bundle.

The notebook reads the parameters as widgets, installs the engine and runs the task. A minimal version:

# Databricks notebook source
# MAGIC %pip install "ubunye-engine==0.9.0"

# COMMAND ----------
dbutils.library.restartPython()

# COMMAND ----------
dbutils.widgets.text("task_dir", "")
dbutils.widgets.dropdown("mode", "PROD", ["DEV", "PROD"])

import ubunye

ubunye.run_task(
    task_dir=dbutils.widgets.get("task_dir"),
    mode=dbutils.widgets.get("mode"),
)

The titanic example's run_titanic.py is a full one, using ubunye.notebook().

docs.title: A GitHub Actions workflow for bundles
docs.text:
This workflow checks pull requests and deploys the bundle on merge. Unlike the generated workflow above, it uses the Databricks CLI, so it can sign in either way. Set either DATABRICKS_TOKEN or the pair DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID and DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET; the CLI picks the service principal when both of the pair are set. Which to choose, and how to make them: Databricks authentication.

name: deploy
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  validate:
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: { python-version: "3.11" }
      - run: pip install -e .[dev]
      - run: ubunye validate -d ./pipelines -u shop -p orders --all
      - run: pytest tests/unit/ -v --tb=short -m "not integration"

  deploy-nonprod:
    if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      DATABRICKS_HOST:          ${{ secrets.DATABRICKS_HOST }}
      DATABRICKS_TOKEN:         ${{ secrets.DATABRICKS_TOKEN }}
      DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID:     ${{ secrets.DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID }}
      DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET: ${{ secrets.DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: databricks/setup-cli@main
      - run: databricks bundle deploy --target nonprod
Sign-in Secrets Personal access token (Free Edition, one user) DATABRICKS_HOST, DATABRICKS_TOKEN Service principal with OAuth (recommended on paid workspaces) DATABRICKS_HOST, DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID, DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET

The engine repo's own bundle workflows (.github/workflows/*_databricks*.yml) work this way.

docs.title: What success looks like
docs.text: databricks bundle deploy logs Uploading bundle files to /Workspace/Users/<you or the principal>/.bundle/... and ends with Deployment complete!. Then run the job with databricks bundle run monthly_orders --target nonprod, or find ubunye-monthly-orders under Jobs & Pipelines in the workspace. In mode: development, Databricks puts [dev <your name>] in front of the job name so two people sharing a workspace don't overwrite each other's jobs.

docs.title: The Python API on Databricks
docs.text:
In a notebook or a notebook job, call the engine from Python instead of the CLI. It uses the Spark session Databricks already started:

import ubunye

# One task
outputs = ubunye.run_task(
    task_dir="/Workspace/pipelines/fraud_detection/ingestion/claim_etl",
    mode="DEV",
    dt="202510",
)

# Several tasks in one pipeline
results = ubunye.run_pipeline(
    usecase_dir="/Workspace/pipelines",
    usecase="fraud_detection",
    pipeline="ingestion",
    tasks=["claim_etl", "feature_engineering"],
    mode="DEV",
    dt="202510",
)

It names the Spark app ubunye:<usecase>.<pipeline>.<task>, so you can find the run in the Spark UI and history server.

Why the Python API on Databricks?

The Python API runs in the notebook's own process, uses the session Databricks already has running, and hands the output tables back to you. The CLI also uses a running session when there is one (--backend not given), but returns nothing you can inspect.

More on the Python API: API reference.

docs.title: Dev notebooks
docs.text:
ubunye init writes a dev notebook for each task, at <task folder>/notebooks/<task>_dev.ipynb. It runs the same steps as the job, one cell at a time:

  1. Parameters: dbutils.widgets for effective_year_month and mode
  2. Setup: installs the engine, loads the config, creates the Databricks backend
  3. Extract: reads all inputs, prints each input's columns (no scan)
  4. Inspect sources: display() each input table
  5. Transform: runs the Task class from transformations.py
  6. Inspect outputs: display() each output table
  7. Load: writes outputs (commented out by default)
  8. Sandbox: the Spark session, for free exploring

For the same steps with less code, use ubunye.notebook() (see the API reference and Notebooks).

The notebook reads the same config.yaml as the job, so dev and production cannot drift apart.

docs.title: Deploying on GCP
docs.text:
This page shows the ways to run a task on Google Cloud, starting with the one that is proven. It is for anyone with a GCP project.

Way Command Status (who says) Dataproc Serverless, engine command ubunye deploy dataproc Proven: the proving ground runs its workloads on Dataproc Serverless and gets the same data as local Spark Dataproc Serverless, companion repo scripts platforms/gcp/submit.sh Written and wired into CI, not yet run

docs.title: Dataproc Serverless with ubunye deploy dataproc (proven)
docs.text:
The problem: you want a task to run on GCP with no cluster to manage. When to use it: this is the default way onto GCP. The command:

ubunye deploy dataproc -d pipelines -u shop -p orders -t clean \
  --project my-project --region europe-west1 --bucket my-bucket \
  --image europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/my-project/ubunye/job:1 \
  --record-out dataproc.json

The image is built with ubunye deploy dockerfile dataproc. Before you start, the image steps, the flags and the real --dry-run output are on One command to the cloud.

docs.title: Dataproc Serverless with the companion repo's scripts (not yet run)
docs.text:
Dataproc Serverless runs Spark batches without a cluster to manage. Like EMR, it takes a Python file for spark-submit, which python -m ubunye exists to be (see Anywhere with spark-submit).

The scripts live in the examples repository (platforms/gcp/), not in this one. The CI jobs there say plainly when they were skipped.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• A clone of the examples repository, and gcloud signed in (gcloud auth login) to the project, with rights to enable APIs and create service accounts, for the one-time setup only.
  • Four values. setup.sh (below) creates them and prints them; put them in your shell, or as GitHub secrets for the examples repo's CI:
Variable What it is Required GCP_PROJECT the project ID yes GCP_BUCKET the bucket for code, data and output yes GCP_REGION the region no, defaults to europe-west1 GCP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT the service account the batch runs as no; without it Dataproc uses the default one

For CI, setup.sh also prints how to let GitHub sign in: keyless Workload Identity (GCP_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_PROVIDER, preferred) or a key file (GCP_SA_KEY).

docs.title: 1. One-time setup
docs.text:
bash platforms/gcp/setup.sh

This turns on the APIs, creates a bucket, and creates a service account that may touch that one bucket and run Dataproc, nothing more. It prints the values above. Prefer the keyless option it suggests: a key that does not exist cannot leak.

docs.title: 2. Submit a task
docs.text:
bash platforms/gcp/submit.sh examples/11_run_anywhere pipelines/portable/ingestion/document_index

The script copies code and data to the bucket and submits the batch. It never passes spark.master; Dataproc owns that choice. See the spark.master rule.

docs.title: 3. Machine learning pipelines
docs.text: Dataproc Serverless accepts a custom container image. This path uses the companion repo's Dockerfiles (platforms/docker/Dockerfile.ml), not ubunye deploy dockerfile. Push the same ML image Kubernetes uses to Artifact Registry and pass it with the batch. The exact commands are comments at the top of platforms/gcp/submit.sh.

docs.title: What about Vertex AI?
docs.text: The same answer as SageMaker on the AWS page. Vertex AI hosts and serves models; it is not a Spark runtime, so pipelines do not run there. A model the registry promoted could be pushed to a Vertex endpoint for serving. That adapter does not exist yet and is listed as planned on the deployment map.

docs.title: Model storage
docs.text: The model registry writes to gs:// paths directly (since 0.5.0) once the gcsfs package is installed. So the whole lifecycle, including where the model files live, can stay inside your GCP project.

docs.title: Deploying on Kubernetes
docs.text:
This page shows how to run pipelines on a Kubernetes cluster. It is for anyone with a cluster and kubectl pointed at it.

There are two ways. Each builds its image differently:

Way Image built with Status ubunye deploy k8s (the engine's command) ubunye deploy dockerfile container Proven on kind (a small Kubernetes that runs inside Docker) The companion repo's manifests (this page) the companion repo's platforms/docker/Dockerfile Run in that repo's CI on a throwaway cluster

The shortest way is the engine's own command: ubunye deploy dockerfile container writes an image's Dockerfile, and ubunye deploy k8s runs a task as a Kubernetes Job in kubectl's current context. See One command to the cloud. The proving ground runs its workloads this way on a kind cluster.

The rest of this page uses the scripts and manifests in the examples repository (platforms/docker/, platforms/k8s/), not this one. They are exercised in CI there against a disposable cluster. Run the commands below from a clone of it.

docs.title: The shape
docs.text: A pipeline on Kubernetes is a container image plus a Job manifest. The image carries Spark, Delta, the JDBC driver and the engine. Your task folders are copied in unchanged. Nothing in any pipeline knows it is inside a container.

docs.title: 1. Build the image
docs.text:
This path uses the companion repo's Dockerfiles, not ubunye deploy dockerfile.

docker build -f platforms/docker/Dockerfile -t ubunye-portable:latest .

For machine learning pipelines there is a second image that adds the open source models with the weights already inside, so pods need no internet:

docker build -f platforms/docker/Dockerfile.ml \
  --build-arg BASE=ubunye-portable:latest -t ubunye-ml:latest .

Push whichever you need to the registry your cluster pulls from.

docs.title: 2. Run a task as a Job
docs.text:
platforms/k8s/job-template.yaml takes any task:

sed -e "s|{{NAME}}|my-pipeline|" \
    -e "s|{{ARGS}}|\"examples/02_ingest_rest_api\", \"weather\", \"ingestion\", \"hourly_forecast\"|" \
    platforms/k8s/job-template.yaml | kubectl apply -f -

The environment variables in the manifest are the whole configuration surface: where the data lives, what kind of table to write, and any secrets your connectors need. Mount them from Kubernetes Secrets in the usual way.

docs.title: 3. Run it on a schedule
docs.text:
Wrap the same spec in a CronJob:

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: ubunye-nightly
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      # the same template as the Job, unchanged

docs.title: Two honest notes
docs.text:
Storage. A pod's disk vanishes with the pod. Point UBUNYE_DATA_ROOT at object storage or a persistent volume, and give the model registry a mounted path or an s3:// style location, which it supports directly since 0.5.0.

One pod or many. The manifests run Spark in local mode inside one pod, which is the honest shape for most scheduled jobs. To fan out across executor pods instead, set SPARK_MASTER to your cluster's API address (k8s://https://kubernetes.default.svc), give the job a service account that may create pods, and set spark.kubernetes.container.image. The task folders do not change: the launcher owns the master, as the spark.master rule says.

docs.title: One command to the cloud: Glue, Dataproc, Kubernetes, Container Apps, EMR
docs.text:
This page shows how to run a task, unchanged, on AWS Glue, GCP Dataproc Serverless, Kubernetes, Azure Container Apps or AWS EMR Serverless with one ubunye deploy command. It is for anyone who has a task working locally and an account on one of those clouds.

The problem: the task runs on your laptop; you want it to run on a cloud and to know it gave the same data. When to use it: any time you deploy to one of these five targets. For Databricks, see Databricks. The command (Glue as the example):

ubunye deploy glue -d pipelines -u shop -p orders -t clean \
  --bucket my-bucket --role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/glue-job --record-out glue.json

"Serverless" here means the cloud starts and stops the machines for you; you manage no cluster. Which targets are proven is on the deployment map.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Each command uses the cloud's own CLI (aws, gcloud, kubectl, az) and its usual sign-in. It:

  1. uploads the task folder as a zip, plus a small entry script (Glue and Dataproc; Kubernetes, Container Apps and EMR carry the task inside the image);
  2. runs the task once through ubunye.run_task, writing a run record;
  3. with --wait (the default), follows the run to the end and reads the run record back from the job's log.

--dry-run prints exactly what would be uploaded and run, and runs nothing.

Shared flags: --env KEY=VALUE sets the task's environment (repeatable), --var KEY=VALUE a template variable, -m the profile and -dt the data timestamp. All flags: CLI reference.

None of these pass spark.master; see the spark.master rule.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Target Sign in with You need AWS Glue aws configure or aws sso login an S3 bucket; an IAM role the job runs as, with access to the bucket and the AWS Glue service role policy (AWSGlueServiceRole) GCP Dataproc gcloud auth login a project with the Dataproc API on; a GCS bucket; an Artifact Registry repository for the image; Docker to build it; optionally a service account for the batch Kubernetes kubectl pointed at the cluster (its current context) a registry the cluster can pull from; Docker to build the image Azure Container Apps az login a resource group, a Container Apps environment, a registry, and a managed identity that may pull from it. Details: Azure AWS EMR Serverless aws configure or aws sso login an EMR Serverless application using your image, a job role, and an S3 bucket for logs. A free plan account cannot use EMR

The examples below use the folder ubunye init -d pipelines -u shop -p orders -t clean makes.

docs.title: AWS Glue
docs.text:
Glue 5 (Spark 3.5, Python 3.11). Glue installs the engine with pip, so you build no image: --engine is the pip requirement (default ubunye-engine), or --engine-wheel uploads a local wheel. Glue supplies Delta itself. --role is the IAM role the job runs as. Workers: --workers (default 2) and --worker-type (default G.1X).

ubunye deploy glue -d pipelines -u shop -p orders -t clean \
  --bucket my-bucket --role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/glue-job \
  --region eu-west-1 --env UBUNYE_DATA_ROOT=s3://my-bucket/data --dry-run

Real output, with the two long launcher scripts cut to ...:

{
  "platform": "glue",
  "job": "ubunye-shop-orders-clean",
  "uploads": [
    {
      "to": "s3://my-bucket/ubunye/shop/orders/clean/bundle.zip",
      "bytes": 2596
    },
    {
      "to": "s3://my-bucket/ubunye/shop/orders/clean/ubunye_entry.py",
      "bytes": 5078
    }
  ],
  "commands": [
    ["python", "-c", "...create or update the Glue job...", "ubunye-shop-orders-clean",
     "{\"Role\": \"arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/glue-job\", \"GlueVersion\": \"5.0\", \"WorkerType\": \"G.1X\", \"NumberOfWorkers\": 2, \"Timeout\": 60, \"MaxRetries\": 0, ...}",
     "--region", "eu-west-1"],
    ["python", "-c", "...start the run, follow it, print its log...", "ubunye-shop-orders-clean",
     "wait", "--region", "eu-west-1"]
  ]
}

[DRY RUN] glue plan for 'ubunye-shop-orders-clean'. Nothing ran.

docs.title: GCP Dataproc Serverless
docs.text:
A batch in a container image. Dataproc mounts Spark and Java; the image carries the engine, Delta's jars and the entry script. This target builds its image with the engine's own ubunye deploy dockerfile:

ubunye deploy dockerfile dataproc --out Dockerfile     # also writes ubunye_entry.py
docker build -t europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/my-project/ubunye/job:1 .
docker push europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/my-project/ubunye/job:1

The image follows Dataproc's rules (no Spark or Java inside, a spark user 1099:1099, tini and procps) and uses Delta built for Scala 2.13, which runtime 2.2 runs. The task itself arrives as an archive at run time, so one image serves every task. Other flags: --runtime (default 2.2), --service-account, --batch.

ubunye deploy dataproc -d pipelines -u shop -p orders -t clean \
  --project my-project --region europe-west1 --bucket my-bucket \
  --image europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/my-project/ubunye/job:1 --dry-run

Real output, the gcloud command shown on fewer lines:

{
  "platform": "dataproc",
  "job": "ubunye-clean-1794306923",
  "uploads": [
    {
      "to": "gs://my-bucket/ubunye/shop/orders/clean/bundle.zip",
      "bytes": 2596
    },
    {
      "to": "gs://my-bucket/ubunye/shop/orders/clean/ubunye_entry.py",
      "bytes": 5078
    }
  ],
  "commands": [
    ["gcloud", "dataproc", "batches", "submit", "pyspark",
     "gs://my-bucket/ubunye/shop/orders/clean/ubunye_entry.py",
     "--project", "my-project", "--region", "europe-west1",
     "--batch", "ubunye-clean-1794306923",
     "--container-image", "europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/my-project/ubunye/job:1",
     "--version", "2.2",
     "--archives", "gs://my-bucket/ubunye/shop/orders/clean/bundle.zip#bundle",
     "--deps-bucket", "my-bucket",
     "--properties=^#^spark.jars=file:///opt/jars/delta-spark_2.13-3.2.0.jar,...",
     "--", "--task", "shop/orders/clean", "--mode", "PROD"]
  ]
}

[DRY RUN] dataproc plan for 'ubunye-clean-1794306923'. Nothing ran.

The number in the batch name changes on every call, because a Dataproc batch id can be used only once.

docs.title: Kubernetes and Azure Container Apps
docs.text:
For a runtime with no managed Spark, the image carries everything: Java, Spark in local mode, Delta, the engine and your pipelines. These targets build their image with the engine's own ubunye deploy dockerfile container. (The companion repo's Dockerfiles are a different path; see Kubernetes.)

ubunye deploy dockerfile container --pipelines pipelines --out Dockerfile
docker build -t myregistry/ubunye-jobs:1 . && docker push myregistry/ubunye-jobs:1

# a Kubernetes Job, in kubectl's current context
ubunye deploy k8s -u shop -p orders -t clean --image myregistry/ubunye-jobs:1 \
  --namespace data --env UBUNYE_DATA_ROOT=s3a://my-bucket/data --record-out k8s.json

The pipelines are inside the image, so these commands take no -d.

The Kubernetes Job has no retries (backoffLimit: 0) and is cleaned up a day after it finishes. Other flags: --cpu, --memory, --timeout.

--dry-run for Kubernetes prints the Job manifest inside its plan. Trimmed, real output:

{
  "platform": "kubernetes",
  "job": "ubunye-clean-6923",
  "uploads": [],
  "commands": [
    ["python", "-c", "...kubectl apply, wait for Complete or Failed, print the logs...",
     "{\"apiVersion\": \"batch/v1\", \"kind\": \"Job\", \"metadata\": {\"name\": \"ubunye-clean-6923\", \"namespace\": \"data\", ...}, \"spec\": {\"backoffLimit\": 0, \"ttlSecondsAfterFinished\": 86400, ... \"image\": \"myregistry/ubunye-jobs:1\", \"args\": [\"--task\", \"shop/orders/clean\", \"--mode\", \"PROD\"], ... \"requests\": {\"cpu\": \"1\", \"memory\": \"2Gi\"} ...}}",
     "1800", "wait"]
  ]
}

[DRY RUN] kubernetes plan for 'ubunye-clean-6923'. Nothing ran.

Azure Container Apps uses the same image:

ubunye deploy container-apps -u shop -p orders -t clean --image myacr.azurecr.io/ubunye-jobs:1 \
  -g my-rg --environment my-env --registry-server myacr.azurecr.io \
  --registry-identity /subscriptions/.../userAssignedIdentities/pull --record-out aca.json

The Container Apps job is created the first time and updated after. Its output, and so the run record, reaches Log Analytics a few minutes after the job ends, and the command waits for it. Before you start, the dry run, and what success looks like: Azure.

docs.title: EMR Serverless
docs.text:
Planned: tested as a plan, not against a live application, because an AWS account on the free plan cannot use EMR. The image comes from the engine's own ubunye deploy dockerfile emr-serverless:

ubunye deploy dockerfile emr-serverless --out Dockerfile     # push it, set it on the application
ubunye deploy emr-serverless -u shop -p orders -t clean \
  --application-id 00fabc123 --role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/emr-job \
  --bucket my-bucket --region eu-west-1 --dry-run

Real output, the Spark settings cut to ...:

{
  "platform": "emr-serverless",
  "job": "ubunye-clean",
  "uploads": [],
  "commands": [
    ["aws", "emr-serverless", "start-job-run",
     "--application-id", "00fabc123",
     "--execution-role-arn", "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/emr-job",
     "--name", "ubunye-clean",
     "--job-driver", "{\"sparkSubmit\": {\"entryPoint\": \"local:///app/ubunye_entry.py\", \"entryPointArguments\": [\"--task\", \"shop/orders/clean\", \"--mode\", \"PROD\"], \"sparkSubmitParameters\": \"...\"}}",
     "--configuration-overrides", "{\"monitoringConfiguration\": {\"s3MonitoringConfiguration\": {\"logUri\": \"s3://my-bucket/logs/\"}}}",
     "--region", "eu-west-1"]
  ]
}

[DRY RUN] emr-serverless plan for 'ubunye-clean'. Nothing ran.

This command starts the run and returns; it does not wait, so it has no --wait or --record-out. The driver's output, with the run record, lands in s3://<bucket>/logs/.

docs.title: What success looks like
docs.text:
Without --dry-run, the command prints progress lines while it waits (on Glue: started <run id>, then the run state every 20 seconds). At the end it prints one line per task and one line per output. The shape:

[OK] glue run success: shop/orders/clean
  <output name>: <rows> rows, <data hash>
  run record: glue.json

If a task fails, the line says [FAIL] and the command exits with a non-zero code. If you asked for --record-out and the record is not in the job's log, it fails too, rather than report success without the record.

docs.title: The run record
docs.text:
The entry script prints the run's record between two markers at the end of the job; --record-out saves it. It is the same run record a local run writes, so ubunye gate and ubunye lineage compare work across clouds: the same task on two platforms must write the same data.

ubunye gate --baseline glue.json --candidate dataproc.json   # the same data?

More: Run records.

docs.title: Several tasks in one launch
docs.text:
Repeat -t to run a pipeline's tasks in that order, in one job:

ubunye deploy glue -d pipelines -u food -p prices -t clean -t monitor \
  --bucket my-bucket --role arn:aws:iam::...:role/glue-job \
  --var out_dir=s3://my-bucket/food --record-out glue.json

The tasks share the job, its session and its disk, so a later task can read what an earlier one wrote, even on a container whose disk goes when it stops. The first task that fails stops the rest, and the deploy fails if any task failed or never ran. With several tasks, --record-out glue.json writes one run record per task: glue.clean.json, glue.monitor.json, also when the job failed.

Things to know:

  • A task name is a folder name: no /, \, or ,, and each task once. A bad list is refused before anything is uploaded or started.
  • The default job name and bundle folder of several tasks is their names joined by - plus a short hash of the list (clean-monitor-29df150d), so two different lists never share them. Pass --job for a name of your own.
  • The tasks share the platform's time limit: Glue's job Timeout (60 minutes) and the container --timeout cover all of them together, not each.
  • The entry script inside an image runs several tasks only if the image was built from this version: rebuild a Kubernetes, Container Apps, Dataproc or EMR image made with an older ubunye deploy dockerfile. (Glue uploads the script on every deploy.)

docs.title: Examples: start here
docs.text:
These examples live in the companion repository ubunye-ai-ecosystems/ubunye-examples. This section is organised by what you want to do: ingest data, build machine learning, keep models honest, work with language models.

Each example on these pages has a row of tabs: Databricks, Laptop, Docker and Kubernetes. Each tab shows how to run that example in that place. The tabs remember your choice: click Databricks once and every example on every page shows the Databricks way. The pipelines themselves never change between tabs. That is the whole point of the engine.

ubunye-ai-ecosystems/ubunye-examples on GitHub

Which engine version? The examples repo installs the engine from PyPI and pins the release its CI last tested: ubunye-engine==0.7.0 (in its requirements.txt and Docker image). The current engine is 0.9.0. The commands below keep the tested pin. To try the examples on 0.9.0, install "ubunye-engine[spark,ml]==0.9.0" instead; that pairing has not been through the examples' CI yet. What changed between versions: Upgrading.

docs.title: More examples in the engine repo
docs.text:
More examples ship inside the engine repository, under examples/. Each runnable one has its own README with the commands:

Folder What it shows Runs on proving/c01_portable_etl one Narwhals transform, the same rows on pandas and Spark, checked with ubunye prove laptop, no Java with pandas real-world/food_prices_africa WFP food prices: clean, then flag price jumps laptop, no Java real-world/olist_ecommerce nine raw tables to an order fact table, with input contracts, quarantine and reconcile laptop, no Java production/titanic_local the Titanic task on Spark and pandas, same run record hashes laptop production/titanic_multitask_local two chained tasks on Spark and pandas laptop production/llm_replay model calls replayed from a committed file: no key, no network, no cost laptop, no Java production/titanic_databricks, titanic_multitask_databricks, jhb_weather_databricks, titanic_ml_databricks the same tasks as Databricks Asset Bundles on serverless compute, writing to Unity Catalog Databricks python_api ubunye.run_task() and ubunye.run_pipeline() from Python laptop with Spark, or Databricks titanic_end_to_end.ipynb the model lifecycle: train, gates, registry, rollback, lineage a notebook, no Spark fraud_detection/claims/claim_etl a sample config and transform: read a Hive table, write to S3.
