A shape to copy, not a runnable demo (it needs your own fraud_db.raw_claims table) your Spark cluster rest_api/customer_sync a sample config.yaml for the REST connector: bearer token, paging, rate limits. A shape to copy; it points at a placeholder API reference only

docs.title: Before you start, once per environment
docs.text:
DatabricksLaptopDockerKubernetes

Sign up for Databricks Free Edition (no card). In the workspace choose Create, then Git folder, and paste the examples repository URL. It is public, so you need no token. Every example is then a notebook you open and run.

You need Python, Java 17 and an internet connection. (This setup uses Spark 3.5, which runs on Java 8, 11 or 17; see Installation.)

git clone https://github.com/ubunye-ai-ecosystems/ubunye-examples
cd ubunye-examples
pip install "pyspark==3.5.3" "delta-spark==3.2.0" "ubunye-engine[spark,ml]==0.7.0" "requests"

The scripts under platforms/ handle Spark, Delta and a local metastore. Examples that read the Databricks sample tables need seeded stand-ins with the same shape, created once:

. platforms/spark_env.sh && python platforms/seed.py

You need Docker only. Build the image once:

docker build -f platforms/docker/Dockerfile -t ubunye-portable:ci .

The machine learning examples use a second image with the open source model weights baked in, so nothing is downloaded at run time:

docker build -f platforms/docker/Dockerfile.ml --build-arg BASE=ubunye-portable:ci -t ubunye-ml:ci .

Any cluster works. For a disposable local one:

kind create cluster --name ubunye
kind load docker-image ubunye-portable:ci --name ubunye

Job manifests live under platforms/k8s/.

docs.title: Why you can trust these pages
docs.text: Every example has been run for real, with its output inspected. One test goes further: it runs the same pipeline on the laptop, in Docker, on Kubernetes, against object storage and on Databricks, then fails the build unless all of them produced the same rows (the hash ignores row order). See Run anywhere.

docs.title: Ingestion
docs.text:
These examples live in the companion repository ubunye-ai-ecosystems/ubunye-examples. Run the commands from a clone of it (setup per place).

Getting data in. Four examples: catalog tables with SQL, a public web API, raw unstructured files, and a real relational database over JDBC.

docs.title: 01 · Tables and SQL
docs.text:
Read a catalog table, push a join down as SQL so the database does the work, and write with merge so re-running never duplicates rows.

DatabricksLaptopDockerKubernetes

Open examples/01_ingest_tables_sql/notebooks/run_customer_revenue.py and press Run all. Or, from a terminal:

databricks bundle run ingest_tables_sql --target dev

Seed the sample-shaped tables once (see Start here), then:

platforms/run_task.sh examples/01_ingest_tables_sql retail ingestion customer_revenue

docker run --rm --entrypoint bash ubunye-portable:ci -c \
  '. platforms/spark_env.sh && python platforms/seed.py && \
   platforms/run_task.sh examples/01_ingest_tables_sql retail ingestion customer_revenue'

Use the job template with this example's arguments:

sed -e "s|{{NAME}}|ingest|" \
    -e 's|{{ARGS}}|"examples/01_ingest_tables_sql", "retail", "ingestion", "customer_revenue"|' \
    platforms/k8s/job-template.yaml | kubectl apply -f -

docs.title: 02 · REST API
docs.text:
Pull a weather forecast from a free public API, with paging, retries and rate limiting, then fan one JSON document out into rows.

DatabricksLaptopDockerKubernetes

Open examples/02_ingest_rest_api/notebooks/run_hourly_forecast.py and run it, or:

databricks bundle run ingest_rest_api --target dev

platforms/run_task.sh examples/02_ingest_rest_api weather ingestion hourly_forecast

docker compose -f platforms/docker/compose.yml run --rm rest-api

sed -e "s|{{NAME}}|rest|" \
    -e 's|{{ARGS}}|"examples/02_ingest_rest_api", "weather", "ingestion", "hourly_forecast"|' \
    platforms/k8s/job-template.yaml | kubectl apply -f -

docs.title: 03 · Unstructured files
docs.text:
Read raw text files with the binary reader, then chunk them into overlapping windows ready for embeddings. The documents are committed to the repository, so nothing is downloaded while running.

DatabricksLaptopDockerKubernetes

Open examples/03_ingest_unstructured/notebooks/run_document_index.py and run it, or:

databricks bundle run ingest_unstructured --target dev

UBUNYE_CORPUS=file:///tmp/ubunye/corpus \
platforms/run_task.sh examples/03_ingest_unstructured docs ingestion document_index

Runs as the first step of the models demo:

docker run --rm --entrypoint /app/platforms/models_demo.sh ubunye-ml:ci

kubectl apply -f platforms/k8s/job-models.yaml

docs.title: 09 · JDBC, a real database
docs.text:
A parallel read from RNAcentral's public PostgreSQL mirror, 54 million rows. The lesson: a JDBC read is single threaded unless you tell it not to be, and this example shows the four settings that split it across connections.

DatabricksLaptopDockerKubernetes

Plainly: serverless cannot run this one. It ships no JDBC drivers and cannot install one, so this example needs a classic cluster on a paid workspace, and it has its own bundle:

cd examples/09_jdbc_ingest && databricks bundle run jdbc_ingest --target dev

Works out of the box. The driver is one Maven coordinate, which the platform script already passes:

platforms/run_task.sh examples/09_jdbc_ingest rnacentral ingestion ingest_rna

docker compose -f platforms/docker/compose.yml run --rm jdbc

sed -e "s|{{NAME}}|jdbc|" \
    -e 's|{{ARGS}}|"examples/09_jdbc_ingest", "rnacentral", "ingestion", "ingest_rna"|' \
    platforms/k8s/job-template.yaml | kubectl apply -f -

docs.title: Language models
docs.text:
These examples live in the companion repository ubunye-ai-ecosystems/ubunye-examples. Run the commands from a clone of it (setup per place).

Working with LLMs inside ordinary pipelines. Two examples: retrieval augmented answers with sources cited, and teaching a small model you own from a large model's labels.

Both run in two ways, chosen by one environment variable. On Databricks they use the workspace's hosted model endpoints. Everywhere else, MODEL_BACKEND=local swaps in open source models that run on a CPU with no endpoint and no API key. The pipelines do not change. Which model answers is business logic, and it lives in one Python file.

docs.title: 05 · RAG, answers with receipts
docs.text:
Chunk documents, embed them, find the chunks relevant to a question, and answer using only what was found, citing the sources. Needs example 03's chunks first.

DatabricksLaptopDockerKubernetes

Run 03 first, then the two notebooks under examples/05_rag_documents/notebooks/, or:

databricks bundle run rag_documents --target dev

pip install sentence-transformers transformers torch --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
MODEL_BACKEND=local \
platforms/run_task.sh examples/05_rag_documents rag knowledge embed_chunks answer_questions

The first run downloads two small models from Hugging Face, about one gigabyte total. After that it is fully offline.

The ml image has the weights baked in, so this works with no internet:

docker run --rm --entrypoint /app/platforms/models_demo.sh ubunye-ml:ci

kubectl apply -f platforms/k8s/job-models.yaml
kubectl logs -f job/ubunye-rag

docs.title: 06 · Fine-tune an open LLM
docs.text:
Distillation, end to end. A large model labels customer reviews once, then a small DistilBERT you own learns from those labels, gets judged on held-out data, and must pass a quality gate before it is registered. The result costs nothing per call and no one can rate limit it.

DatabricksLaptopDockerKubernetes 
databricks bundle run finetune_llm --target dev

Fine-tuning on CPU takes about ten minutes. That is the slowest example in the repository.

MODEL_BACKEND=local STUDENT_MODEL_STORE=/tmp/ubunye/model_store \
platforms/run_task.sh examples/06_finetune_llm reviews nlp label_reviews finetune_classifier

docker run --rm -e WITH_DISTILLATION=true \
  --entrypoint /app/platforms/models_demo.sh ubunye-ml:ci

platforms/k8s/job-models.yaml runs example 05 only. To add the distillation step, add this entry to the container's env: list in that file (next to MODEL_BACKEND):

            - name: WITH_DISTILLATION
              value: "true"

Then apply it and follow the logs:

kubectl apply -f platforms/k8s/job-models.yaml
kubectl logs -f job/ubunye-rag

Give the pod time: the student trains on CPU. A Job's pod settings cannot be changed after it is created, so if ubunye-rag already exists, delete it first with kubectl delete job ubunye-rag.

docs.title: Machine learning
docs.text:
These examples live in the companion repository ubunye-ai-ecosystems/ubunye-examples. Run the commands from a clone of it (setup per place).

Training models and using them. Two examples: the full lifecycle done properly, and the same model built in three frameworks to prove the engine does not care which one you pick.

docs.title: 04 · The full lifecycle
docs.text:
Build features with a deterministic split, train, judge the model on rows it never saw, pass a quality gate, register, promote to production, then score new data with whatever model is in production. A model that fails the gate is never registered at all.

DatabricksLaptopDockerKubernetes

Open the notebooks under examples/04_ml_taxi_fare/notebooks/ in order, or run the whole chain:

databricks bundle run ml_taxi_fare --target dev

Seed once (see Start here), then run the three tasks in order:

TAXI_MODEL_STORE=/tmp/ubunye/model_store \
platforms/run_task.sh examples/04_ml_taxi_fare taxi_fare ml \
  feature_engineering model_training batch_inference

docker run --rm --entrypoint bash \
  -e TAXI_MODEL_STORE=/data/model_store ubunye-portable:ci -c \
  '. platforms/spark_env.sh && python platforms/seed.py && \
   platforms/run_task.sh examples/04_ml_taxi_fare taxi_fare ml \
     feature_engineering model_training batch_inference'

sed -e "s|{{NAME}}|ml|" \
    -e 's|{{ARGS}}|"examples/04_ml_taxi_fare", "taxi_fare", "ml", "feature_engineering", "model_training", "batch_inference"|' \
    platforms/k8s/job-template.yaml | kubectl apply -f -

docs.title: 10 · One model, three frameworks
docs.text:
The same model trained in scikit-learn, PyTorch and TensorFlow, behind three config files that are byte for byte identical. A build check keeps them identical. It ends in a leaderboard honest enough to say "too close to call" instead of crowning a half-percent lead.

DatabricksLaptopDockerKubernetes 
databricks bundle run ml_frameworks --target dev

The three trainers run in parallel, then the judge waits for all three.

TensorFlow needs numpy<2, so install the pinned trio first:

pip install torch --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
pip install tensorflow "numpy<2" "protobuf<5"
BENCH_MODEL_STORE=/tmp/ubunye/model_store \
platforms/run_task.sh examples/10_ml_frameworks fare_bench ml \
  train_sklearn train_torch train_keras select_champion

The ml image already carries all three frameworks, pinned correctly:

docker run --rm --entrypoint bash \
  -e BENCH_MODEL_STORE=/data/model_store ubunye-ml:ci -c \
  '. platforms/spark_env.sh && python platforms/seed.py && \
   platforms/run_task.sh examples/04_ml_taxi_fare taxi_fare ml feature_engineering && \
   platforms/run_task.sh examples/10_ml_frameworks fare_bench ml \
     train_sklearn train_torch train_keras select_champion'

The examples repo has no ready manifest for this one, so here is the Docker command wrapped in a Job. It follows platforms/k8s/job-template.yaml, with the ubunye-ml:ci image and at least 5Gi of memory: three frameworks is a real appetite. Save it as job-ml-frameworks.yaml, then kubectl apply -f job-ml-frameworks.yaml:

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: ubunye-ml-frameworks
spec:
  backoffLimit: 0
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: ubunye
          image: ubunye-ml:ci
          imagePullPolicy: Never # side-loaded into kind
          command: ["bash", "-c"]
          args:
            - >-
              . platforms/spark_env.sh && python platforms/seed.py &&
              platforms/run_task.sh examples/04_ml_taxi_fare taxi_fare ml feature_engineering &&
              platforms/run_task.sh examples/10_ml_frameworks fare_bench ml
              train_sklearn train_torch train_keras select_champion
          env:
            - name: BENCH_MODEL_STORE
              value: /data/model_store
            - name: DATA_DIR
              value: /data
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
          resources:
            requests: { memory: "5Gi", cpu: "2" }
            limits: { memory: "7Gi" }
      volumes:
        - name: data
          emptyDir: {}

Follow it with kubectl logs -f job/ubunye-ml-frameworks.

docs.title: Keeping models honest
docs.text:
These examples live in the companion repository ubunye-ai-ecosystems/ubunye-examples. Run the commands from a clone of it (setup per place).

What happens after training. Two examples: a written contract for incoming data, and a monitor that notices when a live model goes bad and does something about it.

docs.title: 07 · Data quality, a contract enforced
docs.text:
Rules with severities, written in one readable file. Rows that break a rule are set aside with the reason attached, never silently dropped. The run fails loudly when the breach is structural, because quietly quarantining a third of the data is not a fix, it is a cover-up.

DatabricksLaptopDockerKubernetes

Open examples/07_data_quality/notebooks/run_validate_transactions.py and run it, or:

databricks bundle run data_quality --target dev

Seed once (see Start here), then:

platforms/run_task.sh examples/07_data_quality quality contracts validate_transactions

docker run --rm --entrypoint bash ubunye-portable:ci -c \
  ". platforms/spark_env.sh && python platforms/seed.py && \
   platforms/run_task.sh examples/07_data_quality quality contracts validate_transactions"

sed -e "s|{{NAME}}|quality|" \
    -e "s|{{ARGS}}|\"examples/07_data_quality\", \"quality\", \"contracts\", \"validate_transactions\"|" \
    platforms/k8s/job-template.yaml | kubectl apply -f -

docs.title: 08 · Model monitoring and rollback
docs.text:
Three checks that catch three different failures: has the world changed, has the model decayed against its own recorded baseline, and is the live model still the best one in the registry. Then it acts. It rolls back only when a better version actually exists, and says "retrain" with the numbers when a rollback would be theatre. Needs example 04's model first.

DatabricksLaptopDockerKubernetes 
databricks bundle run model_monitoring --target dev

The notebook runs both failure stories: a drifted world, and a bad model promoted by hand. Read the zeros in the output. They are the lesson.

TAXI_MODEL_STORE=/tmp/ubunye/model_store \
TAXI_MODELS_DIR=$PWD/examples/04_ml_taxi_fare/models \
platforms/run_task.sh examples/08_model_monitoring taxi_fare mlops monitor_model

Run example 04 in the same container first, then the monitor, so the registry has a model to watch:

docker run --rm --entrypoint bash \
  -e TAXI_MODEL_STORE=/data/model_store \
  -e TAXI_MODELS_DIR=/app/examples/04_ml_taxi_fare/models ubunye-portable:ci -c \
  ". platforms/spark_env.sh && python platforms/seed.py && \
   platforms/run_task.sh examples/04_ml_taxi_fare taxi_fare ml \
     feature_engineering model_training batch_inference && \
   platforms/run_task.sh examples/08_model_monitoring taxi_fare mlops monitor_model"

The same chain as Docker, inside one Job, so the metastore and the registry survive between the tasks. The examples repo has no ready manifest for this one; this Job follows platforms/k8s/job-template.yaml. Save it as job-monitoring.yaml, then kubectl apply -f job-monitoring.yaml:

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: ubunye-monitoring
spec:
  backoffLimit: 0
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: ubunye
          image: ubunye-portable:ci
          imagePullPolicy: Never # side-loaded into kind
          command: ["bash", "-c"]
          args:
            - >-
              . platforms/spark_env.sh && python platforms/seed.py &&
              platforms/run_task.sh examples/04_ml_taxi_fare taxi_fare ml
              feature_engineering model_training batch_inference &&
              platforms/run_task.sh examples/08_model_monitoring taxi_fare mlops monitor_model
          env:
            - name: TAXI_MODEL_STORE
              value: /data/model_store
            - name: TAXI_MODELS_DIR
              value: /app/examples/04_ml_taxi_fare/models
            - name: DATA_DIR
              value: /data
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
          resources:
            requests: { memory: "2Gi", cpu: "1" }
            limits: { memory: "3Gi" }
      volumes:
        - name: data
          emptyDir: {}

Follow it with kubectl logs -f job/ubunye-monitoring.

docs.title: Run anywhere, proven
docs.text:
These examples live in the companion repository ubunye-ai-ecosystems/ubunye-examples. Run the commands from a clone of it (setup per place).

This is the example the whole engine stands on. One task folder, run on six environments, with a build that fails unless every one of them produced the same rows (the hash ignores row order).

laptop        067da98ea04a7d2f...
Docker        067da98ea04a7d2f...
Kubernetes    067da98ea04a7d2f...
object store  067da98ea04a7d2f...
spark-submit  067da98ea04a7d2f...
Databricks    067da98ea04a7d2f...

Those are real hashes from this example's own runs, not an illustration. (The engine's own cross-cloud results are on Proving ground: latest results.) The only things that change between environments are three variables: where the compute is, what kind of table to write, and where the data lives.

docs.title: Run it yourself
docs.text:
DatabricksLaptopDockerKubernetes 
databricks bundle run run_anywhere --target dev

platforms/local/run.sh

The last line printed is the fingerprint. Compare it with any other environment.

docker compose -f platforms/docker/compose.yml run --rm run-anywhere

kubectl apply -f platforms/k8s/job.yaml
kubectl logs -f job/ubunye-portable

docs.title: Object storage
docs.text: The same task also writes to a real S3 compatible store through the same connector code AWS uses, and must produce the same hash. Against real S3 you change the endpoint and supply credentials. Nothing else moves. Model files can live on object storage too: since 0.5.0 the registry accepts s3:// and gs:// paths directly.

docs.title: AWS and GCP
docs.text:
The engine itself is proven on the clouds. The proving ground runs its workloads with ubunye deploy glue on AWS Glue and ubunye deploy dataproc on GCP Dataproc Serverless (plus Azure, Kubernetes and Databricks), and every environment gets the same data as local Spark. That page has the numbers; how to deploy is on One command to the cloud.

This example's own cloud scripts are a separate path, and not yet run. The setup scripts, submit scripts and build jobs for EMR Serverless and Dataproc Serverless exist in the examples repo under platforms/aws/ and platforms/gcp/. The build jobs say, in plain words, that they were skipped rather than run. Four secrets turn them on with no code change: see AWS and GCP.

docs.title: What it caught
docs.text: The check earned its keep on its first day. Databricks once produced a different hash from everyone else. The pipeline was fine. The data was not: git had quietly changed the line endings of the input files on one platform. Nothing crashed anywhere. Only the hash comparison noticed. That is why this example asserts on output, not on exit codes.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: The words these docs use, each in one or two plain sentences, with a link to the page that explains it in full. Read it once before your first task, or come back when a word is new.

docs.title: Folders and names
docs.text:
Word What it means More pipelines folder The top folder that holds all your use cases. You name it with -d (--usecase-dir), for example -d pipelines. Project Structure use case A folder for one business problem, such as fraud_detection. It holds pipelines. Named with -u. Project Structure pipeline A folder inside a use case that holds tasks which run in order, such as ingestion. Named with -p (--pipeline). Project Structure task One runnable unit of work: read some data, change it, write it. Named with -t. Project Structure task folder The folder that is a task. It holds config.yaml (what to read and write) and transformations.py (your code). In config templates it is {{ task_dir }}. Project Structure

So ubunye run -d pipelines -u fraud_detection -p ingestion -t claim_etl runs the task folder pipelines/fraud_detection/ingestion/claim_etl/.

Older name: package

Before 0.9 the middle level was called a package (--package). The CLI flag still works until 1.0, with a warning. Run records still name this field package, so when you read a record, package is the pipeline. See Upgrading.

docs.title: Running a task
docs.text: Word What it means More profile A named set of engine settings under ENGINE.profiles in config.yaml, such as DEV or PROD. You pick one with -m/--mode; run uses DEV if you say nothing. Names must match exactly, case included. Engine and Profiles backend What actually moves the data: spark (needs Java), databricks (the session a notebook already has) or pandas (no Java, one machine). Pick one with --backend. Execution Backends connector The small plugin that reads from or writes to one kind of place. The format: key picks it, for example format: s3 for files on any path, local or cloud, or format: jdbc for a database. Connectors write mode The mode: key on an output: what happens to data already there. overwrite, append, merge or overwrite_partitions. Inputs and Outputs expectations Checks on the data a task reads and writes, such as "no null ids". A failed check can stop the run, warn, or move bad rows to a quarantine output. Checks run before anything is written. Expectations

docs.title: After a run
docs.text: Word What it means More run record A file a run leaves behind when you pass --lineage: when it ran, how it went, row counts, and a hash of the config, the code and every row read and written. ubunye lineage list and ubunye lineage compare read it. Run Records batch A task with its -dt and --var values. Ubunye refuses to append the same batch twice unless you pass --rerun. Safe Reruns

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
How to install Ubunye Engine, pick the extras you need, and check it works. This is the one page that lists the Python, Java and pandas versions it needs.

Ubunye Engine runs on Python 3.10 or newer (3.10 to 3.13 are tested on every change), on Linux, Windows and macOS.

docs.title: Core install
docs.text:
pip install ubunye-engine

This installs the CLI, config loader, plugin registry, and lineage tracker. The engines that move data are optional extras: pick the one you need.

docs.title: Install extras
docs.text:
pandas (no Java)SparkMLDev (contributors) 
pip install "ubunye-engine[pandas]"

Adds pandas and pyarrow. Runs a task on your laptop or in CI with no Spark and no Java, reading and writing exactly as Spark does. See Execution backends.

pip install "ubunye-engine[spark]"

Adds pyspark. Required for format: hive, format: delta, and format: unity. Add delta for Delta Lake outside Databricks: pip install "ubunye-engine[spark,delta]".

pip install "ubunye-engine[ml]"

Adds scikit-learn and mlflow, which the built-in ML wrappers and the MLflow registry use. ml-torch adds torch as well.

git clone https://github.com/ubunye-ai-ecosystems/ubunye_engine.git
cd ubunye_engine
pip install -e ".[dev]"
pre-commit install

See Contributing for the test tiers.

Extras combine: pip install "ubunye-engine[pandas,spark]".

A warning you can ignore

With the pandas and spark extras together, pip may install pandas 3. PySpark then prints this when Spark starts:

FutureWarning: PySpark does not yet fully support pandas >= 3.0.0. Some features may not work correctly. It is recommended to use pandas < 3.0.0 for now.

This is expected: the run carries on and gives the same result (checked with pandas 3.1 and Spark 4.2). To silence it, install "pandas<3" alongside.

The other extras:

Extra Adds For delta delta-spark 4 Delta Lake on Spark outside Databricks rest requests the rest_api connector objectstore fsspec model artifacts on s3://, gs:// (add s3fs or gcsfs) databricks databricks-sdk ubunye deploy databricks, secret://databricks otel OpenTelemetry SDK and OTLP exporter traces and metrics aws, gcp, azure each cloud's secret store client secret://aws-sm, secret://gcp-sm, secret://azure-kv mcp mcp ubunye mcp, the engine as an MCP server for agents

docs.title: Verify the install
docs.text:
ubunye version

prints the version you installed, for example:

Ubunye Engine v0.9.0

See which engines you can run on, and what each can do:

ubunye backends

With only the pandas extra, part of it looks like this:

pandas
  features:     partitioned_writes, path_io, records
  file formats: csv, json, parquet
  write modes:  append, errorifexists, ignore, overwrite, overwrite_partitions
  distributed:  no   needs Java: no

ubunye doctor goes further: it checks the backends, the plugins and, given a task, the environment variables its config needs, and says what would fail and why.

docs.title: System requirements
docs.text:
Requirement Tested Python 3.10, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 Operating system Linux, Windows, macOS pandas backend pandas 2.2 or newer (pandas 3 works) with pyarrow 14 or newer (24 or newer on Windows) Spark 4 backend Java 17 or 21 Spark 3.5 backend Java 8, 11 or 17

The pandas backend needs no Java at all. To check for Java, run java -version; Spark also finds it through JAVA_HOME. ubunye doctor warns when PySpark is installed and no Java is found.

The oldest versions listed are the ones the package accepts, and CI installs exactly those and runs the tests on them.

Databricks

On Databricks the cluster already has PySpark installed. Install only the core package on the driver: 

%pip install ubunye-engine

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
Your first task, running on your laptop in a few minutes, with no Java and no cloud account. For anyone new to Ubunye. The commands in step 2 are run by the test suite exactly as written, on every change, so they work as shown.

New words (use case, pipeline, task, run record) are explained in Concepts.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
pip install "ubunye-engine[pandas]"

The pandas extra is what lets a task run with no Spark and no Java. (Add [spark] later to run the same task on Spark.)

docs.title: 2. Make a task, check it, run it
docs.text:
ubunye init -d pipelines -u demo -p starter -t filter_adults
ubunye plan -d pipelines -u demo -p starter -t filter_adults --backend pandas
ubunye run -d pipelines -u demo -p starter -t filter_adults --backend pandas --lineage
ubunye lineage list -d pipelines -u demo -p starter -t filter_adults

What each one did:

  1. init made a task folder, and the folder is the whole task. -d is the pipelines folder, -u the use case, -p the pipeline, -t the task:

    pipelines/demo/starter/filter_adults/
    config.yaml          reads data/people.csv, writes output/adults as Parquet
    transformations.py   keeps the people aged 18 and over
    data/people.csv      eight people, some of them children
    notebooks/           a notebook for trying things step by step

    In config.yaml, input and output both say format: s3. That is the file connector: s3 means any file path, on your disk or in a cloud bucket, not only Amazon S3.

  2. plan checked everything it could without moving any data: the input file is there, the transform loads, the write mode makes sense, and the pandas backend can do all of it. It exits 1 if anything would stop the run.

  3. run read the CSV, kept the adults, and wrote pipelines/demo/starter/filter_adults/output/adults/ as Parquet. With --backend pandas that happens in plain Python, no Java involved.

  4. lineage list shows the run record the run left (--lineage wrote it): when it ran, how it went, how many rows came out. Each record also keeps a hash of every row read and written, so two runs can be compared exactly.

    RUN_ID     STARTED              STATUS        DUR  ROWS
------------------------------------------------------------
dede6d1c  2026-11-10T10:34:34  success      0.3s  in:8  out:5

    Your run ID and time will differ.

If a command fails because of the machine (no Java, an old pyarrow, a missing environment variable), ubunye doctor says which, and how to fix it. See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: 3. Change it
docs.text:
Open transformations.py:

class FilterAdults(Task):
    def transform(self, sources):
        people = sources["people"]
        return {"adults": people[people["age"] >= 18]}

Change 18 to 21 and run it again, with --lineage so it leaves a record:

ubunye run -d pipelines -u demo -p starter -t filter_adults --backend pandas --lineage
ubunye lineage list -d pipelines -u demo -p starter -t filter_adults

The list now shows two runs, newest first:

RUN_ID     STARTED              STATUS        DUR  ROWS
------------------------------------------------------------
9913a5f1  2026-11-10T10:34:39  success      0.3s  in:8  out:4
dede6d1c  2026-11-10T10:34:34  success      0.3s  in:8  out:5

Compare them. Put your own two run IDs in place of these:

ubunye lineage compare -d pipelines -u demo -p starter -t filter_adults \
  --run-id1 dede6d1c --run-id2 9913a5f1

  code_hash: sha256:b6e66360... -> sha256:49d550bd...  CHANGED
  Input 'people':
      row_count: 8  (unchanged)
      data_hash: sha256:00d7526f...  (unchanged)
  Output 'adults':
      row_count: 5 -> 4  CHANGED
      data_hash: sha256:622fcbc6... -> sha256:7420fc72...  CHANGED

(Shortened here: the real output prints full hashes, plus the config, schema and environment hashes.) The code changed, the input stayed the same, and the output lost one row.

The line people[people["age"] >= 18] means the same thing in pandas and in Spark, which is why this task can run on either.

docs.title: 4. Run the same folder on Spark
docs.text:
You need Java (which version) and pip install "ubunye-engine[spark]". Change 21 back to 18 in transformations.py, then run without --backend:

ubunye run -d pipelines -u demo -p starter -t filter_adults --lineage

Now check that Spark wrote exactly what pandas wrote. List the runs, then compare the Spark run (the newest) with your first pandas run (the oldest, the same code):

ubunye lineage list -d pipelines -u demo -p starter -t filter_adults
ubunye lineage compare -d pipelines -u demo -p starter -t filter_adults \
  --run-id1 <pandas run id> --run-id2 <spark run id>

When the two backends agree, every hash says (unchanged) and only the time differs:

  status: success  (unchanged)
  duration_sec: 0.27769826199801173 -> 2.659492216000217  CHANGED
  config_hash: sha256:8bd62c96...  (unchanged)
  code_hash: sha256:b6e66360...  (unchanged)
  Input 'people':
      row_count: 8  (unchanged)
      data_hash: sha256:00d7526f...  (unchanged)
  Output 'adults':
      row_count: 5  (unchanged)
      schema_hash: sha256:9c8ec3b8...  (unchanged)
      data_hash: sha256:622fcbc6...  (unchanged)

Same folder, same config, same rows. On Databricks the notebook's session is used automatically.

docs.title: 5. From Python
docs.text:
import ubunye

outputs = ubunye.run_task("pipelines/demo/starter/filter_adults", backend="pandas")
print(len(outputs["adults"]))   # a pandas DataFrame

docs.title: Common errors
docs.text:
Every error says what went wrong, where, and what to try.

More symptoms and fixes: Troubleshooting.

A typo in a field name

Unknown fields in pipelines/demo/starter/filter_adults/config.yaml:

  (top level):
    Unknown field 'ENGNE'
    Did you mean 'ENGINE'?

A template variable with no value

Template resolution failed for .../config.yaml:
  Undefined variable 'region' in config value '.../{{ region }}'. ...

Pass it with --var region=gauteng, or give it a default: {{ region | default('gauteng') }}.

Something the backend cannot do

[ERROR] Run refused for copy: This task cannot run on the pandas backend:
  - input 'orders' uses the 'hive' connector, which needs spark; the pandas backend does not provide it.

ubunye plan --backend pandas finds these before anything runs.

See the full Error Reference.

docs.title: Project Structure
docs.text: A Ubunye project has three levels of folders: a use case holds pipelines, and a pipeline holds tasks that run in order. A task is one folder with a config.yaml (what to read and write) and a transformations.py (how to change the data). The folder path and the ubunye run flags name the same task.

docs.title: Recommended layout
docs.text:
This example has one use case, fraud_detection, with two pipelines. The ingestion pipeline has two tasks, and the claim_etl task folder is shown in full:

my_project/
├── pipelines/                     ← pipelines folder (-d)
│   ├── fraud_detection/           ← use case (-u)
│   │   ├── ingestion/             ← pipeline (-p)
│   │   │   ├── claim_etl/         ← task (-t): this folder is the task folder
│   │   │   │   ├── config.yaml
│   │   │   │   ├── transformations.py
│   │   │   │   ├── data/claims.csv              ← sample input the config reads
│   │   │   │   └── notebooks/
│   │   │   │       └── claim_etl_dev.ipynb      ← notebook for trying it step by step
│   │   │   └── policy_etl/        ← another task in the same pipeline
│   │   └── risk_scoring/          ← another pipeline
│   └── .ubunye/
│       ├── lineage/               ← run records (--lineage), under the -d folder
│       └── leases/                ← which batches already ran (safe reruns)
├── .ubunye/
│   └── model_store/               ← model registry files (wherever your config's store points)
└── pyproject.toml

To run the claim_etl task: ubunye run -d pipelines -u fraud_detection -p ingestion -t claim_etl.

ubunye init -d pipelines -u fraud_detection -p ingestion -t claim_etl makes the claim_etl folder for you. Its starter sample is data/people.csv with a task that keeps the adults (the one in the Quickstart); replace both with your own data and code.

docs.title: Task folder
docs.text:
File Purpose config.yaml Declares inputs, transform, outputs, engine, orchestration transformations.py Python transform (Task subclass) model.py Optional ML model (UbunyeModel subclass), imported by transformations.py data/ Optional sample input. The config reads it through {{ task_dir }}, which is the task folder notebooks/<task>_dev.ipynb Interactive dev notebook (Databricks-ready)

Every task is self-contained. The config is the single source of truth for what runs and where.

docs.title: config.yaml skeleton
docs.text:
This one runs as it stands, on pandas or Spark: it reads the CSV in the task folder and writes Parquet next to it. format: s3 is the file connector; s3 means any file path, local or in the cloud.

MODEL: etl          # or ml
VERSION: "1.0.0"    # semver

ENGINE:             # Spark settings; the pandas backend ignores them
  spark_conf:
    spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: "200"
  profiles:
    DEV:            # the default profile; names are matched exactly, case included
      spark_conf:
        spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: "4"
    PROD:
      spark_conf:
        spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: "400"

CONFIG:
  inputs:
    claims:
      format: s3
      path: "{{ task_dir }}/data/claims.csv"
      file_format: csv
      options:
        header: "true"
        inferSchema: "true"

  transform: {}     # optional: leave out type to use the Task class in transformations.py

  outputs:
    clean_claims:
      format: s3
      path: "{{ task_dir }}/output/clean_claims"
      file_format: parquet
      mode: overwrite   # the write mode

ORCHESTRATION:      # optional: used by `ubunye export`, not by `ubunye run`
  type: airflow
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  retries: 3
  owner: data-engineering

On Spark you can also read and write tables, for example format: hive (with db_name and tbl_name) or format: delta. Those need Spark: the pandas backend cannot serve hive, jdbc, unity or delta, and ubunye plan --backend pandas says so before a run. See Connectors.

docs.title: Environment profiles
docs.text:
A profile is a named set of Spark settings under ENGINE.profiles, picked with -m/--mode. Profiles let you change Spark settings per environment without copying the YAML:

ENGINE:
  spark_conf:
    spark.executor.memory: "8g"
  profiles:
    DEV:
      spark_conf:
        spark.executor.memory: "512m"
        spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: "4"
    PROD:
      spark_conf:
        spark.executor.memory: "32g"

Select at runtime:

ubunye run -d pipelines -u fraud_detection -p ingestion -t claim_etl           # -m defaults to DEV
ubunye run -d pipelines -u fraud_detection -p ingestion -t claim_etl -m PROD

Or via the Python API:

import ubunye

ubunye.run_task(task_dir="pipelines/fraud_detection/ingestion/claim_etl", mode="PROD")

Profile names are matched exactly: -m prod does not find a PROD profile. When a config has profiles and none matches the mode, the run stops with an error that lists the profiles it has. A config with no profiles runs in any mode. More on profiles: Engine and Profiles.
