docs.title: Writing a transform that gives the same answer on pandas and Spark
docs.text: A transform written with Narwhals runs on pandas and on Spark unchanged. Running is not the same as agreeing. This page is for anyone writing a transform that must give the same answer on both. It lists the places where the same line of code gave different numbers, each found by running a real workload on both engines and comparing the run records with ubunye prove. Each has a fix that holds on both. To check your own task, jump to How to know. Why it works this way: ADR 005.

docs.title: Rounding: round halves yourself
docs.text:
.round(4) rounds a half up on Spark and to the even neighbour on pandas. A monthly mean of 921.03125 became 921.0313 on Spark and 921.0312 on pandas; 43 of 6,366 monthly food prices differed this way in the food prices example.

def round4(expr):
    return (expr * 10000 + 0.5).floor() / 10000   # half up, on every engine

Expr.floor needs Narwhals 2.9 or later.

docs.title: Means and sums of floats: add integers
docs.text:
A sum of floating-point numbers depends on the order it is added in, and engines add in different orders (pandas pairwise, Spark partition by partition). The results differ in their last bits, which is invisible until a value sits on a rounding boundary: after fixing the rounding, 7 monthly prices still differed by 0.0001. Turn the values into whole units first; an integer sum is exact in any order:

micro = (nw.col("price") * 1_000_000 + 0.5).floor().cast(nw.Int64)
monthly = prices.with_columns(micro=micro).group_by(...).agg(
    total=nw.col("micro").sum(), n=nw.len(),
).with_columns(mean_price=round4(nw.col("total") / nw.col("n") / 1_000_000))

Money in integer cents from the start (as in the proving workload C01) avoids the question altogether.

docs.title: Casts inside a group-by: cast after it
docs.text:
On pandas, Narwhals 2.26 dropped a .cast(nw.Int64) written inside a group-by that also computed a mean: the counts came out as float64, and the schema no longer matched Spark's bigint (reported to Narwhals as narwhals#4005). Cast after the aggregation:

agg = df.group_by("k").agg(n=nw.len(), m=nw.col("x").mean())
agg = agg.with_columns(nw.col("n").cast(nw.Int64))

docs.title: Replacing text: replace_all, literal
docs.text: str.replace is not implemented for Spark in Narwhals; it raises NotImplementedError. str.replace_all(" KG", "", literal=True) works on both.

docs.title: Casting text to numbers: filter first, then cast
docs.text:
"25 KG" to 25 is a cast of text to a number. When some rows cannot be cast, pandas raises, Spark 3.5 quietly makes them null, and Spark 4 (ANSI mode) raises. Keep only the rows that can be cast, then cast:

weights = df.filter(nw.col("unit").str.contains("^[0-9.]+ KG$").fill_null(False))
weights = weights.with_columns(
    kg=nw.col("unit").str.replace_all(" KG", "", literal=True).cast(nw.Float64)
)

docs.title: Time: say which zone
docs.text: Cutting a timestamp into a day or an hour depends on a time zone. Every Ubunye backend uses UTC unless the task sets spark.sql.session.timeZone. In older versions, local Spark used the machine's own zone without saying so. A task that means local days sets the key. Why it works this way: ADR 007.

docs.title: Days between two dates: count with whole numbers
docs.text:
Narwhals cannot subtract two timestamps on Spark (dt.total_seconds and dt.timestamp are not implemented there), and on pandas dt.ordinal_day() fails on a column with a null in it, which a delivery date often has. The Olist example turns each date into a day number with whole number arithmetic on the year, month and day, which every engine does alike, and subtracts:

def day_number(ts):
    month = ts.dt.month().cast(nw.Int64)
    y = ts.dt.year().cast(nw.Int64) - nw.when(month <= 2).then(1).otherwise(0)
    march_based = nw.when(month >= 3).then(month - 3).otherwise(month + 9)
    day_of_year = (march_based * 153 + 2) // 5 + ts.dt.day().cast(nw.Int64) - 1
    return (y * 365 + y // 4 - y // 100 + y // 400 + day_of_year).cast(nw.Int64)

Two smaller traps met on the way: pandas 2 has no modulo (%) on Arrow backed integers (Ubunye's pandas backend reads into Arrow), and Narwhals has no when().when(): nest a second when inside otherwise.

docs.title: Null group keys: keep them on purpose
docs.text: Spark keeps rows whose group key is null as one group; plain pandas drops them. Narwhals follows Spark only when asked: group_by(..., drop_null_keys=False).

docs.title: How to know
docs.text:
Run the task on both engines with --lineage and compare:

T="-d pipelines -u shop -p orders -t clean"
ubunye run $T --backend pandas --lineage && ubunye prove observe --workload my-task --env pandas-local $T -o evidence
ubunye run $T --backend spark  --lineage && ubunye prove observe --workload my-task --env spark-local  $T -o evidence
ubunye prove report evidence --workload my-task --reference spark-local

prove observe reads the task's latest run record (--run-id picks another), so observe each run right after it.

A data FAIL with schema and rows PASS is usually one of the traps above: compare the two outputs row by row on the columns that are computed.

docs.title: Run records
docs.text:
A run record is what one run leaves behind: what it read, what it wrote, how many rows, a hash of every row, and the code, config and machine it ran with. This guide is for anyone who wants to know what a run did, or whether two runs gave the same data.

  • The problem: a job ran, and you need to know what it read, what it wrote, and whether today's output is the same as yesterday's.
  • When to use it: on every run you may need to explain later, and in CI to catch a change in the data before it merges.
  • The one command: add --lineage to ubunye run.
ubunye run -d pipelines -u demo -p starter -t filter_adults --backend pandas --lineage -dt 2026-11-01

The examples below use the task ubunye init -d pipelines -u demo -p starter -t filter_adults makes, run on the pandas backend. The output is real.

docs.title: Make one
docs.text:
ubunye run -d pipelines -u demo -p starter -t filter_adults --backend pandas --lineage -dt 2026-11-01

Starting task: filter_adults (Mode: DEV, Deploy: client)
[OK] Run complete for filter_adults

ubunye test run writes a run record by default (--no-lineage turns it off). In Python, pass lineage=True to ubunye.run_task or ubunye.run_pipeline.

docs.title: Where it is stored
docs.text:
By default, one JSON file per run under the pipelines folder:

pipelines/.ubunye/lineage/demo/starter/filter_adults/129fca30-185a-427d-b98a-7cf0c8dc9022.json

That is the filesystem store. Jobs that share no disk can share a Delta table instead (--lineage-backend delta). Every store and its flags: Where run records are stored.

docs.title: What it holds
docs.text: Part Fields What it tells you Who run_id, task_path, usecase, package (the pipeline), task_name, profile, model, version Which task ran, with which profile and task version When started_at, ended_at, duration_sec, timings (each read, transform and write) How long it took, and where the time went Outcome status (success, error, running, interrupted), error Whether it worked Inputs and outputs name, location, row_count, schema_hash, data_hash What was read and written, and a hash over every row Code and config code_hash, config_hash, variables (dt, --var, mode) Whether the code or config changed Environment environment (Python, platform, package versions), environment_hash, backend, engine_version What it ran on Other expectations, llm_calls, llm_budget, model_runs, time_zone Data checks, model calls and model training, when the task has them

docs.title: Read one
docs.text:
List the runs of a task, newest first:

ubunye lineage list -d pipelines -u demo -p starter -t filter_adults

------------------------------------------------------------
Task: demo/starter/filter_adults
------------------------------------------------------------
RUN_ID     STARTED              STATUS        DUR  ROWS
------------------------------------------------------------
cf99c8f0  2026-11-10T10:36:01  success      0.2s  in:8  out:5
129fca30  2026-11-10T10:35:55  success      0.3s  in:8  out:5

Show one (the latest, or --run-id), as JSON:

ubunye lineage show -d pipelines -u demo -p starter -t filter_adults

{
  "run_id": "129fca30-185a-427d-b98a-7cf0c8dc9022",
  "task_path": "demo/starter/filter_adults",
  "profile": "DEV",
  "config_hash": "sha256:10b2e1c5...",
  "status": "success",
  "inputs": [
    {
      "name": "people",
      "location": ".../filter_adults/data/people.csv",
      "row_count": 8,
      "schema_hash": "sha256:9c8ec3b8...",
      "data_hash": "sha256:00d7526f...",
      "hash_method": "rows-v1",
      "source_version": {"kind": "files", "files": 1, "bytes": 163, "etags": false, "...": "..."}
    }
  ],
  "outputs": [
    {"name": "adults", "row_count": 5, "data_hash": "sha256:622fcbc6...", "...": "..."}
  ],
  "backend": "pandas",
  "variables": {"dt": "2026-11-01", "mode": "DEV"},
  "code_hash": "sha256:b6e66360...",
  "environment_hash": "sha256:9753dc49...",
  "...": "..."
}

(Shortened here; the real output prints every field.) ubunye lineage trace prints the same run as a readable inputs, transform, outputs picture, and ubunye lineage search -d pipelines searches every task. Every flag: ubunye lineage.

docs.title: Compare two runs
docs.text:
lineage compare puts two records side by side. Here the input file was saved with its rows in the opposite order, then run again:

ubunye lineage compare -d pipelines -u demo -p starter -t filter_adults \
    --run-id1 129fca30-185a-427d-b98a-7cf0c8dc9022 --run-id2 cf99c8f0-dd67-43c5-8e73-5080235048bb

  status: success  (unchanged)
  duration_sec: 0.2550354539998807 -> 0.23477902000013273  CHANGED
  config_hash: sha256:10b2e1c5...  (unchanged)
  code_hash: sha256:b6e66360...  (unchanged)
  environment_hash: sha256:9753dc49...  (unchanged)
  Input 'people':
      row_count: 8  (unchanged)
      schema_hash: sha256:9c8ec3b8...  (unchanged)
      data_hash: sha256:00d7526f...  (unchanged)
  Output 'adults':
      row_count: 5  (unchanged)
      schema_hash: sha256:9c8ec3b8...  (unchanged)
      data_hash: sha256:622fcbc6...  (unchanged)

Same rows in another order: same hash. Now one cell changes (Lerato's age, 22 to 23):

  Input 'people':
      row_count: 8  (unchanged)
      data_hash: sha256:00d7526f... -> sha256:b1b01fe5...  CHANGED
  Output 'adults':
      row_count: 5  (unchanged)
      data_hash: sha256:622fcbc6... -> sha256:1e274b72...  CHANGED

The row counts match, but the hashes catch the change.

A data hash is compared only when both runs made it the same way. Two missing hashes show as "unknown", and a record from before 0.7.0 (which hashed a sample) shows as "not comparable" with a newer one.

docs.title: In CI: ubunye gate
docs.text:
gate compares the latest run with the one before (or any two) and exits 1 when the data changed without a version bump, or the run got slower or lost rows past a limit you set:

ubunye gate -d pipelines -u demo -p starter -t filter_adults

gate: demo/starter/filter_adults  cf99c8f0 -> 99b6d52a
[OK] run succeeded
[FAIL] data adults: changed without a VERSION bump (still 0.1.0); changed: input people

fails.

Setting it up in a pull request: Gate.

docs.title: What the hash promises
docs.text:
The data hash (rows-v1) is made from every row, not a sample.

Promise What it means for you Every row counts All rows are hashed, in the same pass as the row count Row order does not matter A shuffle or repartition gives the same hash Column order does not matter Columns are sorted by name first One changed cell changes it Any different value gives a different hash Null is not NaN The two give different hashes Same on every engine pandas and Spark give the same hash for the same data and types

If the rows cannot be read, the record has no data hash and says why (hash_error). It never puts the schema hash in its place.

docs.title: What an input's hash covers
docs.text:
An output is hashed from what the run wrote. An input is hashed from what the run read, but on Spark that happens at the end of the task, by reading the source again. So the record takes the source's version when the input is read, and again right after the hash. When the two differ, it says so:

"source_version": {"kind": "files", "files": 2, "bytes": 2030, "etags": false, "listing_hash": "sha256:..."},
"source_version_at_hash": {"kind": "files", "files": 2, "bytes": 2034, "etags": false, "listing_hash": "sha256:..."},
"source_changed": true,
"source_note": "The source changed between the read and the hash (2 files, 2030 bytes -> 2 files, 2034 bytes). This digest is of the later state, not of what the task read."

What the version is, by kind of input:

Input Its version Files files, bytes, latest_modified, etags, listing_hash, from Spark's own file index; nothing is read. Where the file system gives no content tags (etags: false: a local disk, HDFS), "unchanged" means the names, sizes and times are the same, and the note says so Delta The read is pinned to one version (by the config, or by the engine when the config names none), so the note says the hash is of what was read, and gives the table's latest_version at the hash as information A SQL query, JDBC, a catalog table that is not Delta "kind": "none", with the reason A listing that failed or took longer than UBUNYE_SOURCE_VERSION_TIMEOUT seconds (default 30) "kind": "none", with the reason Any input on pandas Recorded, but not checked again: the input is in memory, so the hash is of what was read

With LineageRecorder(hash_inputs=False) no version is taken. ubunye lineage trace prints the note, and lineage compare and ubunye gate do not treat such an input's hash as evidence.

docs.title: Large tables
docs.text:
On pandas, a table of 500,000 rows or more is hashed by helper processes. How many, how much memory, and how to cap them: The run record uses helper processes.

Why it works this way: ADR 006, ADR 011.

docs.title: Safe reruns
docs.text:
How Ubunye stops a batch landing twice when you run a task again, and how to replace or finish one on purpose. For anyone who runs jobs on a schedule or reruns a failed day.

  • The problem: a task that appends adds rows each time it runs. Run the same day twice, by hand or by a retry, and that day's rows are in the table twice.
  • When it bites: a scheduler retries a job; you rerun a backfill; a pipeline stopped half way and you start it again; a run crashed after it wrote.
  • The one command: run it again with --rerun to replace the batch, or --resume to finish a pipeline.
ubunye run -d pipelines -u shop -p daily -t load_orders -dt 2026-11-01 --rerun

docs.title: Words used here
docs.text:
• Batch: one task with its -dt and every --var value. -m and -dtf on their own do not name a batch, but -dtf is part of it once -dt is given. A run with no -dt and no --var has no batch, so nothing here applies to it.
  • Append task: a task with at least one output whose write mode is append. An output with no mode counts as append, since most writers default to it.
  • Overwrite task: a task whose outputs all replace what is there (overwrite, overwrite_partitions, merge). These were already safe to rerun.

docs.title: See it work
docs.text:
Two tasks from ubunye init, run on pandas: load_orders appends, summarise overwrites.

Run a finished batch again: refused.

ubunye run -d pipelines -u shop -p daily -t load_orders -dt 2026-11-01 --backend pandas
ubunye run -d pipelines -u shop -p daily -t load_orders -dt 2026-11-01 --backend pandas

Starting task: load_orders (Mode: DEV, Deploy: client)
[ERROR] Run refused for load_orders: shop/daily/load_orders already finished this batch (run 61475466 (finished 2026-11-10T10:35:29Z)) and appends to adults: running it again would add the batch twice.

  Finished: .../pipelines/.ubunye/leases/shop/daily/load_orders/08e84f1b8a561918.finished.json
  Hint: To replace the batch, run again with --rerun (rerun=True in Python). If each run adds new data to the same batch, give each run its own variable, for example --var hour=13.

It exits 1 with one line, no traceback. Nothing was written.

Replace it: --rerun.

ubunye run -d pipelines -u shop -p daily -t load_orders -dt 2026-11-01 --backend pandas --rerun

Starting task: load_orders (Mode: DEV, Deploy: client)
--rerun: replacing the batch written by run 61475466 (finished 2026-11-10T10:35:29Z); its 1 file(s) are removed once this run succeeds.
Replaced the batch: removed 1 file(s) of the earlier run.
[OK] Run complete for load_orders

Finish a pipeline that stopped half way: --resume. Here load_orders finished 2026-11-02 and summarise never ran:

ubunye run -d pipelines -u shop -p daily -t load_orders -t summarise -dt 2026-11-02 --backend pandas --resume

Starting task: load_orders (Mode: DEV, Deploy: client)
[SKIP] load_orders already finished this batch (--resume); kept as it is.
Starting task: summarise (Mode: DEV, Deploy: client)
[OK] Run complete for summarise

In Python: run_task(..., rerun=True), run_pipeline(..., rerun=True) and run_pipeline(..., resume=True). A task skipped by resume is not in the result.

docs.title: The rules, per kind of output
docs.text:
What happens when an append task's batch runs again, after it finished or after a crash:

Output Run again (finished) --rerun After a crash or failure Files on a local or shared disk, pandas Refused The earlier run's files are removed once the new run succeeds The run's own files are taken back Files on a local or shared disk, Spark (parquet, csv, json, orc, avro, text) Refused As for pandas As for pandas Delta (path or table), with replace_where Refused The batch's rows are replaced in one commit The rerun replaces the batch's rows Delta (path or table), no replace_where Refused Appended again, and the run warns at its start A retry adds nothing: Delta skips a batch it already committed, and the run warns that the batch was already there JDBC, with replace_where Refused Staged, then moved in by one transaction that replaces the batch's rows A kill before the commit changes nothing; after it, the rerun replaces the batch JDBC, no replace_where Refused Appended again, and the run says so Named in the log and the run record, not repaired A catalog table that is not Delta Refused Appended again, and the run says so Named, not repaired Spark to object storage (s3a://, abfss://, gs://, dbfs:/) or HDFS Refused Appended again, and the run says so Named, not repaired

For an output in the last three rows that must land once, write it with mode: overwrite_partitions and partitionBy, or overwrite, or merge. How to set replace_where: Files and Delta and JDBC.

docs.title: Overwrite tasks
docs.text: Never refused. An overwrite output is replaced in one step, and overwrite_partitions replaces only the partitions the new data fills, so a rerun of a day replaces that day. Write modes: Inputs and outputs.

docs.title: --rerun
docs.text:
• Replaces a batch a finished run appended. Use it for a backfill or a correction.
  • The earlier run's files are removed only after the new run has committed. A crash before that keeps the old batch (the new files are taken back); a crash after it is finished by the next run.
  • It removes the files the earlier run wrote, wherever they are, even if the output's path changed since. Files moved or compacted by something else since are not found: --rerun then removes nothing and appends, and the log says how many files it removed.
  • Why not replace by default: an hourly job with the same -dt would then delete the morning's rows at noon. If each run adds new rows to the same batch, give each run its own variable instead, such as --var hour=13.

docs.title: --resume
docs.text:
• Skips each task that already finished this batch, with [SKIP], and runs the rest.
  • A task that appends is known to have finished from its output. A task that only overwrites is known to have finished only from its run records: with --lineage it is skipped when its latest run of the batch succeeded; without --lineage it runs again. That is safe (it replaces its output), but it does the work twice.
  • Why not skip by default: in an hourly pipeline (same dt, one task appends, the next overwrites) a silent skip dropped the first task's new rows and exited 0.

docs.title: Two runs at once, crashes and leases
docs.text:
• A lease per batch. While a run works, it holds a lease: a small file under <pipelines folder>/.ubunye/leases/, naming the run, its process, host and a heartbeat. A second run of the same batch is refused while the first lives, naming it. Runs of different batches never block each other.
  • A dead run is taken over. A lease whose process is gone (same machine), or whose file has not been touched for 15 minutes (another machine on a shared disk), belongs to a dead run. The next run takes it over, marks the dead run's record interrupted, and takes back the files it appended.
  • Only a run's own files are removed. Each file is claimed in the lease before it lands. No output folder is ever listed to decide what to delete, so another run's files are never touched.
  • A file that cannot be removed (a reader has it open, common on Windows) stays in the lease: the next run takes it back, or refuses and names the file.
  • A run that lost its lease stops, and its record says interrupted, never success.
  • Do not delete a lease of a run that may be alive: it holds that run's claims.
  • A finished run leaves <key>.finished.json beside its lease. That note is what makes the next run of the batch refuse. Notes are small, one per task and batch, and nothing removes them.
  • On by default. UBUNYE_RUN_LEASE=off turns leases off; then a run appends plainly (Delta replace_where still replaces).

docs.title: What it does not cover
docs.text:
• Cloud jobs on their own disks. The lease and the finished note live in the pipelines folder, so they protect runs that share it: one machine, or a shared disk. A cloud job that starts on a fresh disk sees neither.
  • A different spelling is a different batch. The same -dt with another -dtf, another -m spelling or an extra --var is not refused while the first runs, and does not take back a dead run's files. Rerun with the same values.
  • Batches finished before 0.8 left no note, so they are not refused.
  • macOS: a process start time is not read, so a dead run whose process id was reused looks alive until that process ends.
  • Lineage off, narrow window: a successful run killed after its success is recorded but before it marks its lease done counts as finished when lineage is on. With lineage off, the next run can take its appends back and write the batch itself.
  • Delta retention: Delta forgets a committed batch after delta.setTransactionRetentionDuration, when a table sets it; a retry after that appends again. A config that sets its own txnAppId or txnVersion is left alone.
  • JDBC with replace_where needs a classic Spark session (Spark Connect is refused with a clear error) and a database user that may create and drop a table in the target's schema. The predicate is in the database's SQL dialect.

Why: ADR 008.

docs.title: Model Contract: UbunyeModel
docs.text:
For anyone writing a model class that Ubunye can train, save, register and load.

UbunyeModel is the base class every model you write must fill in. It is the only thing the engine ever calls on your model. The engine itself imports no ML library.

docs.title: The contract
docs.text:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from typing import Any, Dict

class UbunyeModel(ABC):

    @abstractmethod
    def train(self, df: Any) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """Train on df. Returns a metrics dict e.g. {"auc": 0.94, "f1": 0.87}."""

    @abstractmethod
    def predict(self, df: Any) -> Any:
        """Generate predictions. Returns df-like with prediction columns added."""

    @abstractmethod
    def save(self, path: str) -> None:
        """Serialize model to path. Pick any format: pickle, joblib, ONNX, …"""

    @classmethod
    @abstractmethod
    def load(cls, path: str) -> "UbunyeModel":
        """Deserialize from path. Returns a ready-to-predict instance."""

    @abstractmethod
    def metadata(self) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """Return at minimum: library, library_version, features, params."""

    def validate(self, df: Any) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """Optional holdout validation. Default raises NotImplementedError."""
        raise NotImplementedError("validate() not implemented")

docs.title: Why this contract?
docs.text:
The engine never imports sklearn, torch, xgboost, or any ML library. It only calls train(), predict(), save(), and load(). The implementation is entirely yours.

This gives you:

  • Library freedom: wrap any ML framework without engine changes.
  • Testability: test your model class with plain unit tests and a small fake data frame (a MockDF, see below); no Spark needed.
  • Registry integration: ModelRegistry.register() calls save() and stores metadata() and the metrics train() returned.

docs.title: Minimal implementation (sklearn)
docs.text:
# model.py  (in your task folder)
import joblib
from pathlib import Path
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, f1_score
from ubunye.models.base import UbunyeModel

class FraudRiskModel(UbunyeModel):

    def __init__(self):
        self._clf = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=100, max_depth=4)
        self._features = ["amount_sum_30d", "txn_count_30d", "avg_amount_30d", "risk_encoded"]

    def train(self, df) -> dict:
        pdf = df.toPandas()
        X, y = pdf[self._features], pdf["is_fraud"]
        self._clf.fit(X, y)
        proba = self._clf.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
        preds = self._clf.predict(X)
        return {
            "auc": float(roc_auc_score(y, proba)),
            "f1":  float(f1_score(y, preds)),
        }

    def predict(self, df):
        pdf = df.toPandas()
        pdf["fraud_score"]     = self._clf.predict_proba(pdf[self._features])[:, 1]
        pdf["fraud_predicted"] = self._clf.predict(pdf[self._features])
        return df.sparkSession.createDataFrame(pdf)

    def save(self, path: str) -> None:
        Path(path).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        joblib.dump(self._clf, f"{path}/model.pkl")

    @classmethod
    def load(cls, path: str) -> "FraudRiskModel":
        m = cls()
        m._clf = joblib.load(f"{path}/model.pkl")
        return m

    def metadata(self) -> dict:
        return {
            "library":         "scikit-learn",
            "library_version": "1.4.0",
            "features":        self._features,
            "params":          self._clf.get_params(),
        }

docs.title: train(): return value
docs.text:
train() must return a dict of metric name → numeric value. These metrics are stored in the registry and used by promotion gates.

return {
    "auc":      0.92,
    "f1":       0.87,
    "accuracy": 0.95,
    "loss":     0.08,
}

A promotion gate can only check a metric that train() returns. The sklearn model above returns auc and f1, so min_auc works and max_loss would block every promotion. See Promotion gates.

docs.title: predict(): return value
docs.text: predict() receives the same type of object train() received (a Spark DataFrame, a pandas DataFrame, or anything with the methods your model calls) and should return a DataFrame-like with prediction columns added. Return it from your task's transform() under an output name and the engine writes it like any other output.

docs.title: metadata(): required keys
docs.text:
The metadata() dict must contain at minimum:

Key Type Description library string ML library used (e.g. "scikit-learn", "xgboost", "pytorch") library_version string Version string features list of strings Input feature column names params dict Hyperparameters

Additional keys are stored but not validated.

features is also the model's input contract at predict. A ModelTransform predict compares the frame's columns with it before calling the model. Extra columns are fine. By default a missing column is a warning on the log and the run record; with registry.check_features: true the frame is refused with FeatureContractError, which names the missing columns, the model and the version. If your predict() builds some declared features itself, leave the check at its default or set check_features: false. A model that declares no features is not checked. Only names are checked: dtypes are not stored.

Why it works this way: ADR 012.

docs.title: Testing your model (Spark-free)
docs.text:
A MockDF is a tiny stand-in for a Spark DataFrame that you write in your test. It has only the methods your model calls (here toPandas() and count()), so the model can't tell the difference and you need no Spark to test it:

import pytest
from model import FraudRiskModel

class MockDF:
    def __init__(self, rows):
        self._rows = rows
    def toPandas(self):
        import pandas as pd
        return pd.DataFrame(self._rows)
    def count(self): return len(self._rows)

def test_train_returns_metrics(tmp_path):
    model = FraudRiskModel()
    rows = [
        {"amount_sum_30d": 100, "txn_count_30d": 5, "avg_amount_30d": 20, "risk_encoded": 0, "is_fraud": 0},
        {"amount_sum_30d": 900, "txn_count_30d": 2, "avg_amount_30d": 450, "risk_encoded": 2, "is_fraud": 1},
    ] * 50
    metrics = model.train(MockDF(rows))
    assert "auc" in metrics
    assert "f1" in metrics
    model.save(str(tmp_path / "model"))
    loaded = FraudRiskModel.load(str(tmp_path / "model"))
    assert loaded is not None

docs.title: Training in a task
docs.text:
Train and register the model from the task's transformations.py; model.py sits next to it and imports as from model import FraudRiskModel. A model registered inside a run records that run's id. The full example is in Transform: Training a model.

A task's config.yaml cannot run the model by naming type: model: a task always runs its transformations.py. The type is not run: ubunye run warns (FutureWarning), and ubunye plan and ubunye validate report it. To use the registry: settings from config.yaml, call ModelTransform from transformations.py; see Registry settings for a model transform.

See Model Registry for the full registry reference.

docs.title: Abstract enforcement
docs.text:
UbunyeModel is a strict ABC. Any class that does not implement all five abstract methods (train, predict, save, load, metadata) will raise TypeError on instantiation:

class IncompleteModel(UbunyeModel):
    def train(self, df): return {}
    # missing predict, save, load, metadata

IncompleteModel()   # TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class IncompleteModel

This is checked by unit tests and when the model class is instantiated.

docs.title: Model Registry
docs.text:
For anyone who trains models with Ubunye and needs to keep versions, move them from test to live, and roll back. The registry works with any ML library.

  • The problem: you train a new model every week. You need to know which version is live, which data made it, and you need a safe way to swap it.
  • When to use it: as soon as a model leaves your laptop.
  • The one command: ubunye models list --use-case fraud_detection --model FraudRiskModel --store .ubunye/model_store

How a task uses the registry

A task always runs its transformations.py. You train and register a model there, in Python: see Transform: Training a model, the page that owns that topic. Naming type: model under transform: in config.yaml does not run a model: ubunye run warns (FutureWarning) and still runs transformations.py. The transform.params block (with its registry: settings) is read only when your transformations.py hands it to ModelTransform, as shown in Registry settings for a model transform.

docs.title: Lifecycle stages
docs.text:
Stage Meaning development Freshly registered; not yet validated staging Passed quality gates; ready for shadow or canary testing production Live; serving predictions archived Replaced or retired; kept for audit

Every register() call creates a development version. Promotion moves a version up the chain; demotion moves it down or to archived.

docs.title: Storage layout
docs.text:
{store_path}/
└── {use_case}/
    └── {model_name}/
        ├── registry.json          ← version index (all metadata)
        └── versions/
            └── 1.0.0/
                ├── model/         ← opaque artifact (from model.save())
                ├── metadata.json  ← model.metadata() output
                └── metrics.json   ← train() metrics

The engine calls model.save(path). The artifact format (pickle, ONNX, pt, …) is yours.

docs.title: List versions
docs.text:
ubunye models list \
    --use-case fraud_detection \
    --model FraudRiskModel \
    --store .ubunye/model_store

Output:

  Version      Stage          Registered                    Key metrics
  ------------ -------------- ---------------------------- ------------------------------
  1.3.0        production     2024-06-15T02:10:00.512301   auc=0.930, f1=0.880
  1.2.0        staging        2024-06-10T01:45:00.104877   auc=0.910, f1=0.870
  1.1.0        archived       2024-06-01T00:30:00.861020   auc=0.880, f1=0.850

Add --json to list (and to compare) for one JSON document, for scripts and agents. Every models command takes --backend / -b (see Choosing a backend).

docs.title: Show version details
docs.text:
ubunye models info \
    --use-case fraud_detection \
    --model FraudRiskModel \
    --version 1.3.0 \
    --store .ubunye/model_store

Prints the version as JSON: timestamps, metrics, metadata and the id of the run that registered it.

docs.title: Promote
docs.text:
ubunye models promote \
    --use-case fraud_detection \
    --model FraudRiskModel \
    --version 1.3.0 \
    --to production \
    --promoted-by alice \
    --store .ubunye/model_store

Promoting to production automatically archives the current production version. --to takes staging or production. The version must pass the promotion gates stored with the model (see below); --force skips them, prints a warning and records on the version that it was forced.

docs.title: Demote
docs.text:
ubunye models demote \
    --use-case fraud_detection \
    --model FraudRiskModel \
    --version 1.3.0 \
    --to staging \
    --store .ubunye/model_store

--to takes development, staging or archived. Demote only moves a version down: staging only from production, and never to production. Moving up is a promotion, so it goes through promote and its gates. The Python API (ModelRegistry.demote) refuses the same moves with a RegistryError.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
Restores a previous version to production and archives the current one:

ubunye models rollback \
    --use-case fraud_detection \
    --model FraudRiskModel \
    --version 1.2.0 \
    --store .ubunye/model_store

docs.title: Archive
docs.text:
ubunye models archive \
    --use-case fraud_detection \
    --model FraudRiskModel \
    --version 1.1.0 \
    --store .ubunye/model_store

docs.title: Compare metrics
docs.text:
ubunye models compare \
    --use-case fraud_detection \
    --model FraudRiskModel \
    --versions 1.2.0 --versions 1.3.0 \
    --store .ubunye/model_store

Give --versions twice, once per version. --versions 1.2.0 1.3.0 is refused.

Output:

  Comparing fraud_detection/FraudRiskModel: 1.2.0 vs 1.3.0

  Metric               v1.2.0             v1.3.0             Delta
  -------------------- ------------------ ------------------ ----------
  auc                  0.9100             0.9300             +0.0200
  f1                   0.8700             0.8800             +0.0100
  accuracy             0.9400             0.9500             +0.0100

docs.title: Promotion gates
docs.text: A gate is a rule a version must pass before it moves up (to staging or production). If any gate fails, the version does not move.

docs.title: Gate types
docs.text:
Key pattern Passes when min_<metric> The metric is >= the threshold max_<metric> The metric is <= the threshold require_drift_check metadata()["drift_check_passed"] is True (see Drift Detection)

<metric> is a name your model's train() returns. The model on Model Contract returns auc and f1, so its gates are min_auc and min_f1.

Three rules that surprise people

  • A missing metric blocks. A gate on a metric the model never returned (say max_loss when train() returns only auc and f1) fails every time, with Metric 'loss' not found in model metrics.
  • Stored gates cover every version of the model. Gates you pass to register(..., promotion_gates=...) are stored with the model, not with that one version. The newest stored set is checked for every later promotion of any version, including older ones, and including ubunye models promote. Registering 1.0.1 with gates also blocks 1.0.0 if 1.0.0 fails them.
  • gates= on one promote() call replaces the stored gates for that one promotion only.

docs.title: Store gates with the model
docs.text:
mv = registry.register(
    "fraud_detection", "FraudRiskModel", None, model, metrics,
    promotion_gates={"min_auc": 0.85, "min_f1": 0.80},
)

ubunye models promote has no flag for gates. It checks the stored ones.

docs.title: Gates for one promotion
docs.text:
from ubunye.models import ModelRegistry, ModelStage

registry = ModelRegistry(".ubunye/model_store")
mv = registry.promote(
    use_case="fraud_detection",
    model_name="FraudRiskModel",
    version="1.3.0",
    to_stage=ModelStage.STAGING,
    gates={"min_auc": 0.85, "min_f1": 0.80, "require_drift_check": True},
    promoted_by="alice",
)

docs.title: When a gate fails
docs.text:
promote raises PromotionBlockedError (a kind of ValueError, importable from ubunye.core.errors). It names each failing gate with its actual value and threshold. The version stays where it was. The CLI prints the same message as an [ERROR] and exits 1:

Promotion blocked — 1 gate(s) failed:
  - require_drift_check: Drift check: not found or failed in metadata.

  Version:      1.0.1
  Target stage: staging
  Hint: Fix the failing gates or adjust thresholds in promotion_gates config.

ubunye models promote --force skips the gates, prints a warning and records on the version that it was forced.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
from ubunye.models import ModelRegistry, ModelStage, ModelVersion

registry = ModelRegistry(".ubunye/model_store")

# List all versions (newest first)
versions = registry.list_versions("fraud_detection", "FraudRiskModel")

# Get the production artifact path
artifact_path, mv = registry.get_model(
    "fraud_detection", "FraudRiskModel", stage=ModelStage.PRODUCTION
)
# Load via your own model class
from model import FraudRiskModel
model = FraudRiskModel.load(artifact_path)

# Promote
registry.promote("fraud_detection", "FraudRiskModel", "1.3.0", ModelStage.PRODUCTION)

# Rollback to a previous version
registry.rollback("fraud_detection", "FraudRiskModel", "1.2.0")

# Compare
diff = registry.compare_versions("fraud_detection", "FraudRiskModel", "1.2.0", "1.3.0")
# Returns: {"auc": {"a": 0.91, "b": 0.93, "delta": 0.02}, ...}

docs.title: Choosing a backend
docs.text:
Where models live is a plugin: a registry backend. Two ship with Ubunye:

Name What it does filesystem The default. A folder, or an s3://, gs:// or abfss:// URL. No cloud service needed. mlflow The MLflow Model Registry. Each version is a registered model version; stages are aliases. See MLflow Model Registry.

The backend is chosen in one order:

  1. the name you ask for: --backend / -b on every ubunye models command, registry.backend in a model transform, or backend= in Python;
  2. else the UBUNYE_REGISTRY_BACKEND environment variable;
  3. else filesystem.

The host never decides: running on Databricks does not switch you to MLflow. --store (or registry.store) is handed to the backend as it is.

ubunye models list -u fraud_detection -m FraudRiskModel -s .ubunye/model_store -b filesystem

# config.yaml: read by ModelTransform, called from your transformations.py
transform:
  params:
    action: train
    model_class: "model.FraudRiskModel"
    registry:
      store: ".ubunye/model_store"
      backend: filesystem      # optional
      use_case: fraud_detection

from ubunye.models import ModelRegistry, resolve_registry

registry = ModelRegistry(".ubunye/model_store", backend="filesystem")
backend = resolve_registry("filesystem", store=".ubunye/model_store")  # the raw backend

ubunye.models.backends.available() lists the installed names. Asking for one that is not installed fails with that list.

Why it works this way: ADR 010.

docs.title: MLflow Model Registry
docs.text:
--backend mlflow keeps models in the MLflow Model Registry.

  • Where MLflow is is MLflow's business: MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI and MLFLOW_REGISTRY_URI, read the way MLflow reads them.
  • --store is the MLflow experiment that holds one run per version. The run carries the saved model as its model artifact. Use a workspace path on Databricks, for example /Shared/ubunye/models.
  • The model is the registered model {use_case}.{model_name}. Set UBUNYE_MLFLOW_MODEL_NAME to change it, for example main.ml.{use_case}_{model_name} for a three part Unity Catalog name.
  • A version is a registered model version. The Ubunye version string, the stage, the metrics, the metadata, the promotion gates and the lineage run id are version tags (ubunye.version, ubunye.stage, ubunye.metric.<name>, ubunye.meta.<key>).
  • Stages staging and production are also MLflow aliases, so models:/fraud_detection.FraudRiskModel@production loads the production version from any MLflow client. development and archived are tags only: many versions can be in them at once, and an alias points at one.

If the experiment does not exist, Ubunye creates it, and MLflow picks where its artifacts go (./mlruns for a local SQLite store). Create the experiment yourself to choose another place.

The MLflow stage API is never used. It is deprecated, and Unity Catalog has none, so the same backend works there.

export MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI=sqlite:///mlflow.db
ubunye models promote -u fraud_detection -m FraudRiskModel -s ubunye-models \
  -b mlflow --version 1.0.1 --to production

The class used to be MLflowRegistryBackend: a folder registry that also logged a best effort MLflow run. It still works when you build it in Python, and warns that it is deprecated. Models it stored stay in their folder; read them with --backend filesystem.

Why it works this way: ADR 014.

docs.title: Writing a backend
docs.text:
A backend is a class with six methods, the RegistryBackend protocol: register, get, list_versions, promote, demote and delete. Its constructor takes the store string. Register it in your package:

[project.entry-points."ubunye.registry_backends"]
myreg = "my_package.registry:MyRegistryBackend"

pip install your package and --backend myreg works. No edit to Ubunye.

Keep it small. Ubunye does the rest on top of those six methods, for every backend: version numbers when none is given, refusing a duplicate version, promotion gates (stored as the promotion_gates metadata key and checked before promote is called), one production version at a time, rollback, archive and compare. Your backend must:

  • persist the metadata and lineage_run_id it is given and return them in ModelVersionInfo.metadata;
  • report stages with the public names (development, staging, production, archived), whatever it calls them inside;
  • raise VersionNotFoundError for a version or stage it does not have;
  • refuse a demote that moves a version up: call ubunye.models.lifecycle.check_demote(version, current_stage, to_stage) first;
  • return list_versions newest first;
  • return from get an artifact path that YourModel.load() can read.

Prove it with the conformance suite:

import pytest

from ubunye.testing.registry_conformance import RegistryConformance


class TestMyRegistry(RegistryConformance):
    @pytest.fixture
    def backend(self, tmp_path):
        return MyRegistryBackend(str(tmp_path / "store"))

docs.title: Auto-versioning
docs.text:
When register() is given version=None, the registry bumps the patch component of the highest existing version:

(no versions yet) → 1.0.0
1.0.0 → 1.0.1
1.2.3 → 1.2.4

To pin a specific version, pass it:

registry.register("fraud_detection", "FraudRiskModel", "2.0.0", model, metrics)

A version that already exists is refused with VersionExistsError.

docs.title: Lineage integration
docs.text:
A model registered inside a run (from a task's transformations.py) gets that run's ID in ModelVersion.lineage_run_id, unless you pass lineage_run_id= yourself. Run with --lineage so there is a run record to look the ID up in:

ubunye run -d pipelines -u fraud -p ml -t train --lineage
ubunye models info --use-case fraud_detection --model FraudRiskModel \
    --version 1.3.0 --store .ubunye/model_store
# → "lineage_run_id": "abc123..."

ubunye lineage show -d pipelines -u fraud -p ml -t train --run-id abc123...

This lets you trace exactly which data, config hash, and code produced each model version.

docs.title: The run record names the model (0.9)
docs.text:
The link also goes the other way. When a ModelTransform trains or scores, the run record gets a model_runs entry:

  • train: the model, the version registered, the stage it reached (or development), and the gate result: passed, blocked with the gate, metric, value and threshold that blocked it, no gates, or none when no promotion was asked.
  • predict: the model, the version and the stage it was loaded from.
ubunye lineage trace -d pipelines -u fraud -p ml -t train
#   MODELS
#     train FraudRiskModel 1.3.0 -> staging (gates passed)

ubunye lineage show prints the same entries as JSON. Why it works this way: ADR 012.

docs.title: Registry settings for a model transform
docs.text:
Key Default What it does on_blocked raise A promotion the gates block fails the run. record keeps the run going; the version stays in development and the record says which gate blocked it. stamp_columns false Predict: add model_version and model_stage columns to the scored rows (pandas and Spark). Refuses to overwrite a column of that name. check_features not set Predict: compare the frame with the version's declared features. Not set: warn, record, and call the model. true: refuse the frame with FeatureContractError. false: no check. 
transform:
  params:
    action: predict
    model_class: model.FraudRiskModel
    registry:
      store: .ubunye/model_store
      use_case: fraud_detection
      use_stage: production
      stamp_columns: true
      check_features: true

ubunye run always runs the task's transformations.py (see the box at the top of this page), so call the transform from it:

from ubunye.core.interfaces import Task
from ubunye.plugins.transforms.model_transform import ModelTransform


class Score(Task):
    def transform(self, sources):
        params = self.config["CONFIG"]["transform"]["params"]
        return {"scored": ModelTransform().apply(sources, params, None)["predictions"]}

docs.title: Pattern: Drift Detection
docs.text:
For anyone who trains a model with Ubunye and wants to stop a model going live when today's data no longer looks like the data it learned from.

  • The problem: the data a model sees changes over time, and its predictions get worse without any error. You only find out when someone complains.
  • When to use it: you score or retrain a model on a schedule, and you want a number that says "the inputs have moved", plus a gate that blocks promotion when they have.
  • The one command: ubunye run -d pipelines -u fraud -p drift -t psi -dt 2026-11-02 --lineage

The whole guide runs on your laptop on the pandas backend with small sample data. Every output below is real.

docs.title: What is drift?
docs.text:
Type What changed Data drift The values of the input features moved since training (amounts got bigger, say) Concept drift The link between the features and the answer changed Prediction drift The model's outputs moved

This guide measures data drift with PSI (Population Stability Index): one number per feature that compares how the values spread out in the training set with how they spread out now. A common reading:

PSI Meaning below 0.1 no real change 0.1 to 0.2 some change, keep an eye on it 0.2 or more big change: this guide calls it FAIL

docs.title: The project
docs.text:
project/
├── lake/fraud/                    # data: on a real lake, your Delta tables
│   ├── training_set.parquet       # the rows the model learned from
│   └── features.parquet           # the feature table: same columns, new rows
└── pipelines/                     # the pipelines folder (-d)
    └── fraud/                     # use case
        ├── drift/psi/             # task 1: measure drift, keep the history
        │   ├── config.yaml
        │   └── transformations.py
        └── ml/train/              # task 2: train, and promote only if drift passed
            ├── config.yaml
            ├── model.py
            └── transformations.py
Make the sample data (make_data.py)

Run this once from project/. The feature table's last week has bigger amounts than the training set, so it drifts.

# Small sample data: a training set and a feature table with two weeks of rows.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)


def rows(n, amount_mean, start, days):
    amount = rng.gamma(2.0, amount_mean / 2.0, n)
    count = rng.poisson(6, n) + 1
    risk = rng.integers(0, 3, n)
    fraud = ((amount > amount_mean * 1.5) & (risk >= 1)) | (rng.random(n) < 0.01)
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "event_date": (pd.Timestamp(start) + pd.to_timedelta(rng.integers(0, days, n), unit="D")).strftime("%Y-%m-%d"),
        "amount_sum_30d": amount.round(2),
        "txn_count_30d": count,
        "avg_amount_30d": (amount / count).round(2),
        "risk_encoded": risk,
        "is_fraud": fraud.astype(int),
    })


rows(800, 500, "2026-09-01", 30).to_parquet("lake/fraud/training_set.parquet", index=False)
# Last week the amounts jumped: the feature table drifts from the training set.
features = pd.concat([rows(200, 500, "2026-10-20", 7), rows(200, 900, "2026-10-27", 7)])
features.to_parquet("lake/fraud/features.parquet", index=False)

docs.title: Step 1: Measure drift
docs.text:
The task compares the training set (reference) with the last 7 days of the feature table (current). Both hold the same feature columns, so PSI compares like with like. Each run adds its rows, stamped with run_date, so you keep a history.

# pipelines/fraud/drift/psi/config.yaml
MODEL: etl
VERSION: "1.0.0"

CONFIG:
  inputs:
    reference:              # the rows the model was trained on
      format: s3
      path: lake/fraud/training_set.parquet
      file_format: parquet
    current:                # the feature table: same columns, newer rows
      format: s3
      path: lake/fraud/features.parquet
      file_format: parquet

  transform:
    params:
      run_date: "{{ dt }}"
      window_days: 7

  outputs:
    drift_metrics:          # one row per feature per run, kept as history
      format: s3
      path: lake/fraud/drift_metrics
      file_format: parquet
      mode: append
    drift_alerts:           # only the features that failed
      format: s3
      path: lake/fraud/drift_alerts
      file_format: parquet
      mode: append

{{ dt }} is the date you pass with -dt (see Jinja). The write mode is append, so each run adds to the history instead of replacing it.

# pipelines/fraud/drift/psi/transformations.py
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from ubunye.core.interfaces import Task

FEATURES = ["amount_sum_30d", "txn_count_30d", "avg_amount_30d"]
N_BINS = 10
PSI_LIMIT = 0.2


class DriftTask(Task):
    def transform(self, sources: dict) -> dict:
        params = self.config["CONFIG"]["transform"]["params"]
        run_date = pd.Timestamp(params["run_date"])
        since = run_date - pd.Timedelta(days=params["window_days"])

        ref = sources["reference"]
        cur = sources["current"]
        dates = pd.to_datetime(cur["event_date"])
        cur = cur[(dates > since) & (dates <= run_date)]

        rows = []
        for col in FEATURES:
            psi = _psi(ref[col], cur[col])
            rows.append({
                "run_date": run_date.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"),
                "feature": col,
                "psi": round(psi, 4),
                "status": "PASS" if psi < PSI_LIMIT else "FAIL",
            })
        metrics = pd.DataFrame(rows)
        return {
            "drift_metrics": metrics,
            "drift_alerts": metrics[metrics["status"] == "FAIL"],
        }


def _psi(ref: pd.Series, cur: pd.Series) -> float:
    """Population Stability Index of one numeric column."""
    edges = np.unique(np.quantile(ref, np.linspace(0, 1, N_BINS + 1)))
    edges[0], edges[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf
    r = np.histogram(ref, edges)[0] / len(ref)
    c = np.histogram(cur, edges)[0] / len(cur)
    r, c = np.clip(r, 1e-6, None), np.clip(c, 1e-6, None)
    return float(np.sum((c - r) * np.log(c / r)))

Check it, then run it for two weeks:

ubunye plan -d pipelines -u fraud -p drift -t psi --backend pandas -dt 2026-10-26
ubunye run  -d pipelines -u fraud -p drift -t psi --backend pandas -dt 2026-10-26 --lineage
ubunye run  -d pipelines -u fraud -p drift -t psi --backend pandas -dt 2026-11-02 --lineage

What success looks like:
